1.title: Coaching philosophy, role & scope of practice
1.key_concept: A coaching philosophy is the written set of values, priorities and non-negotiables that makes your decisions predictable under pressure — it decides what you do when the athlete is tired, injured, or ahead of plan. Athlete-centred coaching means the athlete's goals, context and autonomy drive programming; the coach supplies structure, expertise and honest feedback, not ego. Scope of practice defines the boundary: train, condition, coach technique, educate on general recovery and fuelling — do not diagnose, rehabilitate, prescribe individualised diets, or treat psychological conditions (exact legal limits vary by country, so check your own jurisdiction and certification). Duty of care obliges screening, safe environments, informed consent, confidentiality and timely referral. Trust is built over time through competence, consistency, clear rationale and visible care for the athlete as a person.
key_facts: Philosophy = values → priorities → decision rules; written down, or it tends to collapse under race-week pressure.
Athlete-centred ≠ athlete-led: athlete owns the goal, coach owns the method and the veto on unsafe work.
In scope: training design, technique coaching, load management, general nutrition/hydration and sleep education, monitoring, motivation.
Out of scope: diagnosing injury/illness, rehab prescription, individualised medical nutrition therapy, supplement/drug advice, psychological therapy.

Refer out on: red-flag pain, pain unresolved after roughly 2–3 weeks (a practical rule of thumb, not a legal threshold), neurological symptoms, chest pain/syncope, signs of REDs or disordered eating, mental-health distress, uncontrolled chronic disease. Pregnancy is not automatic exclusion — it calls for medical clearance and programme modification.
Refer, don't abandon → keep coaching what is safe and pain-free (e.g. SkiErg/row and upper-body work while a lower-limb issue is managed by a physio).

Duty of care essentials: pre-participation screening (PAR-Q+ or equivalent — a screening tool, not medical clearance), informed consent, competent supervision, safe equipment and sled surface, emergency action plan, insurance, current CPR/first-aid.
Confidentiality: athlete data (health, times, body composition) is disclosed only with consent — coaching a Doubles pair does not license sharing one partner's medical information with the other.

A practical trust checklist (a working heuristic, not a formal published model): competence, consistency, clarity of rationale, and care. Broken promises and unexplained programme changes are among the fastest ways to lose buy-in.

Professional boundaries: avoid dual relationships and blurred coach/friend/partner roles; document decisions and sessions. Ego test: if you cannot explain WHY a session exists in one sentence the athlete understands, the session is probably yours, not theirs.
1.training_link: Write your philosophy in one page and hand it to every new HYROX athlete at intake — it pre-answers why you will cap their compromised-run volume or pull them from a sled session. When an athlete reports groin pain during sandbag lunges, your job is to stop the movement, document it, refer to a physio, and keep them training whatever is genuinely pain-free — SkiErg, row, upper-body strength — while the diagnosis happens. Never fill the gap with your own diagnosis; fill it with safe training and a clear, physio-agreed return criterion.

glossary.def: The explicit set of values and priorities a coach uses to make consistent decisions about training, risk and communication.

1.exam_focus: Recognising the scope-of-practice boundary in a coaching scenario — what you may handle yourself versus what triggers referral, and how duty of care and confidentiality apply while you keep the athlete training safely.

2.title: Communication, cueing & feedback
2.key_concept: Coaching language is a motor-learning intervention, not decoration. Attentional-focus research indicates that external cues — aimed at the movement's effect on an implement, the floor or the environment — tend to beat internal cues about body parts on retention, transfer, movement economy and force output. The constrained-action hypothesis is the leading explanation: an internal focus makes the athlete consciously police a system that runs better automatically. Feedback divides into knowledge of results (the outcome) and knowledge of performance (how it was produced). Both help early; constant feedback can breed dependency, so fade it as skill consolidates. Deliver it briefly, and autonomy-supportively — choice + rationale + the athlete's perspective — rather than controlling.
key_facts: External focus (effect on implement/environment) generally outperforms internal focus (body part) for retention, transfer, economy and force output; the effect appears across skill levels, though effect sizes vary by task and some studies find no difference.
Constrained-action hypothesis: internal focus imposes conscious control → disrupts automatic self-organising motor processes. It is the dominant explanation, not a proven mechanism.

Within external cues, focus distance can matter: more distal external targets have outperformed near-body external ones in several studies (e.g. "push the far wall away" vs "push the handle") — a smaller and less consistent effect than external-vs-internal.
KR = outcome info (split, reps, distance). KP = process/technique info (kinematics, sequencing).
KR is often intrinsically available in HYROX training (clock, erg monitor) → the coach adds most value with KP.
Guidance hypothesis: high feedback frequency can raise acute practice performance while impairing retention, because the athlete leans on the coach instead of building error detection.
Fading schedules: summary/average feedback, bandwidth feedback (only when error exceeds tolerance), faded frequency (e.g. ~100% → ~50% → ~25% across a block), self-controlled (athlete requests it).

Concision is a practical coaching heuristic rather than a research-derived constant: roughly one cue per set, a handful of words, one focus at a time — long instruction adds cognitive load, and information processing degrades under fatigue.
Autonomy-supportive language (meaningful choice, rationale, "you can…") is associated with higher intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy and learning than controlling language ("you must…").

OPTIMAL theory (Wulf & Lewthwaite) combines enhanced expectancies, autonomy support and external focus; the external-focus limb has the strongest support, while several enhanced-expectancies findings have failed to replicate.
Cue individuality: a cue is a means, not truth — keep whichever wording produces the target movement, discard the rest.

Under high fatigue (late-race stations) fall back to ONE pre-agreed anchor cue the athlete can self-deliver; in a HYROX race the coach is not alongside, so cues must already be rehearsed as self-talk.
2.training_link: Build each athlete a short, personal cue sheet — one external cue per station ("push the far wall away" on the sled push, "stamp the floor" on burpee broad jumps, "drive the handles past the hips" on the SkiErg) — and rehearse those exact words in training so the athlete can self-deliver them on race day, since you will not be beside them for the 8 x 1 km and the eight stations. In sessions, let the monitor supply KR and spend your voice on KP, then fade: cue every set early in a block, roughly every second set mid-block, then only when the fault exceeds your bandwidth. Offer choices where they are real (sled grip, lunge breathing pattern, wall-ball set structure) and explain the why.

glossary.def: Attention directed at the intended effect of a movement outside the body — the sled, the ball, the floor, the rope. Thought to preserve automaticity.

glossary.def: Attention directed at one's own body segments or muscle actions. Useful for isolating a fault or a rehab pattern, but usually less effective for performance output.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Feedback about the outcome of the attempt — time, distance, reps, whether the standard was met.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Feedback about how the movement was executed — positions, sequencing, tempo, rhythm — independent of whether the outcome was hit.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The proposal that frequent augmented feedback acts as a crutch: it boosts practice performance but blocks the athlete's own error-detection, hurting retention.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Feedback given only when performance drifts outside a preset error tolerance; silence itself signals "that was acceptable".
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="7" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 14h28M34 20h22M34 26h16" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A schedule that systematically reduces feedback frequency across a block as competence rises.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="7" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 14h28M34 20h22M34 26h16" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The athlete decides when to ask for feedback; the control itself appears to support learning and motivation.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="7" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 14h28M34 20h22M34 26h16" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Communication that offers meaningful choice, explains rationale, and acknowledges the athlete's perspective, in place of directives and pressure.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="7" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 14h28M34 20h22M34 26h16" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The demand a cue or instruction places on limited working memory; effective capacity falls with fatigue and arousal, so cue length must fall as the race progresses.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

2.exam_focus: Expect to be asked to classify or rewrite a cue as external vs internal, and to select an appropriate feedback type (KR vs KP) and fading schedule for an athlete's stage of learning.

3.title: Motivation, adherence & behaviour change
3.key_concept: For most amateur HYROX athletes, adherence limits results at least as much as programme design — a good plan half-completed loses to a modest plan completed. Self-determination theory frames motivation on a continuum from amotivation → external regulation → introjected → identified → integrated → intrinsic, with quality of motivation shaped by three basic needs: autonomy (choice and ownership), competence (visible mastery), relatedness (belonging). Support those and regulation tends to internalise → sessions get done unsupervised. Undermine them (controlling language, arbitrary loads, constant outcome comparison) and motivation is more likely to collapse when the coach isn't present. Goal setting converts motivation into behaviour: outcome goals give direction but sit outside athlete control; performance and process goals are controllable and self-reinforcing. Habits — cue → routine → reward, stable context, low friction — carry training through low-motivation weeks better than willpower alone.
key_facts: SDT basic needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness → satisfy all three for durable adherence.
Motivation continuum: amotivation → external → introjected → identified → integrated → intrinsic; more internalised regulation is generally associated with better persistence.
Extrinsic rewards (prizes, leaderboards) can crowd out intrinsic interest when experienced as controlling; the same reward given as informational feedback on competence tends not to.

Three goal types, not a ranking — use all three: outcome (finish top 10 — uncontrollable, gives direction), performance (sub-1:20 — self-referenced standard), process (wall ball break scheme and breathing pattern — fully controllable day to day).
SMART: specific, measurable, achievable/agreed, relevant, time-bound; set short-, mid- and long-term goals together so each feeds the next.

Habit loop = cue → routine → reward (a practical coaching model, not a lab construct); stable time/place plus an implementation intention ("if X then Y") improves follow-through compared with intention alone.
Bandura's self-efficacy sources, generally ordered strongest first: mastery experience > vicarious (peer modelling) > verbal persuasion > interpretation of physiological/emotional states.
Adherence red flags: session-completion % drifting down, silent logging gaps, repeatedly skipping the disliked station, sessions quietly shortened rather than missed outright.
Recreational athlete → autonomy, enjoyment, flexible weekly minimums; competitive athlete → precise KPIs, block structure, tighter compliance.
Frequent low-stakes wins (station PBs, roxzone splits) generally maintain competence better than a single distant race goal.
Motivational interviewing basics: open questions, reflective listening, roll with resistance, elicit the athlete's own change talk.
Behaviour change usually holds better with 1–2 targeted habits at a time than with a full lifestyle overhaul.
3.training_link: Give every athlete one controllable process goal per station block — e.g. "first 50 wall balls unbroken, then sets of 25 with a 5-breath reset" — and review it against the log weekly, not against the race date. When a recreational client's adherence dips, expand autonomy before adding volume: let them choose the run day or swap the sled push session for a carry medley, keeping the weekly minimum intact. For your competitive athletes, protect competence by scheduling a testable win (1000 m SkiErg PB, roxzone transition drill, sandbag lunge split) every 3–4 weeks so hard blocks still deliver visible mastery.

glossary.def: Framework holding that motivation quality depends on satisfying autonomy, competence and relatedness. The better these needs are met, the more the athlete trains for internal reasons.

glossary.def: Doing the training because the activity itself is satisfying — enjoyment, curiosity, mastery — rather than for an external payoff.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: Extrinsic motivation the athlete has personally endorsed: the work isn't fun but they value the result, so it holds up well over a training block.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A goal defined by executable actions under the athlete's direct control (pacing, split strategy, technique cue), independent of race outcome.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: The athlete's belief they can execute a specific task at a specific standard. Task-specific rather than a general trait, and built mainly by successful attempts.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A pre-committed if–then plan linking a concrete cue to the intended behaviour, which reduces reliance on in-the-moment willpower.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The proportion of prescribed training an athlete actually completes as intended — the practical ceiling on any programme's effect.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Absence of intent to act, usually from perceived incompetence, an unattainable goal, or seeing no link between effort and outcome.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: A collaborative conversational style that draws the athlete's own reasons for change out of them instead of the coach supplying arguments.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

3.exam_focus: Expect to be given an athlete scenario and asked to identify the SDT need being undermined and rewrite an outcome goal as controllable process/performance goals that improve adherence.

4.title: Recovery physiology & sleep
4.page_refs: Sports Medicine: Optimizing Health, Recovery & Performance
4.key_concept: Recovery is not one process but four running on different clocks: substrate (muscle glycogen, hours→24 h), fluid and electrolytes (hours), tissue repair of myofibrils and connective tissue (1–3+ days), and central/autonomic restoration of drive, mood and motor control (hours→weeks). Training supplies the stimulus; recovery converts it into adaptation — so the coach programmes the dose AND the restoration. Sleep is the highest-leverage modality: slow-wave sleep carries the largest nocturnal growth-hormone pulse and supports immune function and physical restoration, while REM consolidates motor skill and regulates mood. Chronic restriction is associated with higher injury and illness risk, higher RPE at a fixed workload, and slower reaction time. Passive modalities (CWI, compression, massage) are secondary, largely perceptual, and CWI used habitually can blunt strength/hypertrophy adaptation.
key_facts: Substrate: muscle glycogen resynthesis runs ≈5%/h with adequate CHO (up to ~7%/h with aggressive early feeding); full restoration ~20–24 h. Fast turnaround (<8 h) → 1.0–1.2 g/kg/h CHO for the first ~4 h. Tissue: protein ~1.6–2.2 g/kg/day in ~0.3–0.4 g/kg doses — daily total matters far more than the narrow 'anabolic window'.
Rehydration: replace ~125–150% of the fluid deficit WITH sodium — plain water alone drops plasma osmolality, drives diuresis, and leaves restoration incomplete.

Sleep architecture: ~90 min cycles, 4–6/night. SWS is front-loaded (largest GH pulse, immune and physical restoration); REM is back-loaded (motor consolidation, mood) — so cutting the last 2 h of sleep removes disproportionately more REM.

Athlete target ~7–9 h/night, with many practitioners pushing 8–10 h in heavy blocks. In the adolescent-athlete literature, sleeping <8 h/night was associated with roughly 1.7× the odds of injury — an association, not a demonstrated cause.

Sleep extension (raising time-in-bed toward ~10 h for several weeks) has improved sprint times, reaction time, shooting accuracy and mood in trained athletes — the best-evidenced recovery intervention available.
Naps: 20–30 min avoids sleep inertia; ~90 min completes a full cycle. Keep naps to the early afternoon, several hours before bedtime, so overnight sleep pressure stays intact.
CWI ~11–15 °C for ~10–15 min reduces soreness and perceived fatigue; genuinely useful in congested competition and multi-day settings where the goal is next-day performance.

CWI used regularly AFTER resistance work blunts hypertrophy/strength adaptation (attenuated mTOR-pathway and satellite-cell signalling) → avoid it in strength-building blocks; endurance adaptation appears less affected, though the evidence there is mixed.
Compression and massage: fairly consistent reductions in perceived soreness, small and inconsistent effects on objective force restoration — low-cost, low-risk, not a substitute for sleep or fuel.
Active recovery clears blood lactate faster, but lactate clearance ≠ recovery of force or glycogen; its real value is blood flow, mobility and psychological reset.
4.training_link: In a HYROX build, treat sleep as programmed work: audit your athlete's actual time-in-bed before you add a single interval session, and in a peak block push toward 8–10 h plus a 20–30 min early-afternoon nap on double days. Save cold water immersion for congested weeks and race-week turnarounds — do not let them ice down after the sled and lunge strength work that is meant to build the qualities those stations demand. After a full simulation, prioritise the things that actually restore: if the next hard session falls inside ~8 h, feed 1.0–1.2 g/kg/h carbohydrate for four hours; otherwise a normal high-CHO meal pattern across the day is enough. Replace ~125–150% of body-mass loss with sodium-containing fluid, then programme an easy aerobic shakeout the next morning rather than a massage table.

glossary.def: The deepest non-REM stage, concentrated in the first half of the night. Associated with the largest growth-hormone pulse, immune function and physical restoration.

glossary.def: Rapid-eye-movement sleep, concentrated in the later cycles. Supports motor-skill consolidation, learning and emotional regulation.
