glossary.def: Transient grogginess and impaired reaction time on waking from deep sleep. Why naps are kept to 20–30 min or extended to a full ~90 min cycle.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Deliberately increasing habitual time in bed above normal for a training or competition block, as an active intervention rather than simply avoiding deprivation.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Submersion in roughly 11–15 °C water for ~10–15 min post-exercise to reduce perceived soreness and thermal load; may suppress the inflammatory signalling that drives strength adaptation.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: When a recovery intervention suppresses the very stress signal the training was meant to create, reducing the long-term training effect despite the athlete feeling better acutely.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Low-intensity aerobic work (typically well below threshold) after or between hard efforts, used to promote blood flow and clearance without adding meaningful training stress.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A short-term performance dip from deliberately heavy loading that supercompensates into a gain once recovery is applied. Becomes non-functional overreaching or overtraining if restoration never arrives.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

4.exam_focus: Expect to be tested on matching a recovery modality to the training goal — specifically recognising that cold water immersion aids short-turnaround performance restoration but blunts strength/hypertrophy adaptation, while sleep is the highest-evidence intervention.

5.title: Monitoring load & readiness
5.page_refs: Sports Medicine: Optimizing Health, Recovery & Performance
5.key_concept: Monitoring closes the loop between what you prescribe (external load: km run, sled metres, reps, kg, watts) and what the athlete actually absorbs (internal load: HR-derived load, RPE, perceived strain). The same session lands differently depending on sleep, heat, fuelling and life stress, so the relationship between external and internal load — not either number alone — signals adaptation or drift. Session-RPE (RPE × duration) gives a cheap universal load unit; weekly sums, monotony and strain describe distribution. Acute:chronic ratios, HRV and resting-HR trends, and short wellness questionnaires are convergent but noisy indicators, and the evidence behind most of their published cut-offs is weaker than their popularity suggests. None diagnoses anything alone. Coaching value comes from consistent daily collection, individual baselines, trend-reading over single points, and a pre-agreed rule for what a red flag triggers.
key_facts: External load = work done (km, sled m, reps, kg, watts). Internal load = the athlete's response (HR, sRPE, perception). Prescribe external, adapt from internal.
sRPE = RPE (0–10 CR10) × session duration in min → arbitrary units (AU). Collect roughly 30 min post-session (at minimum ~10–15 min) so the last hard interval doesn't dominate the rating.

Weekly load = Σ daily sRPE. Monotony = weekly mean daily load ÷ SD of daily loads; Strain = weekly load × monotony. Typical monotony sits near 1–2; values above ~2 are the usual flag. High load combined with high monotony (everything the same, no easy days) is the pattern Foster's early observational work linked to illness and stagnation — a useful planning heuristic, not a validated predictive threshold.

ACWR = acute (≈7 d) ÷ chronic (≈28 d) load. The 0.8–1.3 'sweet spot' / >1.5 'danger zone' thresholds are NOT validated — mathematical coupling (acute load sits inside chronic load), small samples and arbitrary binning undermine them. Use ACWR directionally, never as a gate.

HRV: log vagally-mediated indices (RMSSD or lnRMSSD) under standardised conditions — same time daily, ideally on waking, same posture (supine or seated), same breathing approach, same device and app, before caffeine or training. Judge against the athlete's own rolling 7-day mean ± SD; absolute values are close to meaningless between people.

Meaningful signal = 7-day rolling mean drifting outside the athlete's normal range, or a suppressed rolling mean with rising rolling SD (instability). One low morning after a hard session or a late night is expected, not alarming.

Resting HR: an increase of roughly 5–10 bpm above baseline sustained across several days, especially alongside ↓ HRV and ↓ wellness, points to illness, dehydration, heat strain or non-functional overreaching. Treat it as a prompt to investigate, not a diagnosis.

Wellness questionnaire (5 items, 1–5: sleep quality, fatigue, muscle soreness, stress, mood) takes <60 s. Review evidence suggests simple subjective measures often track accumulated load at least as sensitively as objective device metrics. Compliance beats sophistication.

Objective performance checks are the arbiter: submaximal HR at a fixed run pace (↑ HR at the same speed, or ↓ output at the same HR = drift), HR recovery over 60 s, CMJ height, grip strength, morning body mass (an acute drop >2% suggests dehydration, though food and glycogen shifts confound it).

Red-flag response ladder: (1) verify — is it real, is it multi-day, is it corroborated by a second measure? (2) fix the cheap causes — sleep, fuel, hydration, life stress. (3) modify — cut intensity first, then volume; keep easy movement, drop the hard station or interval work. (4) refer if fever, chest symptoms, injury pain, disordered eating or a persistent mood change appears. Never use the data punitively — athletes stop reporting honestly.
5.training_link: Set your HYROX athlete up with a 60-second daily entry — sleep, fatigue, soreness, stress, mood, resting HR — plus sRPE logged within about 30 minutes of every session, and treat the 7-day rolling means as your dashboard rather than any single morning. When wellness drops for two or three straight days alongside a suppressed HRV trend, cut intensity before volume: keep the easy aerobic running, but drop the compromised-run intervals and the heavy sled and sandbag-lunge work, since heavy pushing/pulling and eccentric-loaded lunges drive the soreness that wrecks the following week. Corroborate with something objective — HR at a fixed 5:30/km, or wall-ball rep-cadence decay — so you are steering by performance drift rather than a wearable's colour.

glossary.def: The objectively measured work prescribed or completed — running distance and pace, sled metres, reps, load lifted, power output. Independent of the athlete's internal state.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The physiological and psychological cost of that work to this athlete on this day — heart-rate-based load, session-RPE, perceived strain.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A whole-session load unit: the athlete's 0–10 effort rating multiplied by session duration in minutes, expressed in arbitrary units.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Weekly mean daily load divided by the standard deviation of daily loads. High values mean every day looks the same — no real hard/easy contrast. Typically ~1–2 in a well-varied week.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Weekly load multiplied by monotony — a single number combining how much work was done with how undifferentiated it was.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Recent load (roughly the last week) divided by accumulated load (roughly the last month). A rough index of whether current work exceeds prepared capacity; its published cut-offs are not reliable.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The natural log of RMSSD, a vagally-mediated HRV index. Logging compresses the skewed raw scale, improving day-to-day sensitivity against a personal baseline.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The minimum shift in a monitored variable that exceeds normal day-to-day noise for that individual, so it is worth acting on rather than ignoring.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Functional overreaching: a short-term performance dip that rebounds to or above baseline within days to about two weeks of unloading. Non-functional: the dip persists for weeks to months with mood, sleep and HR disturbance. The two are separated retrospectively by how long recovery takes — you cannot reliably tell them apart in the moment.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Rising heart rate at a fixed running pace (or falling pace at fixed heart rate) across a session or across weeks — a marker of accumulated fatigue, heat strain or lost aerobic durability.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

5.exam_focus: Expect to be tested on computing session-RPE, weekly load, monotony and strain; on interpreting an ACWR or HRV/resting-HR trend against its known evidential limitations; and on describing the concrete decision ladder a coach follows when a multi-day red flag appears.

6.title: Overreaching, overtraining & fatigue management
6.page_refs: Sports Medicine: Optimizing Health, Recovery & Performance
6.key_concept: Training stress sits on a continuum whose stages can only be named retrospectively, by how long performance stays suppressed. Acute fatigue clears in hours-days. Functional overreaching (FOR) is a deliberate overload block: performance dips, then rebounds above baseline within roughly days to ~2 weeks of reduced load. Non-functional overreaching (NFOR) is the same dip without the rebound - weeks to months to recover, no performance gain. Overtraining syndrome (OTS) is a diagnosis of exclusion: months or longer of unexplained underperformance plus mood, sleep, endocrine and immune disruption, with medical causes (iron deficiency, thyroid dysfunction, RED-S/low energy availability, infection, depression) ruled out first. Recovery timeline is the practical discriminator - severity of symptoms on any given day is not - and because the label only arrives after the fact, prevention beats diagnosis.
key_facts: Continuum: acute fatigue → FOR (rebounds above baseline) → NFOR (no rebound) → OTS (chronic, requires medical exclusion).
Timelines: FOR days–~2 wk; NFOR weeks–months; OTS months or longer. Labels are retrospective only.
OTS = diagnosis of exclusion → rule out iron/ferritin deficiency, thyroid dysfunction, RED-S/LEA, EBV or other infection, depression, sleep apnoea.
Underfuelling (low energy availability) is a very common driver of presentations labelled 'overtraining', and is often the first thing to check.

Best functional marker = a repeatable standardised test. At FIXED SUBMAXIMAL pace/power, look for rising HR-cost and/or rising RPE. At MAXIMAL effort, look for the opposite: blunted HRmax and reduced peak output.
Suppressed HRmax plus suppressed peak blood lactate at genuinely all-out effort is the classic overreached signature (an inability to drive maximal work, not improved lactate clearance).
Monitor 7-day rolling HRV/RHR (never single days) plus sleep, body mass, mood and session-RPE load; mood and perceived effort often shift before measurable performance does.

How training load is DISTRIBUTED matters, not just its total: sharp week-to-week spikes and high monotony (little easy-hard variation within the week) are associated with breakdown. Note that acute:chronic workload ratio methods are popular but methodologically contested - treat them as a prompt to look closer, not a verdict.

Concurrent risk in HYROX: heavy eccentric exposure comes mainly from sandbag lunges and burpee broad jump landings (plus running volume). Sled push and sled pull are largely CONCENTRIC and cause little muscle damage - they tax metabolic and neuromuscular capacity instead. Residual muscle damage degrades running economy and can masquerade as lost aerobic fitness.

Prevention (practical heuristics, not hard rules): 3:1 or 2:1 load-to-deload week cycling, at least one true rest day, a hard-easy split rather than uniformly moderate work, and energy plus protein intake matched to load.

Using FOR on purpose: a ~2-3 wk overload block, accepting a dip, then a taper of roughly 10-14 days that cuts volume substantially while retaining intensity - then confirm the rebound on a benchmark before racing.
Treatment: NFOR → 1-3 wk load reduction (relative rest, not zero); OTS → months of medically supervised graded return.
6.training_link: Build a fixed benchmark you can repeat every 3-4 weeks - e.g. 4 x 500 m row at a set pace, or a 2 km run at a set submaximal pace - and track HR and RPE at that fixed output rather than chasing PBs. If HR-cost or RPE climbs at unchanged pace while mood and sleep dip, cut load 30-50% for a week before you start rewriting the programme. In a concurrent HYROX build, keep the genuinely eccentric-heavy work (sandbag lunges, burpee broad jump landings) away from key run sessions so residual soreness does not corrupt your run paces; sled push and pull are concentric-dominant and cause less damage, but they still carry a real metabolic and neuromuscular cost, so schedule them on effort grounds rather than soreness grounds. Whenever a deload fails to restore output, check fuelling and energy availability before assuming the programme is the problem.

glossary.def: Short-term planned overload causing temporary performance decline that rebounds above baseline after reduced load of days to about two weeks.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Accumulated overload where performance stays depressed for weeks to months and no rebound follows; a stalled overload, not yet a syndrome.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Long-term maladaptation with unexplained underperformance lasting months or longer plus systemic symptoms, diagnosed only after medical and nutritional causes are excluded.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The rebound above prior baseline that occurs when recovery follows an overload dose large enough to disturb, but not to exceed, adaptive capacity.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Low day-to-day variation in training load WITHIN a week, calculated as mean daily load divided by the standard deviation of daily load. High monotony combined with high load raises strain even when the weekly total looks unremarkable.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Session RPE (0-10) multiplied by session duration in minutes, giving an internal load in arbitrary units (AU) that can be summed and compared across running, erg and strength work.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Energy intake minus exercise energy expenditure, expressed relative to fat-free mass, falling too low to support normal physiological function; the nutritional root of many OTS-like presentations.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M14 12v18M14 12h12" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M30 30c8-2 16-10 30-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: A label applied only after other plausible explanations have been tested and ruled out, which is why OTS cannot be assigned from performance data alone.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A planned period of reduced training volume, usually with some intensity retained, that lets accumulated fatigue dissipate so adaptation can surface.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Muscle lengthening under tension (lunge descent, landing from a broad jump). It is the main driver of exercise-induced muscle damage and delayed soreness, unlike concentric-dominant work such as sled pushing.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

6.exam_focus: Distinguishing FOR, NFOR and OTS by recovery timeline and whether performance rebounds - and knowing that OTS is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring medical referral rather than a coaching call.

7.title: Common HYROX injuries & risk factors
7.page_refs: Sports Medicine: Optimizing Health, Recovery & Performance
7.key_concept: HYROX injuries are predominantly overuse rather than traumatic: repetitive high-volume running interleaved with loaded pushing, pulling, carrying and hinging under deep fatigue. Four regions dominate the presentations coaches actually see — Achilles/calf, knee (patellofemoral, ITB), lumbar spine, shoulder. Note up front that formal HYROX injury surveillance is still thin (mostly small retrospective surveys), so reason from mechanism and from general endurance/strength injury literature rather than from sport-specific incidence figures. Mechanism is usually load-tolerance mismatch: tissue capacity rises slowly (tendon, bone) while training load spikes fast. Risk splits into intrinsic (prior injury — the most consistently reported predictor, age, ankle/hip mobility, strength or side-to-side asymmetry, running mechanics, sleep and energy availability) and extrinsic (weekly volume and its rate of change, sled loads and floor friction, footwear, surface, race density, coaching quality). Most cases trace back to a training error a coach could have seen coming.
key_facts: Prior injury to the same site is the most consistently reported predictor of a future injury there; screen history first.

Achilles/calf is a primary concern area on mechanistic grounds: forefoot-dominant sled push, 8 km of fatigued running, and burpee broad jump rebounds all load the plantarflexors repeatedly. Treat this as reasoned exposure, not a measured injury rate.
Sled push 50 m → forefoot-only ground contact with sustained plantarflexion under heavy horizontal load; sled pull 50 m → repeated hinge and row pattern, loading low back, elbow flexors and shoulder.

Burpee broad jump 80 m stacks several mechanisms at once: repeated landings on fatigued legs, lumbar flexion/extension cycling, and loaded chest-to-floor for the anterior shoulder. Mechanism density is a reasonable coaching argument for caution — it is not an established injury ranking.
Sandbag lunges 100 m: front-loaded, deep knee flexion, hip-flexor and patellar tendon load, plus a spinal flexion moment if the bag slides forward.

Farmers carry 200 m: sustained grip and heavy axial load — upper trap and cervicothoracic fatigue, low-back compression, and a lateral-flexion moment if the athlete lists to one side or the loads are uneven.

Wall balls (100 reps, all individual divisions): repeated near-overhead flexion under fatigue can irritate the subacromial region (subacromial pain syndrome); the deep squat volume loads the patellofemoral joint.

SkiErg and row: repeated lumbar flexion when the hinge collapses drives low-back pain and erector fatigue; rowing volume is also associated with low-back and, in high-volume rowers, rib stress problems. Avoid over-precise pathoanatomical labels — 'disc injury' is rarely diagnosable at the gym floor.
Training-error pattern: too rapid a rise in running volume or intensity, back-to-back hard compromised sessions, no deload, sudden sled-load jumps, and racing every 4–6 weeks without a rebuild block.

Bone stress injuries (tibia, metatarsal, femoral neck) should prompt a low-energy-availability screen. RED-S affects athletes of all sexes; ask about fuelling in everyone, and add menstrual history where applicable.

Rule of thumb: keep weekly running-volume change modest — the familiar ≤10%/week figure is a useful teaching convention, though a randomised trial (Buist et al., 2008) found a graded 10%-style progression did not lower running injury rates versus a standard build. Use it as a brake on obvious spikes, not as a validated safety threshold, and change ONE variable at a time (volume, intensity, or load).

For Achilles/patellar tendinopathy, progressive loading beats rest: graded strength work through heavy slow resistance and then energy-storage/plyometric work. Isometrics are commonly used for pain relief, but the evidence for a reliable analgesic effect is mixed.
7.training_link: Screen every new athlete for prior Achilles, knee and low-back history before you write a single compromised-run session — that history dictates how fast you can add running volume and burpee broad jump exposure. Build calf and posterior-chain capacity year-round (heavy slow calf raises, hinge strength) so the sled and the fatigued kilometres land on tissue that can take them, and change only one variable per week — volume, intensity, or sled load. When an athlete reports a niggle, audit the last three weeks of programming first; the training error is nearly always there. Be honest with athletes that these are mechanism-based judgements, not guarantees drawn from HYROX injury statistics.

glossary.def: Tissue breakdown from repeated submaximal loading that exceeds the tissue's adaptation rate, with no single traumatic event. Onset is gradual and usually traceable to a load spike.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M30 8v12l14 14" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="30" cy="20" r="3.5" fill="#e0556b"/></svg>

glossary.def: The gap between the mechanical load applied and the capacity the tissue has actually built. Injury sits at the point where applied load crosses tolerance.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Something inside the athlete that alters injury risk — injury history, age, mobility limits, asymmetry, running mechanics, sleep, energy availability.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Something in the environment or programme — weekly volume, rate of load change, sled friction and load, footwear, surface, competition density, coaching.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Load-related tendon pain and dysfunction with degenerative rather than primarily inflammatory changes. Responds to graded mechanical loading; provoked by abrupt volume or plyometric spikes.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A continuum from bone stress reaction to frank stress fracture, caused by repetitive impact outstripping bone remodelling. Common in tibia and metatarsals; frequently paired with underfuelling.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M30 8v12l14 14" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="30" cy="20" r="3.5" fill="#e0556b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport — impaired physiological function arising from chronic low energy availability, with effects on bone, endocrine, immune and metabolic health. Affects male and female athletes.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Running performed immediately after a loaded station, with altered mechanics from local fatigue. Necessary for HYROX specificity but a concentrated injury exposure.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Recent (roughly one-week) load compared with a rolling several-week average. Popular as a spike-detection prompt, but the method has drawn substantial statistical criticism and should never be treated as a validated injury predictor — a conversation starter, not a verdict.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

7.exam_focus: Matching a specific station's mechanical demand to the tissue it stresses, and correctly separating intrinsic from extrinsic risk factors in a case scenario where a training error caused the overuse injury — while stating risk claims with the confidence the underlying evidence actually supports.

8.title: Return to training & reconditioning
8.page_refs: Sports Medicine: Optimizing Health, Recovery & Performance
8.key_concept: Reconditioning is load management matched to biology, not to the calendar alone. Inflammation (roughly the first 0–5 days) protects — gentle, pain-free movement only. Proliferation (roughly day 3 to 6 weeks) lays down disorganised collagen that responds to progressive tensile load. Remodelling (6 weeks out to 12+ months) aligns fibres and demands near-full, sport-specific stress. Mechanotransduction cuts both ways: underloading delays healing as surely as overloading re-injures. The mature position is criteria PLUS a biological time floor — clear on pain behaviour, symmetry and capacity benchmarks, but never before the tissue has had the minimum time it physically needs. In HYROX the sequence matters: restore tissue capacity → rebuild running volume → layer station work last, since sled, lunge and burpee-jump loads stack high force onto deep fatigue.
key_facts: Healing stages overlap: inflammation ~0–5 d → proliferation ~d3–6 wk → remodelling ~6 wk–12+ mo. All windows are approximate and vary widely by tissue, site, severity and age.
Optimal loading beats rest once the acute phase settles. Prolonged unloading reduces tendon and bone stiffness, collagen alignment and neuromuscular drive.

Criteria-based progression outperforms time-based alone — but time is not irrelevant. Some tissues (bone, ACL graft ligamentisation) have hard biological floors, so the defensible model is 'criteria met AND minimum healing time elapsed'.

Limb Symmetry Index = injured ÷ uninjured × 100. ≥90% is the commonly used minimum gate; it is a convention, not a validated cut-point. Pairing it with pre-injury or normative absolute values is safer, since the uninjured limb detrains too.

Test a battery, not one number: isometric/isokinetic strength, a single-leg hop series, calf-raise endurance (adult norms commonly cited around 20–25 single-leg reps, with wide variability), and re-testing under fatigue.
Widely used pain heuristic (not a validated rule): ≤3/10 during loading, no worse the next morning, settles within 24 h → the load was probably acceptable.

Bone stress injury: high-risk sites (femoral neck, anterior tibial cortex, navicular, talus, medial malleolus, base of 5th metatarsal, sesamoids) need true offloading plus imaging-informed, medically supervised timelines; low-risk sites generally progress faster.

Return to run via walk-run intervals on flat, non-technical ground; progress frequency → duration → intensity, changing one variable at a time. The '10% per week' cap is a practical heuristic with weak direct evidence, not a validated threshold.

Reintroduce stations at reduced load or distance — around 40–60% of race demand is a reasonable practical starting point, not a published standard — unfatigued first, then in a compromised (post-run) state only once the unfatigued work is clean.

There is no published HYROX-specific injury-epidemiology ranking of the stations. On mechanical reasoning, sled push/pull and sandbag lunges plausibly carry the greatest re-introduction risk after lower-limb injury (high force, deep flexion, performed pre-fatigued), with burpee broad jump as the plyometric landing gate.
8.training_link: Give your returning athlete a clearance battery rather than a date: single-leg calf raises toward roughly 25 reps, hop-test LSI at or above the conventional 90% gate (retested after a 10-minute row so you see it under fatigue), and pain that never exceeds 3/10 or lingers past 24 hours — while still respecting any minimum healing time the tissue needs. Rebuild running first on flat ground with walk-run intervals, keeping weekly volume growth modest (the familiar ~10% heuristic is a sensible brake, not a law) and changing only one variable at a time. Bring stations back unfatigued and light — reduced-load sled, shortened lunge distance, step-back burpees — and only combine run plus station once two consecutive clean weeks are logged.

glossary.def: The process by which cells convert mechanical load into biochemical signals that drive tissue remodelling. It is why graded loading, rather than continued rest, becomes the primary healing stimulus once the acute phase settles.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Advancing an athlete when objective thresholds (strength, symmetry, capacity, pain response) are met rather than simply when a set number of weeks has passed. Best applied alongside, not instead of, minimum biological healing times.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The injured limb's performance expressed as a percentage of the uninjured limb on the same test. Widely used, but flattering when the uninjured side has also detrained, so it should be read next to absolute values.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Repeating a clearance test after a fatiguing bout so it reflects the state the athlete actually competes in. Symmetry that collapses under fatigue is not clearance.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: The volume and magnitude of load a structure can absorb before symptoms rise. Reconditioning raises capacity; the training plan is then kept underneath it.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M30 8v12l14 14" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="30" cy="20" r="3.5" fill="#e0556b"/></svg>

glossary.def: A continuum from stress reaction to frank stress fracture, caused by repetitive loading outpacing bone remodelling. Classified high- or low-risk according to site vascularity and loading mechanics.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M30 8v12l14 14" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="30" cy="20" r="3.5" fill="#e0556b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Removing the provocative load while maintaining systemic conditioning through unaffected modalities, so aerobic and strength qualities do not decay during healing.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: In the commonly taught tendon continuum model, a reactive tendon shows a short-term, largely non-inflammatory swelling response to a load spike that settles when load is reduced; a degenerative tendon has long-standing matrix disorganisation. Degenerated tissue itself does not reliably reverse — heavy slow resistance works largely by strengthening the surrounding intact tendon and the muscle-tendon unit.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

8.exam_focus: Expect to be given an injured athlete's test results or timeline and asked to justify progressing, holding or regressing them using criteria (limb symmetry, capacity benchmarks, pain response) alongside — not instead of — the minimum healing time the tissue requires.

9.title: Force, torque, levers & impulse
9.key_concept: Every HYROX station is a force problem. Force changes motion (F = ma); applied off an axis it creates torque (force x perpendicular moment arm), so joint demand depends on limb geometry, not load alone. Human limbs are predominantly third-class levers: mechanical disadvantage traded for endpoint speed and range. Velocity change comes from impulse (F x t = m x delta-v), so both the magnitude and the duration of force application matter — this is what separates a sled start from a broad jump. Ground reaction force is the external force that accelerates the athlete's centre of mass; on sleds, propulsion must exceed friction (Ff = mu x N), and N rises with any downward component of the push. Work = F x d, power = F x v, and gross efficiency = external mechanical work / metabolic energy cost.
key_facts: F = ma; net force -> acceleration. Zero net force = constant velocity (steady sled speed is not zero effort — it means propulsion exactly equals friction).
Torque = F x perpendicular moment arm. Same load, longer moment arm -> higher joint torque (sandbag drifting forward, wall ball held away from the chest).

Lever classes (standard textbook examples): 1st = axis in the middle (atlanto-occipital / head on neck); 2nd = resistance in the middle (plantarflexion at the ankle, MA > 1); 3rd = effort in the middle (elbow flexion, and most human limb arrangements, MA < 1).
Mechanical advantage = effort moment arm / resistance moment arm. Third-class levers sacrifice force for endpoint velocity and range of motion.
Impulse = F x t = change in momentum. It can be increased by applying more force, applying it for longer, or both — the trade-off between the two is task-specific.

Sled start: static friction typically exceeds kinetic friction, so the force requirement is greatest at 0 m; here longer, forceful contacts are useful because the sled is slow and there is time to apply force.
Jumps (e.g. burpee broad jump) are the opposite impulse case: contact time is short and largely fixed, so extra impulse must come mainly from higher force, not longer contact.

GRF has 3 orthogonal components: vertical (support and vertical propulsion), anterior-posterior (braking then push-off), and mediolateral (normally small; a large one usually reflects instability rather than useful propulsion).

Friction Ff = mu x N. For dry sliding friction mu depends on the sled skid and floor surface and is roughly independent of contact area; N = sled weight plus any downward component of the athlete's push.
Directing push force more horizontally reduces the added normal force and therefore the friction; a more upright, downward-directed push increases resistance.

Work = F x d (joules). For a given athlete and technique, sled work over the 50 m push is roughly fixed regardless of pace, because friction force and distance are unchanged. Power = work / time = F x velocity, so pace changes power, not total work.

Gross mechanical efficiency in cyclic whole-body work is roughly 20% (commonly reported in the ~18-25% range depending on task, intensity and measurement method). The remaining ~80% appears as heat, so thermal load accumulates across a race of 8 runs and 8 stations.
9.training_link: Coach the sled start as an impulse problem: have your athlete set a low body angle so the push line is closer to horizontal, drive the hands forward rather than down, and accept a few long, hard first strides instead of scrambling short ones — breaking the sled loose is the expensive part, and once it is moving only kinetic friction has to be beaten. Contrast that with the broad jump, where contact time is short and the only lever left is peak force. On lunges and wall balls, cue the load close to the trunk: a sandbag drifting a few centimetres forward silently raises hip and spinal torque with no change in kilograms. When an athlete says a station 'felt heavier' late in a race, check moment arms, posture and grip position before assuming a strength deficit.

glossary.def: Perpendicular distance from the line of action of a force to the joint axis. It is the multiplier that converts an external load into joint torque.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 30h44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M30 30l0-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="26,34 34,34 30,28" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Force multiplied by the time over which it acts. It equals the change in momentum, so a moderate force applied for longer can produce the same velocity change as a large brief force.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 30h44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M30 30l0-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="26,34 34,34 30,28" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: The equal-and-opposite force the ground applies to the athlete, per Newton's third law. Its vertical, fore-aft and side-to-side components determine support, propulsion and non-propulsive motion.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 30h44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M30 30l0-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="26,34 34,34 30,28" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: A dimensionless ratio describing how strongly two surfaces resist sliding. The static coefficient is usually greater than the kinetic one, which is why a stationary sled is hardest to break loose.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="20" width="22" height="12" rx="2" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".75"/><path d="M36 26h26M56 20l6 6-6 6" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Ratio of effort moment arm to resistance moment arm in a lever. Values above 1 favour force output; values below 1 favour endpoint speed and range of motion.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Rate of doing mechanical work, equal to force times velocity. It distinguishes how fast an athlete completes a fixed amount of work from how much work is done.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: External mechanical work expressed as a fraction of total metabolic energy consumed. It is influenced by movement economy, technique and muscle fibre characteristics, so it should not be read as a single trainable number.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A lever with the effort applied between the axis and the resistance. It is the dominant human arrangement and requires muscle force well above the external load.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 30h44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M30 30l0-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="26,34 34,34 30,28" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

9.exam_focus: Expect to compute or reason about how moment arm, friction and impulse determine the force required at a station — especially calculating sled friction from mu and normal force, applying impulse-momentum to both slow (sled) and fast (jump) contacts, and distinguishing work from power when race times differ.

10.title: Kinetic chain, posture & movement analysis
10.key_concept: The body works as a linked kinetic chain: force generated at one segment is transmitted through adjacent joints, so a deficit anywhere can leak output elsewhere in the chain. The joint-by-joint model is a coaching heuristic (not a validated law) proposing that joints alternate in primary need — foot stable, ankle mobile, knee stable, hip mobile, lumbar spine stable, thoracic spine mobile, scapula stable, glenohumeral mobile — while acknowledging every joint needs some of both. A braced trunk raises intra-abdominal pressure and stiffens the trunk so hips and shoulders can move against a rigid base. Movement analysis is systematic: define the task and its standard, observe from multiple planes across several repetitions, work out which joint is limiting, then prioritise the fault closest to the root cause rather than the loudest symptom. Fatigue reliably re-exposes faults that look resolved in a fresh athlete.
key_facts: Kinetic chain = linked segments; energy transfers proximal→distal in sequenced efforts (throw, jump) and force is received distal→proximal from ground reaction (running, sled push).

Joint-by-joint alternation (heuristic, useful for generating hypotheses rather than proving them): foot stable → ankle mobile → knee stable → hip mobile → lumbar stable → thoracic mobile → scapula stable → GH mobile.

Restriction at a mobile joint is commonly associated with compensatory motion nearby (e.g. limited ankle dorsiflexion → heel rise, forward torso pitch and greater lumbar flexion at the bottom of a lunge or wall ball). Treat this as a hypothesis to test, not a certainty — the link is associative, not proven causal.

Bracing = coordinated 360° co-contraction of diaphragm, transversus abdominis, obliques, multifidus and pelvic floor → ↑intra-abdominal pressure → ↑trunk stiffness. Not hollowing; not sustained breath-holding across long sets.

Valsalva raises IAP the most and does increase trunk stiffness, but it is appropriate only for brief maximal efforts; it also spikes arterial blood pressure and impairs venous return, so it is contraindicated for athletes with uncontrolled hypertension or cardiovascular disease. HYROX stations demand rhythmic bracing with continuous breathing.

IAP increases trunk stiffness and reduces the buckling/shear demand placed on passive spinal structures — but it does not reduce total spinal compression; co-contraction adds compressive load. Stability is bought with stiffness, not with unloading.

Ankle dorsiflexion: ~10 cm on the knee-to-wall (weight-bearing lunge) test is a widely used working minimum; healthy adults commonly fall roughly in the 9–14 cm range and normative data vary by population and method. The ~35–40° figure often quoted is tibial inclination from vertical, which is not the same measure as goniometric ankle dorsiflexion ROM (~10–20°). Below the working minimum, expect heel rise, valgus and torso pitch under load.

Knee valgus has candidate causes above and below the knee: proximally, weak or poorly recruited gluteus medius and hip external rotators; distally, restricted dorsiflexion or foot pronation collapse driving tibial internal rotation. Test both rather than assuming.

Overhead rib flare and lumbar extension usually point to limited thoracic extension and/or shoulder flexion (mobility) or loss of anterior trunk control letting the ribcage tip off the pelvis (stability).

Analysis sequence: task/standard → observe 3–5 reps from ≥2 views (sagittal + frontal) → note the deviation → test whether it is mobility, motor control, strength/stability, or fatigue → prioritise the proximal/root fault.
Fatigue compensations to watch for: ↑trunk flexion, ↓hip extension, knee valgus, ↑lumbar extension overhead, forward head, and on post-station runs ↓stride length with ↑ground contact time.
Fault priority order: pain/safety → spine position → the joint restricting the pattern → cosmetic detail.
One cue at a time; re-test at a comparable rep number and fatigue level to confirm the change is real rather than a fresher-athlete artefact.
10.training_link: Analyse your athlete on the movements the race actually punishes, and do it fatigued. Film the sandbag lunges deep into the 100 m and the wall balls past the halfway mark of the 100 reps, not fresh, because that is when ankle and thoracic restrictions surface as torso pitch, knee valgus and a rising ribcage. If dorsiflexion is the limiter, no amount of 'chest up' cueing fixes the lunge — restore ankle range and re-test the same movement. Coach rhythmic bracing with breath on the 50 m sled push and the 200 m farmers carry (exhale on effort, ribs down); if a short Valsalva is used at all, keep it to the first hard metres of the push, and screen the athlete for blood-pressure or cardiovascular contraindications before coaching it.

glossary.def: The linked series of body segments and joints through which force is produced and transmitted; output is often limited by the weakest or least-controlled link.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 30h44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M30 30l0-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="26,34 34,34 30,28" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: A coaching framework proposing that joints alternate in primary need between mobility and stability up the body, so a fault at one joint may be driven by its neighbour. A hypothesis-generating heuristic, not an established biomechanical law.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Pressure generated inside the abdominal cavity by coordinated diaphragm, abdominal wall and pelvic floor contraction; it stiffens the trunk and reduces the buckling and shear demand on passive spinal tissue, while adding to overall spinal compression.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Deliberate 360° abdominal co-contraction that raises IAP and holds the ribcage over the pelvis, creating a rigid base for limb force output.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Motion borrowed from an adjacent segment when the intended joint cannot supply the required range, strength or control; usually appears first under load or fatigue.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A screen is a standardised battery scored against fixed criteria; an analysis is task-specific observation of the actual competition movement to identify the limiting joint.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M30 8v12l14 14" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="30" cy="20" r="3.5" fill="#e0556b"/></svg>

glossary.def: The joint whose restriction or lack of control forces the rest of the chain to deviate; addressing it often resolves several downstream faults at once.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Alignment where the ribcage stacks over the pelvis so the diaphragm and pelvic floor oppose each other and IAP can be generated efficiently.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Closed chain = distal segment fixed against a surface or meeting substantial resistance (sled push, lunge, run stance); open chain = distal segment free to move through space (leg extension, the release of a wall ball throw). Many real tasks sit on a continuum rather than fitting one label cleanly.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 30h44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M30 30l0-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="26,34 34,34 30,28" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

10.exam_focus: Applying the joint-by-joint model to trace an observed HYROX station fault back to its limiting joint, and prioritising which fault to correct first.

11.title: Sled push & pull mechanics
11.key_concept: Both sleds are friction problems, not just strength problems. Resistance ≈ μ × normal force, so surface, sled mass and the direction of the athlete's force vector decide the cost. On the push, a forward trunk lean with locked arms aligns force horizontally, but any downward component adds to normal force → more friction; steps shorten, frequency rises, contact time lengthens, flight phase disappears — the athlete sits at the high-force/low-velocity end of the force-velocity curve. On the pull, a braced hip hinge and body lean turn bodyweight into the prime mover, a slightly upward rope angle unloads the sled, and continuous rope tension avoids repeatedly re-breaking static friction.
key_facts: Sled push (station 2) and sled pull (station 3) are 50 m each, run as 4 × 12.5 m lengths; loads scale by division and sex (Pro heaviest, Open lighter). Quoted sled loads are the total prescribed weight — check the current rulebook rather than memorising numbers, as they have been revised between seasons.

Resistive force ≈ μ × N. μ is a property of the skid/floor pair, not of the athlete, so the same prescribed kg produces different real resistance on different lanes. Treat any specific μ value as illustrative — it is not published or measured for race venues.

Competition lanes are standardised artificial turf, so venue variation is smaller than gym-to-gym variation. It is still real: turf pile, wear, moisture and skid condition all shift μ, which is why athletes report the 'same' sled feeling different at different events.
Static friction exceeds kinetic friction, so the hardest moment is breaking the sled from rest. Avoid stopping mid-length — a stall costs time and forces a fresh static break.
A downward-angled push vector adds to the normal force and therefore to friction; an upward-angled rope pull subtracts from it. The push can only add effective load, the pull can shed some.

Trunk angle is a trade-off, not a number to hit: flatter improves force-vector alignment but reduces usable hip/knee extension range and raises calf, hip-flexor and lumbar demand, while too upright leaks force vertically. Coaches commonly cue roughly 45°, but this is a heuristic — there is no established optimal angle, and it varies with athlete height, load and handle height.

Contact height matters: HYROX sleds offer high and low handle positions. A lower contact generally lets a shorter or flatter-leaning athlete keep the force vector more horizontal, while a higher contact is easier to brace against and gives more room for leg drive; taller athletes often prefer the high handles. It is an individual fit question best tested under race load.
Arms straight, elbows locked, shoulders packed, ribs down → skeletal force transmission; bent arms turn the triceps and shoulders into a fatiguing isometric link and shorten effective push range.
Under heavy load stride length ↓, stride frequency ↑, ground contact time ↑, flight phase disappears; forefoot/midfoot contact with full ankle-knee-hip triple extension each step.

Heavy sled work sits at the force end of the force-velocity curve — typical race push velocities are well under 1 m/s (a 50 m push taking 60–90 s averages roughly 0.55–0.85 m/s), so force production rather than leg speed is the limiter.

Sled pull: the athlete works from inside a marked box and pulls the sled to the line, then walks back to reset — so the pull is repeated bouts of high tension separated by walking, not one continuous effort. Staggered or wide stance, hip hinge, hips loaded, spine braced, rope drawn toward the hip/belt line, driven by lats, posterior chain and bodyweight lean. Hand-over-hand is the most common technique; grip and forearms are a common early failure point.

Sled push is close to concentric-only, with little eccentric loading, which plausibly explains its low reported soreness cost relative to the force involved and why athletes tolerate it fairly frequently. Sled pull adds grip and back fatigue that carries forward into the farmers carry three stations later.
11.training_link: Rehearse on more than one floor — the same prescribed load can feel very different on gym rubber, carpet or turf, so do not let an athlete's only reference be a fast home surface. Program near-race-load pushes for force quality alongside lighter, faster pushes for stride mechanics, and let the athlete trial both handle heights under load rather than assuming one is correct. Cap pull volume with grip work that respects the farmers carry three stations later. Cue set for the push: body angle → straight arms → short fast steps → never let it stop. For the pull: tension first, then hinge and lean.

glossary.def: The transition area between runs and stations; the cumulative time spent in it is reported separately. Sled overreach shows up here as slow walking and a delayed start to the next run.

11.exam_focus: That resistance is μ × normal force — and therefore that body angle, arm position, handle height and rope angle change how heavy the sled effectively is, independent of the plates on it.

12.title: Farmers carry, sandbag lunge & wall ball mechanics
12.key_concept: Stations 6-8 are a chain of trunk-and-grip limited tasks that arrive on pre-fatigued legs. Farmers carry is an anti-lateral-flexion, anti-rotation gait task: load hangs at the sides, so for most athletes the limiter is forearm flexor endurance plus the ability to keep ribs stacked over pelvis while walking fast. Sandbag lunges add a posterior yoke load that shifts the centre of mass behind and above the trunk, demanding thoracic extension and a controlled knee-to-floor descent. Wall balls close the race as a cyclical front-loaded squat-to-throw: depth and target must both be legal, and rhythm depends on absorbing the catch into the next descent rather than stopping it.
key_facts: Order: Farmers Carry 200 m (station 6) → Sandbag Lunges 100 m (station 7) → Wall Balls (station 8; 100 reps in all individual divisions). Each is preceded by a 1 km run, so all three land on heavily fatigued legs; there is no run after the wall balls.

Open-division loads for context (Pro is heavier): carry ~2×24 kg men / 2×16 kg women, sandbag ~20 kg men / 10 kg women, wall ball ~6 kg to a 3.0 m target men / 4 kg to a 2.7 m target women. Confirm current-season standards before programming — organisers do revise them.

Carry limiter for most athletes = grip endurance (sustained isometric finger flexors, restricted local blood flow) before trunk or leg endurance gives out. Setting the implements down is permitted, but every stop-and-re-grip costs time and rhythm, so plan drops rather than being forced into them.

Carry posture: ribs down, scapulae set, neutral neck. Letting the trunk side-bend or the shoulders sag passively raises metabolic cost and brings grip failure forward. Shorter, quicker steps generally beat long strides.

Breathe with a low-grade brace, not a Valsalva — a sustained full breath-hold across 200 m of carrying raises intrathoracic pressure and blood pressure and prevents the ventilation needed to clear CO2 during a long submaximal effort.
Sandbag sits high on the traps/upper back → posterior and superior COM shift → higher trunk-extensor demand and a stronger tendency to round the thoracic spine and lose a vertical torso.

Lunge standard: the rear knee must contact the floor each rep. Front shin roughly vertical to slightly inclined; driving from the front-foot heel/mid-foot increases glute-hip contribution and reduces a quad-only pattern.

Step length trade-off: a longer lunge means fewer reps over 100 m but a higher cost per rep and a greater hip-flexor stretch. Rep counts vary widely with height and stride choice — count your own athlete rather than assuming a number.

Wall ball standards: hip crease below the top of the knee at the bottom, and the ball must strike the target zone. Both must be met on the same rep or it is a no-rep, and a no-rep late in the set is expensive because the work has already been paid for.
Wall ball efficiency: catch high, let the ball ride the descent (absorb, don't stop it), full hip and knee extension into the throw, arms guiding rather than launching.

Wall balls finish the race in a heavily fatigued, high-ventilation state, and the squat-plus-overhead pattern gives breathing little mechanical room. Planning break sets that sum to the full requirement (e.g. 25/25/25/25 or 20/20/20/20/20) keeps cycle time stable better than grinding to a stall.
12.training_link: Train your athlete's grip and trunk in the state they will actually meet them: put 60-90 s heavy carries immediately after a hard 1 km run rep, so forearm and postural failure show up in training instead of on the floor at station 6. For lunges, rehearse the exact sandbag position and knee-touch standard under fatigue, and lock in a step length they can repeat for the full 100 m rather than one that only looks strong fresh. On wall balls, coach a fixed break plan that sums to the full requirement (say 25/25/25/25 with short rests) and drill target accuracy when they are breathless — a no-rep at rep 80 costs more than a slightly slower cycle time.

glossary.def: Trunk function of resisting sideways bending when load is offset or asymmetric. The primary core demand of a loaded carry, held isometrically while gait continues.

12.exam_focus: Identifying the specific biomechanical limiter of each of the final three stations — grip and anti-lateral-flexion on the carry, posterior-load trunk extension and knee-touch mechanics on the lunge, depth-plus-target standards and catch-and-drive cycling on wall balls — and prescribing the correct coaching correction under fatigue.

13.title: Race format, divisions & rules
13.key_concept: HYROX is a fixed, standardised race: 8 x 1 km runs, each run followed by one functional station, always in the same order — SkiErg 1000 m, Sled Push 50 m, Sled Pull 50 m, Burpee Broad Jump 80 m, Row 1000 m, Farmers Carry 200 m, Sandbag Lunges 100 m, Wall Balls (100 reps). Because the sequence and distances never change, splits are far more comparable across athletes and events than in obstacle or CrossFit racing — though not perfectly so, since sled friction, flooring, venue layout and roxzone length differ between venues. Divisions (Open, Pro, Doubles, Relay) alter load and work-share, not sequence. The roxzone — all transit between run and station — is unavoidable race time. Standards are judged: missed reps are corrected or penalised, so technique under fatigue is a performance variable, not just a safety one.
key_facts: Fixed order, never varies: Ski → Sled Push → Sled Pull → Burpee Broad Jump → Row → Farmers Carry → Sandbag Lunges → Wall Balls; a 1 km run precedes every station (8 km of running total, plus roxzone transit, so total distance covered exceeds 8 km).
Sleds are 4 x 12.5 m lengths each (50 m push, 50 m pull); burpee broad jump 80 m; farmers carry 200 m; lunges 100 m.

Wall balls: 100 reps in EVERY individual division per the current Singles Rulebook (earlier seasons set women's Open at 75 — a classic outdated-fact trap); target height differs by sex (roughly 10 ft / 3.05 m men, 9 ft / 2.70 m women), ball weight by division (approximately 6 kg open men, 9 kg pro men; 4 kg open women, 6 kg pro women — confirm against the current rulebook, loads have been revised between seasons).

Pro vs Open: heavier loads on sled push, sled pull, farmers carry, sandbag and wall ball. SkiErg, Row and Burpee Broad Jump are unchanged, as are all distances and rep counts. Pro is open registration — no qualifying time is required to enter it.

Doubles: both partners run every metre of all 8 km together; station work is shared in any split they choose. Total station work is one athlete's worth, not two (note mixed doubles uses the 75-rep wall ball count). Relay: 4 athletes, each covering two of the eight run+station rounds.

Roxzone = the transition corridor; its time counts in the official result. Reported totals commonly fall in the region of 5–10 min, but this varies substantially with venue layout and is an observed range, not a rule.
Age groups run in ~5-year bands (from the youngest eligible category up through the oldest masters bands), used for rankings and world-championship qualification, not for changing loads.

Judging: reps not meeting the standard are no-repped and must be redone; rules infractions can escalate to a time penalty served in a penalty area (magnitude is set by the current rulebook — verify it rather than assuming a figure). Common faults: incomplete hip/knee extension, ball missing target, sandbag dropped from the shoulders, dropping the farmers handles rather than setting them down under control, sled not fully crossing the line, non-continuous burpee or a jump that is not a two-foot take-off.

Standards to drill: full lockout/extension on lunges (rear knee touch, stand tall), wall ball squat depth (hip crease below top of knee) + target contact, burpee with chest and thighs to the floor and a two-foot broad jump take-off.
Coach must know: the format is a compromised-running event — station choice affects the following run split, so the race plan is 16 linked segments plus roxzone, not 8 runs and 8 workouts.
13.training_link: Because the order is fixed, build your athlete's season around the two or three stations that actually cost them time — commonly sleds, lunges and wall balls, though confirm this from their own splits rather than assuming — and always rehearse them into the run that follows, not in isolation. Programme sled push at race load immediately before a 1 km time trial so they learn what leg-flooded running feels like, and drill judged reps (rear knee touch, hip crease below top of knee, ball on target) at rep counts past 60 so the standard survives fatigue. If they are moving to Pro or Doubles, change nothing about pacing until you have re-tested station splits under the new load or work-share. Remember that sled times in particular are venue-sensitive, so treat cross-event sled comparisons with caution.

13.exam_focus: Expect to reproduce the exact station order and rep/distance standards, and to explain how division (Open/Pro/Doubles/Relay), judged standards and roxzone time shape a coach's race plan and training priorities.

14.title: The eight stations — demands overview
14.key_concept: The eight stations are best understood not as eight separate tests but as eight different ways of taxing one continuously running aerobic engine. For most athletes most stations sit at or above threshold, so each is a mixed oxidative/glycolytic effort whose real cost is often paid on the kilometre that follows rather than on the station clock. A useful coaching classification has three axes: dominant musculature (upper pull, upper push, hip/knee extension, grip, trunk), mechanical character (is the leg musculature loaded eccentrically? is it a sustained high-tension effort that impairs local perfusion?), and time cost. As a general pattern, high-force and eccentric leg work (sled push, burpee broad jump, sandbag lunges, wall balls) degrades the following run more than the upper-body ergs do — though the size of that effect varies a lot between athletes. Race strategy therefore means pacing the leg-heavy stations to protect run pace.
key_facts: Fixed order, 8 runs of 1 km alternating with 8 stations: Run→SkiErg 1000 m→Run→Sled Push 50 m→Run→Sled Pull 50 m→Run→Burpee Broad Jump 80 m→Run→Row 1000 m→Run→Farmers Carry 200 m→Run→Sandbag Lunges 100 m→Run→Wall Balls (100 reps, all individual divisions).

The race is aerobic-dominant overall, but most stations are performed at or above threshold, so glycolytic contribution spikes locally while aerobic capacity does the clearing between efforts. Loads and standards vary by division (Open, Pro, Doubles, Relay) and have been revised across seasons — always check the current rulebook rather than memorising weights.

SkiErg 1000 m: a double-pole pull-down driven by lats, triceps and trunk flexion, with a real hip-hinge and leg contribution that athletes often under-use. Low leg-damage cost, but a common site of an early-race HR spike. Typical age-group split roughly 4:00–5:00; faster athletes go under 4:00. All station times below are broad approximations, not standards.

Sled Push 50 m: high-force horizontal leg extension. Sustained high-tension effort raises intramuscular pressure and transiently impairs local perfusion, so metabolites accumulate fast. Times swing widely with floor surface and friction — roughly 1:00 to over 3:00 at the same fitness level. Commonly reported as the single biggest disruptor of the following run.

Sled Pull 50 m: hand-over-hand rope pull loading posterior chain, upper back and grip, with the legs largely braced rather than driving through range. Roughly 1:30–3:00. Usually less downstream run cost than the push, though grip fatigue can carry over to farmers carry.

Burpee Broad Jump 80 m: whole-body, with a high ventilatory cost and repeated eccentric landings. Roughly 3:00–5:00 and highly technique-sensitive. Typically among the worst run disruptors, alongside sled push.
Row 1000 m: legs-back-arms drive sequence recruiting large muscle mass, roughly 3:45–4:30 for age-groupers. Leg fatigue is genuine but concentric and non-impact, so run cost is usually moderate.

Farmers Carry 200 m: usually grip-, forearm- and trunk-limited before it is metabolically limiting; roughly 1:30–2:15. Often the least disruptive station relative to its duration, but it is still race-pace work — treating it as true rest is a mistake.

Sandbag Lunges 100 m: loaded unilateral work with a large eccentric component and an anterior load. A frequent cause of cramping and a slow, choppy final run, though this varies with an athlete's lunge-specific training history.
Wall Balls last: repeated squat-to-front-press against a target-height standard; roughly 4:00–7:00 or longer, with high no-rep exposure because technique degrades as fatigue rises.

Roxzone is the timed transition area; the clock never stops, and roxzone time is the race total minus run and station work time. It spans 15 traverses in and out of the station area (8 run→station entries + 7 station→run exits; the race ends on wall balls) and commonly totals somewhere in the 4–8 minute range for age-groupers, less for elites. Gains there come from efficient lines, quick set-up and purposeful movement — not from sprinting in and arriving unable to work.
14.training_link: Audit race splits station-by-station AND run-by-run, then find which run drops most versus the athlete's fresh 1 km pace — that names the station to fix, most often sled push, burpee broad jump or lunges. Train those under fatigue in compromised-running blocks (station → immediate 400–1000 m at goal pace) rather than only as fresh strength work. Separately, drill the low-cost items — farmers carry efficiency and roxzone transitions — as skill and pacing wins, since time saved there costs comparatively little physiologically.

glossary.def: The timed transition area between runs and stations. Its cumulative total is a legitimate performance metric and often contains minutes of avoidable loss.

glossary.def: Running under the fatigue of a preceding station. In practice, measured as the drop in run pace relative to the athlete's fresh 1 km pace — the primary currency of HYROX pacing decisions.
