glossary.def: Efforts such as the sled push or a heavy carry where high intramuscular pressure transiently impairs local blood flow, accelerating metabolite accumulation and slowing clearance.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Fatigue and muscle damage from lengthening contractions — lunges, burpee landings. Well documented to impair subsequent running economy more than concentric-only work of similar effort.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The number of reps in a station a judge can invalidate. High-rep, standard-dependent stations (wall balls, burpee broad jump) carry the most risk.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The clock time a station consumes in isolation, kept separate from its downstream cost on the following run.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="26" cy="12" r="4" fill="#67e8b0"/><path d="M26 16v10l-8 8M26 26l8 8" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="52" cy="18" r="6" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".7"/></svg>

glossary.def: A station where hand and forearm endurance fails before the aerobic or leg systems do — typically sled pull and farmers carry.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="26" cy="12" r="4" fill="#67e8b0"/><path d="M26 16v10l-8 8M26 26l8 8" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="52" cy="18" r="6" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".7"/></svg>

glossary.def: Deliberately holding a submaximal effort on a leg-heavy station to preserve the following kilometre, accepting a slower station split in exchange for a faster net race time.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

14.exam_focus: Expect to be asked to match each station to its dominant musculature and energy demand, and then to justify which stations most compromise the following run and how a coach should pace or train them.

15.title: Roxzone, transitions & lost time
15.key_concept: The roxzone is the transition corridor an athlete crosses between every run and every station, and the clock never stops inside it. Because 8 runs alternate with 8 stations and the race ends on the final station, an athlete makes 15 traverses, so seconds compound into minutes. Reported roxzone totals vary widely by venue layout and athlete: elites commonly land in the low single-digit minutes while many mid-pack and novice finishers give up roughly 8-12 min or more. Roxzone time is largely not fitness — it is the residue of walking, chalking, fiddling with kit, hunting a free lane, hesitating at the sled, and waiting for breath to settle. Because HYROX reports it as its own split, it is measurable and trainable: a discrete, low-cost performance variable a coach can attack before touching engine work.
key_facts: Roxzone = transition area; clock runs continuously → all transit is race time.
Race order is fixed: SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump, Row, Farmers Carry, Sandbag Lunges, Wall Balls, each preceded by a 1 km run.
8 runs + 8 stations, finishing on a station → 15 roxzone traverses (8 run→station entries, 7 station→run exits).
Roxzone time ≈ total time − (run time + station work time); HYROX reports it as its own split.

Typical observed spread (varies by venue and floor plan): elite roughly 3-5 min; competent age-grouper roughly 5-8 min; novice/mid-pack often 8-12+ min. Treat these as rough field norms, not fixed standards.
Transitions add venue-dependent extra movement, so total distance covered exceeds the 8 km of scored running. The exact added distance differs from event to event.
Common leaks: walking instead of jogging, chalk ritual, glove/shoe/belt fiddling, lane hunting, standing recovery, misreading station setup.
Roxzone is often the cheapest split to improve — it needs little or no aerobic adaptation, mainly rehearsal and pre-set decision rules.
15 s saved per traverse × 15 traverses = 225 s ≈ 3:45 — a saving that can rival what a short training block yields in run pace.

Rule infractions cost time outside the roxzone budget: some faults require repeating reps, others a prescribed penalty run under the current rulebook, so technique compliance protects the transition plan.
Wall Balls close the race: 100 reps in all individual divisions — there is no station→run transition after it.
15.training_link: Pull your athlete's roxzone total from their last race result and set it as an explicit KPI alongside run pace — many age-groupers have several minutes sitting there, and it is usually cheaper to claim than an engine adaptation. In sessions, never let them walk out of a station: rehearse the exact entry sequence (chalk once or not at all, gloves pre-set, hands on the implement quickly) and make the first 20 m off every station a jog, not a recovery stroll. Time the transitions in training the same way you time the intervals, so the roxzone becomes a scored element rather than a rest period.

glossary.def: The marked transition corridor athletes cross between each run and each station. All time spent in it counts toward the finishing time.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The aggregate of all transition segments in a race, reported separately from run time and station work time.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: One passage through the roxzone — either run→station or station→run. A standard individual race contains 15.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 30h52" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="14" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="30" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#ffb86b"/><rect x="46" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

glossary.def: Time recorded on the station itself, from first contact with the implement to completion of the prescribed work.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="26" cy="12" r="4" fill="#67e8b0"/><path d="M26 16v10l-8 8M26 26l8 8" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="52" cy="18" r="6" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".7"/></svg>

glossary.def: Any in-race period where the athlete is neither running nor working a station — chalking, waiting, walking, resetting kit.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Coaching shorthand for a pre-rehearsed sequence for entering a station (lane choice, grip, first-rep cue) that removes decision-making under fatigue.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Additional prescribed distance issued for certain station rule infractions; a separate time cost from ordinary roxzone transit.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

15.exam_focus: Expect to be asked to calculate roxzone total from a results breakdown, to reason about the 15-traverse structure, and to justify why reducing transition time can be a higher-yield coaching intervention than marginal run-pace gains.

16.title: Pacing strategy & race modelling
16.key_concept: A HYROX race model is an accounting exercise: finish time = total run time + total station time + roxzone time. Build it bottom-up from tested station splits and a run pace the athlete can hold compromised, not from fresh 5 km pace. Because every run is bracketed by hard station work, run pace tends to decay across the eight legs; the model should budget for that decay rather than assume it away. Even-to-slightly-negative pacing is generally the most robust approach: going out fast raises metabolic and ventilatory cost early, taxes the sleds and burpees, and tends to produce a back-half decline that station gains rarely repay.
key_facts: Finish = Σ8 run splits + Σ8 station splits + roxzone (transitions). Model all three or the prediction is wrong.
Roxzone is real time, not free: commonly ~4-8 min total across the race for age-group athletes, less for elites; ↑ with fatigue, poor equipment setup, big venues.
The race has 15 roxzone changeovers, not 8: 8 run→station plus 7 station→run. Wall balls end at the finish line, so there is no run after station 8.

Race run pace is NOT fresh pace. A common coaching rule of thumb is ~30-60 s/km slower than fresh 5 km pace, wider for weak-aerobic athletes — treat it as a starting estimate to be replaced by testing, not a law.
Run-split shape is the diagnostic: run 1 is usually fastest (adrenaline, fresh legs, and it can also be distorted by start congestion) → the honest baseline is runs 2-3.
Positive split = classic error. Time banked early is generally repaid at a worse rate later, but the exchange rate is athlete-specific — do not quote a fixed conversion.
Highest-cost stations for subsequent running: sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jump. Because they are stations 2, 3 and 4, the degradation surfaces on runs 3, 4 and 5.
Even pacing (flat runs) or slight negative (last 2-3 runs fastest) suits a sustained effort of roughly 60-120 min held at or below the athlete's maximal steady state.
Wall balls are the terminal variable: a blown pacing plan often shows up as fragmented WB sets rather than as a slow run.
Benchmark predictors: 5 km time + tested 1000 m SkiErg/Row + sled times + unbroken WB capacity → build the model; validate with a half-simulation.
Sled times are typically the largest source of model error — surface friction and setup vary venue to venue; model a range, not a point.
16.training_link: Before you set a target, make your athlete run a tested 1 km at goal race pace immediately after a hard sled push and a 1000 m row — that number, not their 5 km PB, is what goes in the model. Then write the model as a card: eight run splits, eight station splits, a roxzone allowance, and a stated 'do not exceed' pace for runs 1 and 2. Coach the first 2 km as the discipline test — many coaches use a rough guide of roughly 10-15 s faster than the modelled split as the point to rein it in, because an overcooked opening tends to be repaid with interest from the sandbag lunges onward.

glossary.def: A written, per-segment time budget for all 8 runs, 8 stations and the roxzone that sums to a target finish. It is the pacing plan in numbers.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 30h52" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="14" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="30" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#ffb86b"/><rect x="46" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

glossary.def: The transition area and the time spent in it moving between run and station. Counted in official finish time and treated as a trainable segment.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The pace an athlete can sustain on a 1 km leg immediately after a station, with elevated lactate and heart rate. In practice slower than fresh pace.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Second half slower than the first. In HYROX it usually reflects an early pace or sled effort above the athlete's sustainable intensity.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Second half faster than the first, produced by a conservative opening. Uncommon in HYROX but the most forgiving strategy when the model is uncertain.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: The progressive slowing of successive run legs across the race; the size and onset point of the decay indicate where the pacing plan broke.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Shorthand for the highest intensity at which lactate production and clearance stay balanced — the maximal lactate steady state / critical speed region. Above it, blood lactate rises continuously and time to exhaustion shortens sharply.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: 4 runs + 4 stations in race order, at target pace, used to validate a race model without the recovery cost of a full sim.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

16.exam_focus: Constructing or correcting a race model — computing a run-pace target from a finish goal minus station and roxzone time, and diagnosing a positive-split failure from a set of run splits.

17.title: Athlete profiling — runner vs strength-dominant
17.key_concept: Profiling asks one question: which quality is costing this athlete the most time? A HYROX race is 8 x 1 km runs alternating with 8 stations in a fixed order (SkiErg, sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jump, row, farmers carry, sandbag lunges, wall balls), so every athlete covers identical work — which means the limiter shows up as a comparison, not as a raw number. Compare the athlete's rank on the run segments against their rank on the stations within the same division and field. Endurance-dominant athletes typically bleed time on the sleds, lunges and wall balls; strength-dominant athletes tend to hold station times but show run splits that drift late. Layer race splits with gym testing (a fresh run benchmark, compromised-run repeats, relative strength, unbroken capacity, grip endurance) to confirm, since a single race can be distorted by pacing, illness or a bad day. Then bias training toward the weakness while maintaining the strength.
key_facts: Fixed format: 8 x 1 km runs alternating with 8 stations in a set order — SkiErg, sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jump, row, farmers carry, sandbag lunges, wall balls. Everyone does the same work, so profiling is always a relative comparison.

Rough time distribution for most age-group athletes: running is the single largest block (commonly around half the clock), stations the next largest, roxzone a smaller share (often on the order of 5–10%). Treat these as ballpark splits that vary widely by athlete and division, not fixed constants.

Roxzone (transition time) is measured, not dead time, and is itself a profiling signal — a disproportionately long roxzone usually points to aerobic recovery cost or poor course/transition habits rather than to station strength.
Profile from RANK/percentile within division and field, not raw times — raw times confound course layout, conditions and how deep that particular field was.

Run-split drift = (mean of runs 5–8 − mean of runs 1–4) ÷ mean of runs 1–4. There is no validated cut-off in the research literature; coaches commonly treat drift beyond roughly 8–10% as a practical flag for a durability/aerobic limiter or over-aggressive early pacing rather than a strength problem.
Endurance-dominant signature: run splits rank well, station times rank poorly, with the sleds usually the largest outlier; often lower relative strength and limited local muscular endurance.
Strength-dominant signature: station times rank at or above field pace while run splits rank poorly and degrade through the second half, often with a long roxzone spent recovering.

Balanced profile: no segment sits more than a few percentile points off the athlete's own average percentile. Gains then come mostly from roxzone, pacing discipline and station technique rather than from one big physical hole.

The sleds are the classic strength-dominant advantage (high horizontal force output plus a heavy glycolytic cost); wall balls and sandbag lunges load local muscular endurance instead. Profile force-dominant and endurance-dominant stations separately — an athlete can be strong on one and weak on the other.
Grip (farmers carry, sled pull, and to a lesser extent the ergs) can be an isolated limiter that looks like a conditioning problem until it is tested on its own.

Bias training toward the limiter, but keep the dominant quality at a maintenance dose (commonly around 1–2 quality sessions per week; the detraining literature broadly supports that reduced frequency with preserved intensity holds an adaptation). Re-profile each block (~8–12 weeks) because training the limiter moves it.
17.training_link: Pull your athlete's official splits and rank every run and every station against their division before you write a single session — if their sleds sit around the 70th percentile and their runs around the 25th, you are looking at a strength-dominant athlete, and the block needs aerobic volume plus compromised-run work rather than more heavy pushing. Confirm with a second data point (a gym test or a prior race) before committing, since one race can be distorted by pacing or conditions. Retest with a benchmark such as 4 x (1 km run + 1 station) and watch whether run-split drift is shrinking. Keep at least one weekly session on the strong quality so you close the gap without giving back the advantage they already own.

glossary.def: The physical or technical capacity whose improvement would return the most race time. Identified by comparing segment ranks across the race, not by which segment felt hardest.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The percentage slowdown of the second half of the runs relative to the first half. Used as a practical durability and pacing index, not a validated diagnostic threshold.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Running with pre-fatigued legs and elevated ventilation immediately after a station. The specific quality HYROX rewards, and the reason a fresh 5 km time alone can overrate a runner.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Force capacity expressed per kilogram of bodyweight. Relevant because station loads are fixed by division, so a lighter athlete must move the same implement — though on the sled push body mass itself also contributes, so relative strength is a useful indicator rather than a complete predictor.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The ability of a specific muscle group to sustain repeated submaximal contractions before force output falls. A governing quality in wall balls and sandbag lunges, and a contributor in burpee broad jumps alongside technique and whole-body cost.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The cumulative transition time between runs and stations across the race. A trainable segment reflecting decision speed, aerobic recovery between efforts and course familiarity.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: An athlete's rank on one run or station expressed against their division field. The core profiling unit, because it normalises for course, conditions and field quality.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Deliberate allocation of extra quality sessions to the limiter while holding the dominant quality at a maintenance dose.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The tendency to train the quality that already produces good sessions, reinforcing the strength and widening the gap on the limiter.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

17.exam_focus: Given race splits or test data, correctly identify the athlete's limiting quality and prescribe the appropriate training bias — including maintaining, rather than abandoning, the dominant quality.

18.title: Energy systems & the HYROX demand profile
18.key_concept: HYROX sits firmly on the aerobic end of the energy continuum: elite finishers are under ~60 minutes and most age-groupers take ~75-110 minutes of near-continuous work, so oxidative phosphorylation supplies the overwhelming majority of total ATP. But the demand profile is not steady-state. Sled push/pull, burpee broad jumps and wall balls impose bouts whose power demand outruns O2 delivery, so phosphagen and fast-glycolytic pathways spike repeatedly -> metabolites (H+, Pi, ADP) accumulate locally, then must be cleared on the following run and in the roxzone. Substrate use skews heavily to carbohydrate because race intensity sits at or just under the second threshold; fat's relative share is greater only in the lower-intensity portions (transitions, easier segments). The key coaching idea: whole-race anaerobic ATP is a SMALL fraction of the total, yet its local muscular cost is what actually shapes the race. Performance = aerobic ceiling x ability to repeatedly tolerate and recover from those spikes.
key_facts: All three systems run simultaneously at all times; 'dominance' is a question of duration and intensity, not an on/off switch.

Phosphagen (ATP-PCr): highest power, dominant for roughly the first 6-10 s of an all-out effort. PCr resynthesis is O2-dependent (fast-component half-time on the order of 30 s, near-complete in ~3-5 min) -> a better aerobic base means faster station-to-station recovery.
Fast glycolysis: main contributor from roughly 10-15 s out to ~2 min, peaking in the first ~30 s. High flux raises H+ and inorganic phosphate — the 'heavy legs' after a sled.

Oxidative: dominant beyond ~2-3 min. Across a full HYROX race the aerobic system supplies well over 90% of total ATP (best estimates for continuous efforts of this length are ~95%+); the anaerobic share is small in total but concentrated in the stations.
Lactate is a fuel and a shuttle, not the fatigue agent — it is oxidized in the heart, in slow-twitch fibres and in other muscle beds, and converted back to glucose in the liver.

Fatigue during and after a station is best explained by inorganic phosphate (Pi) accumulation, ADP rise and local substrate depletion, with H+/acidosis contributing; the older 'lactic acid causes fatigue' model is outdated.

Race intensity for a competitive athlete is high — commonly reported in the upper-80s to low-90s %HRmax, at or just below the second threshold — so carbohydrate is the dominant oxidized fuel. (Published HYROX-specific physiology is still thin; treat any single number as an estimate.)
Crossover concept: CHO overtakes fat as the main oxidized fuel somewhere around ~45-65% VO2max, shifting rightward with endurance training. Race pace is far above this in every case.

Total glycogen in a trained athlete is roughly 400-600 g (muscle ~300-500 g at ~15 g/kg wet muscle, liver ~80-110 g), i.e. ~1600-2400 kcal — comfortably enough for one race, but depletion is a real factor for 100+ min finishers and across a full race-simulation day.

Exogenous CHO ceiling: ~60 g/h from glucose-only sources, up to ~90 g/h with glucose+fructose blends (gut-trained athletes tolerate more). For efforts under ~75 min, a small dose or even a CHO mouth-rinse is usually sufficient.

Running is 8 x 1 km; the other 8 efforts are the stations, in fixed order: SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump, Row, Farmers Carry, Sandbag Lunges, Wall Balls. Stations plus roxzone commonly account for roughly 40-55% of total race time -> HYROX is not a running race with obstacles, it is repeated threshold running with strength-endurance interruptions.
Cumulative fatigue: each glycolytic spike raises the metabolic cost of the next run, so splits usually drift slower even at constant effort — plan pacing around it rather than fight it.
18.training_link: Train the aerobic ceiling as the primary lever — the large majority of your athlete's race is oxidative, and a bigger engine is also what restores PCr and clears metabolites before the next 1 km. Then rehearse the spikes specifically: compromised-running sets (a sled or a wall-ball block straight into 400-1000 m at goal pace) teach the athlete to run through metabolic disturbance instead of walking it off in the roxzone. Fuel it like a threshold endurance event, not a strength session: well-fed and CHO-topped-up going in (a genuine multi-day glycogen load is only worth it for longer finishing times), roughly 30-60 g CHO/h in-race for athletes finishing near or beyond 90 min, and avoid long fasted sessions in race week.

glossary.def: Immediate ATP resupply from stored ATP and phosphocreatine, requiring no oxygen. Highest power output, smallest capacity — largely spent within seconds and restored aerobically.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Breakdown of glucose/glycogen to pyruvate and onward to lactate when pyruvate production outpaces mitochondrial uptake. High rate, moderate capacity; the pathway carrying the sleds and burpee broad jumps.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="8" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 20h16M44 14l6 6-6 6" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="60" cy="20" r="5" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

glossary.def: Mitochondrial ATP production from carbohydrate and fat using oxygen. Lowest power, by far the largest capacity — the engine that carries a HYROX race.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="8" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 20h16M44 14l6 6-6 6" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="60" cy="20" r="5" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

glossary.def: Brooks' model of the intensity-driven shift in fuel mix: as relative intensity rises, carbohydrate's share of oxidized fuel increases and fat's falls. Endurance training shifts the crossover point rightward but does not remove it.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Transport of lactate from producing fibres/muscles to sites that oxidize it as fuel or reconvert it to glucose. Explains why blood lactate can fall during a steady run that follows a hard station.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption — elevated O2 uptake after an effort, used to resynthesize PCr, restore ion gradients and return to homeostasis. (The legacy term 'oxygen debt' describes the same observation with an outdated mechanism.) In HYROX this is largely paid down while still running.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A segment where power demand exceeds what aerobic metabolism can supply, producing a sharp rise in anaerobic ATP contribution and blood lactate — typically the sleds, burpee broad jumps and wall balls.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="8" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 20h16M44 14l6 6-6 6" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="60" cy="20" r="5" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

glossary.def: Informal shorthand used in these notes for the highest sustainable aerobic power/pace (formally: critical power, or the second threshold). It sets both realistic race pace and how fast each station's metabolic disturbance is repaid.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="8" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 20h16M44 14l6 6-6 6" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="60" cy="20" r="5" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

18.exam_focus: Expect to justify why HYROX is predominantly oxidative yet punctuated by repeated glycolytic spikes, to distinguish the small whole-race anaerobic ATP share from its large local effect, and to translate that into a fuelling or session-design decision.

19.title: VO2max, thresholds & running economy
19.key_concept: Endurance performance sits on three separable pillars. VO2max is the ceiling — the maximal rate you can take in, transport and use oxygen. LT1 (aerobic threshold) marks the first clear rise above resting lactate and defines the top of truly easy work; LT2 (anaerobic/lactate threshold, approximated by MLSS or critical speed) is the highest intensity where lactate production and clearance still balance, and it largely sets the fraction of VO2max you can hold for roughly 30–60 minutes. Running economy — oxygen (or energy) cost per unit distance at a given speed — decides how much of that fractional ceiling converts into pace. In HYROX, where seven of the eight runs are entered in a pre-fatigued state, economy and LT2 often discriminate finish time better than a raw VO2max number, though all three qualities matter and none should be dismissed.
key_facts: VO2max = ceiling; LT2 = usable fraction of it; economy = pace produced per unit O2. Sustainable race pace depends on all three interacting.
VO2max tends to plateau after roughly 2–3 yrs of consistent training in already-trained athletes, while LT2 and economy stay trainable for years → weight coaching accordingly.

LT1 ≈ first sustained lactate rise above baseline (often near ~2 mmol·L⁻¹, but highly individual); LT2 ≈ MLSS / critical speed, commonly ~3–5 mmol·L⁻¹ — the 4 mmol 'OBLA' figure is a population convention, not a physiological law.
Trained endurance athletes typically sit around 75–90% of VO2max at LT2; untrained roughly 50–65%. Ranges are approximate and vary by test protocol.
Running economy is expressed as mL O₂·kg⁻¹·km⁻¹ (or kcal·kg⁻¹·km⁻¹); ↓ cost at a fixed speed = better economy.
Two athletes, same VO2max → the more economical one generally runs faster. Economy accounts for a substantial share of the performance variance among VO2max-matched runners.
VO2max training: 3–5 min intervals at ~90–100% vVO2max, work:rest ≈ 1:1 to 2:1, accumulating roughly 12–25 min at intensity.
LT2 training: continuous threshold/tempo 20–40 min, or cruise intervals (e.g. 5–6 × 6 min) at ~LT2 pace with short rests.
LT1 / aerobic base: high volume of easy work below LT1 → ↑ mitochondrial density, capillarisation, fat oxidation and lactate clearance capacity.
Heavy strength work (~80–90% 1RM) and plyometrics ~2×/wk over 8–14 weeks typically improve economy by a few percent, usually with little or no change in VO2max or body mass.
HYROX-specific economy = compromised running: economy degrades after sled work and lunges, so train the fatigued state rather than only fresh 5 k pace.

Field proxies when lab lactate isn't available: talk test ≈ LT1; a ~30 min solo TT (average HR/pace over the final 20 min) or ~60 min max-effort pace ≈ LT2. Treat these as estimates, not measurements.
19.training_link: Estimate your athlete's LT2 with a 30-minute solo time trial (average HR/pace over the final 20 min) and re-test every 8–12 weeks — that anchor drives run pacing far more usefully than a watch-estimated VO2max. Build the block around easy sub-LT1 volume plus roughly 2 threshold sessions weekly, keep heavy strength and plyometrics in year-round to protect economy, and reserve short VO2max blocks for when LT2 has crept close to the ceiling. Then transfer it: run repeats immediately off sleds and lunges so economy is trained in the pre-fatigued state the race actually delivers. Remember the race shape — the opening 1 km is run fresh, the remaining seven follow SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump, Row, Farmers Carry and Sandbag Lunges respectively, and Wall Balls closes the race with no run after it.

glossary.def: The highest rate of oxygen consumption achievable during maximal exercise, usually in mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. It sets an upper limit on aerobic power output but does not by itself determine race pace.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The lowest intensity at which blood lactate rises measurably and consistently above baseline. It marks the ceiling of genuinely low-strain, high-volume training.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The highest intensity at which lactate appearance and clearance remain in equilibrium. Above it, lactate and associated fatigue accumulate progressively until task failure.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Maximal lactate steady state — the reference expression of LT2, verified by constant-load trials in which blood lactate rises by no more than about 1 mmol·L⁻¹ between roughly the 10th and 30th minute.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The metabolic cost of covering a given distance at a submaximal speed. Lower oxygen or energy cost per kilometre means more speed for the same aerobic investment.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: The percentage of VO2max an athlete can sustain for a given race duration, largely governed by the position of LT2.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The slowest running velocity that elicits VO2max; a practical prescription anchor for maximal-aerobic interval work.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The asymptote of the speed–duration relationship, separating the heavy and severe intensity domains. A field-derived close analogue of MLSS, though the two are not identical.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The elevated energy cost of running when entered in a pre-fatigued state — the operative version of economy in HYROX, where runs 2 through 8 each follow a station.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

19.exam_focus: Expect to be asked to distinguish VO2max, LT1/LT2 and running economy as separate trainable qualities — and to justify why economy and threshold, especially under compromised (post-station) running, are strong drivers of HYROX finish time relative to a raw VO2max value.

20.title: Lactate, buffering & fatigue
20.key_concept: Lactate is not a waste product and not the direct cause of acidosis. Fast glycolysis produces pyruvate faster than mitochondria can accept it; the LDH reaction (pyruvate + NADH + H+ → lactate + NAD+) regenerates NAD+ so glycolytic ATP flow continues. Lactate then shuttles — cytosol → mitochondria, fast fibres → slow fibres, muscle → blood → heart, liver, brain, other muscle — as a fuel and a signalling molecule (gluconeogenic substrate, mitochondrial biogenesis signal). The H+ load that accompanies hard work comes chiefly from ATP hydrolysis during high glycolytic flux, and is buffered by bicarbonate, intramuscular phosphates, proteins and carnosine. Blood lactate is a marker of the balance between appearance and disappearance, not the toxin itself.
key_facts: Lactate production ≠ acidosis. H+ arises mainly from ATP hydrolysis when glycolytic flux is high; the LDH step itself consumes a proton.
LDH: pyruvate + NADH + H+ → lactate + NAD+ → regenerating NAD+ keeps glycolysis (and its ATP output) running.
Cell-to-cell and intracellular lactate shuttles: MCT transporters move lactate into oxidative fibres, heart, liver (Cori cycle) and brain, where it is oxidised or reconverted.
Blood lactate = appearance minus disappearance. A steady value means matched rates, not 'no lactate being made'.

Thresholds: LT1 (first sustained rise above baseline) and LT2 (highest sustainable steady state). LT2, MLSS and critical power are related but NOT identical — critical power typically sits slightly above MLSS.

There is no universal threshold lactate value. MLSS commonly falls somewhere around 2–6 mmol/L and is highly individual; the familiar fixed 4 mmol/L 'OBLA' is a testing convention, not a physiological constant.

Buffers: bicarbonate (extracellular); inorganic phosphate, proteins and carnosine (intracellular). β-alanine supplementation raises muscle carnosine over several weeks; sodium bicarbonate acutely raises extracellular buffering.

Fatigue during high-intensity work is multifactorial: inorganic phosphate accumulation is now considered a major direct impairer of cross-bridge force and Ca2+ handling, with acidosis contributing alongside it plus rising afferent feedback and RPE. Classic textbook claims that H+ alone explains the force loss are overstated.

HYROX stations such as the sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jumps and wall balls drive high glycolytic flux through large muscle groups; sustained high intramuscular tension in the sleds and wall balls also restricts local perfusion, so lactate and H+ rise sharply.
The run after a station is the clearance phase: submaximal aerobic work oxidises lactate. Start that run too hard and appearance keeps outpacing disappearance.

Better-trained athletes clear faster (greater MCT1 expression, mitochondrial density and capillarity). Raising the pace at which lactate stays in steady state — not suppressing lactate — is the adaptation target.
20.training_link: Coach the roxzone exit, not just the station. After a sled push or wall balls an athlete leaves with a large local H+ and lactate load, so the opening stretch of the next run should be deliberately conservative before settling onto target pace — that submaximal aerobic window is where lactate is actually shuttled and oxidised. Exact numbers are a coaching heuristic rather than a validated prescription: something on the order of 150–200 m at roughly 15–30 s/km slower than goal pace is a sensible starting point to test and individualise. Build the clearance machinery directly with threshold and sub-threshold running to raise LT2, plus repeated station-into-run compromised blocks so the athlete rehearses running well while acidotic.

glossary.def: The movement of lactate from where it is produced to sites that oxidise or reconvert it — within a cell, between fibre types, or between organs via the blood.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Monocarboxylate transporters that co-transport lactate with a proton across membranes. MCT4 predominates in glycolytic fibres and favours export; MCT1 predominates in oxidative tissue and favours uptake.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The highest intensity at which blood lactate appearance and disappearance still balance over a sustained effort. Above it, lactate and H+ climb progressively until work rate falls.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The asymptote of the power–duration relationship, marking the boundary of the severe-intensity domain. Closely related to MLSS but usually a slightly higher intensity — the two should not be treated as the same test.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The tissue's ability to absorb H+ without a large pH fall — bicarbonate outside the cell; phosphates, proteins and carnosine inside.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A muscle dipeptide that buffers intramuscular H+. Muscle content is raised by several weeks of consistent β-alanine supplementation.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Hepatic conversion of blood lactate back to glucose, which can return to the muscle — lactate recycled as fuel rather than discarded.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The fall in muscle and blood pH during high-intensity work, driven by H+ accumulation. Associated with rising lactate, but not caused by lactate.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The rate at which lactate is taken up and oxidised or reconverted elsewhere. It shapes how quickly an athlete recovers between hard efforts.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

20.exam_focus: Expect to be tested on lactate as fuel and signal, on H+ (with inorganic phosphate) rather than lactate as the fatigue agent, on the individuality of threshold lactate values, and on applying the shuttle-and-clearance model to pacing the run immediately after a high-glycolytic HYROX station.

21.title: Compromised running — the physiology
21.key_concept: Compromised running is running on legs and lungs already loaded by station work. Economy degrades mainly for peripheral reasons: the muscles just taxed arrive at the run with depleted phosphocreatine, accumulated H+ and inorganic phosphate, and impaired excitation-contraction coupling, so more motor units — including higher-threshold type II units — are recruited to hold the same pace, and oxygen cost per metre rises. Central drive is simultaneously reduced by afferent feedback from fatigued muscle. Perfusion is still partly committed to recently working limbs, to skin for heat loss and to hard-working respiratory muscles, so the legs are competing for a finite cardiac output. Mechanics change too: stride shortens, ground-contact time lengthens, hip extension and leg stiffness fall, elastic return is poorer. Same pace now costs higher HR, VO2 and RPE.
key_facts: Running economy = O2 (or energy) cost at a fixed submaximal speed; post-station it ↑ (worse) even when pace is unchanged.

Peripheral fatigue dominates early post-station: PCr depletion, ↑H+/Pi, impaired Ca2+ release and reduced myofibrillar Ca2+ sensitivity → force per active fibre ↓ → extra motor-unit recruitment → ↑VO2 at the same speed.

Central fatigue = ↓voluntary drive to the motoneuron pool, driven partly by group III/IV afferent feedback from fatigued muscle. The same afferent traffic raises perceived effort, which is a large part of why athletes settle out of the roxzone rather than surge.

Blood-flow competition: a finite cardiac output is shared between recently loaded muscle (post-exercise hyperaemia), skin for heat dissipation, and the respiratory muscles — so O2 delivery per unit of locomotor muscle falls.

Note the direction of each reflex: the LOCOMOTOR muscle metaboreflex raises blood pressure and sympathetic tone to defend flow TO the working muscle. It is the RESPIRATORY muscle metaboreflex that redistributes flow AWAY from the legs when ventilatory work is high. Do not conflate them.

Heavy ventilatory work after SkiErg and Row is the classic HYROX trigger for the respiratory metaboreflex. Mechanistically this is well established in laboratory loading studies; its exact size during a real race has not been quantified, so treat it as a plausible contributor, not a measured one.

Mechanical signature of the compromised run — robust findings: stride length ↓, ground-contact time ↑, hip extension ↓, leg/ankle stiffness ↓, braking impulse ↑. Cadence usually holds or rises slightly relative to the shortened stride. Vertical oscillation is inconsistent across studies — do not teach it as a reliable marker.

Station-specific carry-over: sled push and sled pull are near-purely concentric, high-force, heavily glycolytic work that hammers quads and glutes; sandbag lunges pre-fatigue the same hip and knee extensors used for propulsion; ski, row and farmers carry load posture, grip and trunk → early-run postural collapse.
HR drifts up and stays elevated across the 8 runs while pace ↓ — cardiovascular drift plus rising RPE, not the arrival of a new aerobic limit.

The first couple of hundred metres out of the roxzone is the worst window; economy partially recovers as PCr resynthesises (fast-component half-time commonly reported around 20-30 s, with several minutes needed for full restoration) — but only if pace is controlled rather than surged.

Race-order fact worth memorising for transfer questions: the 8 stations run SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump, Row, Farmers Carry, Sandbag Lunges, Wall Balls, each preceded by a 1 km run. Wall balls is LAST — there is no run after it, so wall-ball fatigue cannot compromise a subsequent run. Run 8 is the one that follows sandbag lunges.

Best trainable adaptations: aerobic/mitochondrial base for faster metabolite clearance and PCr resynthesis, muscle buffering and lactate transport capacity, strength-endurance in the exact station patterns, and repeated station→run transitions so pacing and mechanics are rehearsed under fatigue.
21.training_link: Stop programming runs and stations as fully separate sessions. For most HYROX athletes the binding limiter is the run immediately out of the roxzone rather than standalone 1 km speed — confirm that for the individual athlete before you reorganise their whole block, because a genuinely slow runner still needs run speed. Build blocks like 50 m sled push → 1 km at target race pace, repeated 4-6 times, and coach the pattern they will actually need out of the zone: quick turnover on a deliberately short stride, tall posture, then lengthen the stride as the legs come back. Track the gap between fresh 1 km pace and compromised 1 km pace. Shrinking that gap is the adaptation this session targets; raising fresh pace is a separate and still-necessary job.

glossary.def: Running performed immediately after a fatiguing non-running task, so pace must be produced by muscles already partially depleted and by a partly suppressed central drive.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: The oxygen or energy cost of covering a set distance at a set submaximal speed. Lower cost = better economy; fatigue typically worsens it.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Loss of force-generating capacity arising at or distal to the neuromuscular junction — substrate depletion, metabolite accumulation and disrupted calcium handling inside the fibre.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A fatigue-related reduction in neural drive from the brain and spinal cord to the working muscle, reducing voluntary activation independently of the contractile state of the muscle.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Sensory nerves in muscle that report mechanical and metabolic stress to the CNS; their firing raises perceived effort, inhibits central drive and triggers cardiovascular reflexes.

glossary.def: A pressor reflex triggered by metabolite build-up in working locomotor muscle. It raises blood pressure and sympathetic outflow, which acts to preserve perfusion of that muscle.

glossary.def: The equivalent reflex arising from fatiguing respiratory muscles. Because it drives sympathetic vasoconstriction in the limbs, it shifts blood flow toward the breathing muscles and away from the legs — the version that matters most for a post-SkiErg or post-Row run.

glossary.def: The HYROX transition area an athlete crosses between the running track and the station area; the window in which reacquiring efficient running mechanics is hardest.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The capacity to repeat sub-maximal high-force contractions with minimal force decay — the quality that keeps sled, lunge and carry work from wrecking the following run.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A progressive rise in heart rate at a constant workload, accompanied by falling stroke volume and rising RPE, driven by heat strain, plasma-volume loss and rising sympathetic tone.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

21.exam_focus: Explaining why running economy degrades after station work by correctly separating peripheral fatigue, central fatigue and blood-flow competition — including which metaboreflex points which way — and prescribing station→run compromised-running work as the specific fix.

22.title: Durability & fatigue resistance
22.key_concept: Durability is the retention of physiological qualities — running economy, threshold pace/power, force output, movement quality — after substantial accumulated work, as opposed to those qualities measured fresh. Two athletes with identical lab thresholds can diverge sharply late in a HYROX because one's threshold and economy erode faster. It is described as drift: HR–pace (or HR–power) decoupling, economy drift, and the downward shift of threshold after a set work dose. Proposed drivers include glycogen availability, mitochondrial and fat-oxidation capacity, muscle damage and neuromuscular fatigue, thermal and hydration strain, and fuelling — the relative weighting of these is still debated. It appears to be trained by long aerobic exposure, pre-fatigued quality work, and repeated station-run coupling.
key_facts: Durability = fatigue resistance of physiological qualities, not a separate energy system → fresh VO2max/threshold values overstate late-race capacity.

Common field metric: aerobic decoupling (Pa:HR or Pw:HR) = % drift in pace-per-beat between first and second half of a steady effort; <5% is a widely used practitioner rule of thumb for good durability, not a validated diagnostic threshold.

The durability construct was formalised mainly in cycling, where it is typically probed after a prior-work dose of roughly 1500–3000 kJ; running and hybrid work has no equivalent standard, so use time-under-load or a fixed pre-fatigue block instead.

Threshold pace/power can shift downward after heavy prior work — treat fresh threshold as a ceiling, not a target for the closing runs. The size of the shift is individual and must be measured, not assumed.
Economy tends to degrade with fatigue: ↑ metabolic cost at the same speed via altered kinematics, ↑ ventilatory cost, ↑ core temp, ↓ tendon stiffness/reactivity.

HYROX-specific: the race is 8 × 1 km runs alternating with 8 stations in fixed order — SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump, Row, Farmers Carry, Sandbag Lunges, Wall Balls. Run 1 is the only fresh run; runs 2–8 each start straight out of the Roxzone after a station.

Mapping stations to the run they precede: SkiErg → run 2, Sled Push → run 3, Sled Pull → run 4, Burpee Broad Jump → run 5, Row → run 6, Farmers Carry → run 7, Sandbag Lunges → run 8. Wall Balls closes the race with no run after it.
Because sled push and sled pull load the quads heavily, runs 3 and 4 are the classic split-penalty runs; sandbag lunges sit immediately before run 8, so lunge cost shows up in the final run.

Field measurement options: split degradation curve (run 1 → run 8 %), HR drift at fixed pace, a benchmark effort repeated late in a session, heart-rate recovery after a station, RPE at a fixed pace late in a session.

Training levers: long Z2 sessions (roughly 90–150 min), pre-fatigued quality (station block → threshold run), compromised-running blocks, back-to-back days, and occasionally low-CHO easy aerobic work — never low-CHO for hard sessions.

Fuelling supports durability: carbohydrate intake protects glycogen and helps preserve late pace. Around 60 g/h suits efforts of roughly 1–2 h; 90 g/h and above needs glucose plus fructose and a trained gut, and is aimed at longer work than a typical HYROX race.
Dehydration beyond about 2% body mass is associated with higher heart rate and greater cardiovascular strain, especially in heat; the size of any performance effect in the field is debated.
Periodisation: accumulated-fatigue and high-volume durability blocks belong in general/specific preparation, several weeks out, so adaptation can occur and fatigue can be dissipated before a taper.
22.training_link: Stop judging your athlete's HYROX ceiling from a fresh 5 km or a rested threshold test — test it late instead: after a 45–60 min station-plus-run block, have them repeat a 1 km at goal race-run pace and record HR, RPE and mechanics. Build durability with one compromised-running session a week (e.g. 6 rounds of [one station at race distance + 1 km run] at goal effort) plus a genuine 90–150 min Z2 day, fuelled well enough that the session trains durability rather than just depleting glycogen. Bias the station choice toward sled push and sled pull, since those feed runs 3 and 4, and rehearse sandbag lunges into run 8 at least once a block. Track decoupling and run-1-to-run-8 degradation monthly; falling drift at the same pace is your evidence the block worked.

glossary.def: The degree to which an athlete's physiological qualities (economy, threshold, power) resist deterioration after prolonged or accumulated work.

glossary.def: The percentage drift in the pace-per-heartbeat (or watts-per-heartbeat) ratio between the first and second half of a steady-state effort; a practical field index of durability.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="8" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 20h16M44 14l6 6-6 6" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="60" cy="20" r="5" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

glossary.def: The gradual rise in heart rate at a constant workload, associated with plasma-volume loss, rising core temperature and reduced stroke volume.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The increase in oxygen or metabolic cost of running at a fixed speed as fatigue accumulates, usually paired with degraded mechanics.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Deliberately placing a high-quality interval or threshold effort after a fatiguing block, so the target quality is trained in the state it must be expressed in.

glossary.def: Running immediately off a station under local muscular fatigue and disturbed breathing, replicating a HYROX Roxzone exit.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: The percentage slowdown from the fastest to the slowest race run, used as a field measure of pacing discipline and durability.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: A planned stretch of days or sessions where recovery is intentionally incomplete, to drive adaptation in the fatigued state before a taper restores freshness.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The transition area in a HYROX race between a run and a station; time spent in it counts toward the total, and it is where compromised running begins.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

22.exam_focus: Expect to be asked to define durability, calculate or interpret HR–pace decoupling from given data, identify which stations precede which runs, and prescribe a session that develops fatigue-resistant running specific to HYROX station-to-run transitions.

23.title: Energy availability & body composition
23.key_concept: Energy availability (EA) is the dietary energy left for physiological function after training is paid for, expressed per kg of fat-free mass: EA = (intake kcal − exercise energy expenditure kcal) / kg FFM. It is not the same as energy balance — an athlete can hold stable weight while chronically under-fuelling. Sustained low EA downregulates the hypothalamic-pituitary axis → suppressed sex hormones, low T3, blunted IGF-1, impaired bone remodelling, GI and immune disruption, mood and sleep decay. That syndrome is RED-S (the 2023 IOC consensus restyles it 'REDs'). In HYROX the trap is structural: high-volume running plus strength work raises exercise cost while athletes chase a lighter running weight, so EA falls exactly when repeated-effort power and sled work need it most.
key_facts: EA = (energy intake − exercise energy expenditure) ÷ fat-free mass (kcal/kg FFM/day).
Rough anchors: ~45 kcal/kg FFM/day ≈ optimal; ~30–45 = subclinical/reduced; <30 = low EA, the commonly cited risk threshold. Treat these as orientation, not diagnosis — response is individual.

Threshold caveat: the ~30 kcal/kg FFM/day figure comes largely from short-term laboratory work in young, regularly menstruating women. Male thresholds are much less well defined; men appear to tolerate somewhat lower EA before measurable endocrine disruption, so a 'normal' number never rules out a problem.
Weight stability ≠ adequate EA — the body defends mass by downregulating RMR, NEAT and endocrine output.
RED-S = syndrome of impaired function from problematic low EA; broadens the older female-athlete-triad model (energy deficiency, menstrual dysfunction, low BMD) to many more systems and to men.

Endocrine markers: ↓LH pulsatility, ↓oestrogen/testosterone, ↓T3, ↓IGF-1; amenorrhoea/oligomenorrhoea in women, low libido + low free testosterone in men. Cortisol often rises, though this finding is less consistent than the others.
Systems affected extend beyond reproduction: bone, metabolic/thyroid, immune, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular (unfavourable lipid and endothelial changes), and psychological.
Bone: ↓formation with maintained/↑resorption → ↓BMD, ↑stress-fracture risk; running-dominant HYROX loading amplifies exposure.
Performance costs: ↓glycogen, ↓power and repeated-sprint ability, ↓training adaptation, ↑illness/injury days, slower recovery between sessions.
Low EA is often unintentional — appetite suppression post-run, high training volume, busy schedules — not necessarily disordered eating.
HYROX body-comp trade-off: excess mass costs on 8 km of running; too little lean mass costs on sled push/pull, carries and wall balls → target lean mass retention, not minimum weight.

Time deliberate body-composition change to a general-preparation/off-season block with lower training volume and a modest deficit (a commonly used rate is ~0.5–1% body mass per week), not to a race-specific block where session quality and recovery are the priority.

Coaches screen and refer; they do not diagnose or prescribe clinical treatment. LEAF-Q is a validated athlete-facing screening questionnaire for women. The RED-S CAT is a clinician's assessment and return-to-play tool — know it exists, but it is not a coach's instrument.
23.training_link: When an athlete's sled push times, wall-ball unbroken sets or compromised-running splits stall while bodyweight is drifting down, treat it as an energy-availability question before you touch the programme. Estimate EA over a normal training week, and ask directly about menstrual status, sleep, libido, mood, GI symptoms and any stress-fracture history. Then fix the easy structural gaps first: carbohydrate before and immediately after run-heavy sessions, and a genuine post-session feed that survives contact with a busy day rather than getting skipped. Keep body-composition talk framed as retaining lean mass for the sleds and carries, schedule any intentional deficit into a low-volume general-preparation block, and refer to a sports physician or registered dietitian whenever red flags appear — you screen, they diagnose.

glossary.def: Dietary energy remaining after exercise energy expenditure, normalised to fat-free mass. The fuel actually left for growth, repair, immunity and reproduction.

glossary.def: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport — the cluster of endocrine, bone, metabolic, cardiovascular, GI, immune, psychological and performance impairments arising from problematic LEA in either sex. The 2023 IOC consensus statement writes it 'REDs'.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Total body mass minus fat mass; the metabolically active denominator used to normalise EA between athletes of different sizes.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Energy cost of purposeful training above what the athlete would have expended at rest for that same period.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M14 12v18M14 12h12" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M30 30c8-2 16-10 30-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: Loss of menses driven by suppressed GnRH/LH pulsatility under energy deficit, rather than by a structural or primary endocrine disease.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Long hours spent in a large energy gap during the day even when 24-hour totals look adequate; observational work associates this pattern with hormonal disruption independently of daily totals.

glossary.def: Force or power output per kg body mass — the metric that matters for sled and carry stations relative to running economy trade-offs.

glossary.def: Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire; a validated screening instrument covering GI symptoms, injury history and menstrual function to flag risk for referral.

glossary.def: RED-S Clinical Assessment Tool — a clinician-operated risk-stratification and return-to-play framework (red/amber/green). Referenced here so coaches recognise it, not so they administer it.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

23.exam_focus: Calculating energy availability from intake, exercise expenditure and fat-free mass, then interpreting the result against LEA thresholds — including their limits, especially in male athletes — and choosing the correct coach-scope action: screen and refer, not diagnose.

24.title: Carbohydrate periodization & fuelling
24.key_concept: Carbohydrate periodization means matching daily and per-session carbohydrate intake to the fuel cost of the work, rather than eating a flat number all week. Carbohydrate becomes the dominant and effectively rate-limiting fuel as intensity rises toward and above threshold, so high-glycolytic HYROX sessions (race sims, compromised-run intervals, sled work) demand high availability, while easy aerobic or technical days can run leaner. Protein stays high and evenly spread to defend adaptation under concurrent stress; fat fills the remaining energy and supports hormonal function and fat-soluble vitamin absorption. Deliberate low-carbohydrate-availability training appears to amplify some mitochondrial signalling, but the evidence that it improves actual performance is inconsistent, and it reliably degrades session intensity — so it is a small, targeted tool, never the default. Race day is always fuelled high.
key_facts: Daily CHO scales with load (Burke-style tiers): light/technical ~3–5 g/kg → moderate (~1 h/day) ~5–7 → hard, high-volume (1–3 h/day) ~6–10 → very high double-day or carb-loading ~8–12 g/kg.
Protein for concurrent (strength + endurance) training ~1.6–2.2 g/kg/day, split into 4–5 feeds of ~0.3–0.4 g/kg; leucine-rich sources post-session.

Fat = remainder of energy; a common practical floor is ~0.5–1.0 g/kg/day (endocrine function, fat-soluble vitamins, essential fatty acids, satiety) — when energy must drop, trim carbs on easy days first rather than dropping fat to near zero.
Muscle glycogen ~300–500 g in a trained athlete — commonly described as enough for roughly 60–90 min of hard continuous work, so a HYROX race sits at or beyond the edge of a single tank.

HYROX format context: 8 × 1 km runs alternating with 8 stations in fixed order — SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump, Row, Farmers Carry, Sandbag Lunges, Wall Balls. Elite finishers are around 55–65 min; typical Open finishers land roughly 75–110 min, so fuelling plans must cover well past the 60 min mark.
Pre-session: ~1–4 g/kg CHO taken 1–4 h out; the closer to the start, the smaller, lower-fibre and lower-fat the feed.

During: <45–60 min → generally none needed (mouth rinse optional); ~1–2.5 h → ~30–60 g/h; >2.5–3 h → up to ~90 g/h using multi-transportable carbohydrate (glucose:fructose, classically 2:1, with 1:0.8 favoured in more recent work).

Post-session, when the recovery window is short (<8 h): ~1.0–1.2 g/kg/h CHO for the first ~4 h plus ~0.3 g/kg protein; with 24 h or more to recover, total daily intake matters far more than precise timing.

Carb-loading before a race: ~8–12 g/kg/day for 24–48 h with reduced training and low fibre; expect ~1–2 kg of associated water-weight gain (glycogen is stored with roughly 3 g water per gram, though estimates vary).

'Train low' variants: sleep-low/train-low, fasted easy aerobic, and a low-availability second session of a double day. Documented downsides: reduced session intensity, higher RPE, increased muscle protein breakdown, and — if repeated chronically — drift into low energy availability and RED-S, with associated immune and bone consequences.

Gut training: rehearse the exact race-day carb rate and product in sims — tolerance for high hourly intakes is trainable over roughly 2–6 weeks. Corollary rules: never train low on a quality session, and never compete low.
24.training_link: For your HYROX athlete, tier the week: high-carb days on race sims, compromised-run intervals and heavy sled sessions; moderate on easy aerobic or skill days; keep protein flat at ~1.8–2 g/kg every day regardless. Because a typical Open race runs roughly 75–110 min with heavy glycolytic loading at the sled push and pull, burpee broad jumps and wall balls, treat it as a genuine in-race fuelling event rather than a short effort: drill a ~1–2 g/kg low-fibre breakfast 2–3 h out, ~30 g CHO in the last 30 min pre-start, and at least one rehearsed gel or drink mid-race (check current event rules on carrying personal nutrition, and use the roxzone water stations). If you use train-low at all, restrict it to an easy morning run inside a base block, and pull it entirely in race week.

glossary.def: Planned day-to-day and session-to-session variation of carbohydrate intake so availability matches the fuel demand and adaptive goal of each session.

glossary.def: Strategy of performing selected low-intensity sessions with reduced carbohydrate availability to target mitochondrial adaptation, while all hard sessions and races are fully fuelled. Signalling effects are well demonstrated; performance benefits remain equivocal.

glossary.def: A glucose plus fructose blend that uses two separate intestinal transporters (SGLT1 and GLUT5), raising the ceiling of usable carbohydrate per hour above the ~60 g/h limit of glucose alone.

glossary.def: Short-term high-carbohydrate intake combined with reduced training that raises muscle glycogen above normal resting levels before a race.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M32 8h16l-3 26a5 5 0 0 1-10 0Z" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 22h12" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Attenuation of strength or hypertrophy adaptation when endurance work is added; associated with low energy and carbohydrate availability, and mitigated by adequate fuel, protein and session spacing.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Energy intake minus exercise energy expenditure, expressed per kg fat-free mass, falling too low to support normal physiological function — commonly operationalised as below ~30 kcal/kg FFM/day. LEA is the underlying driver of RED-S.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M14 12v18M14 12h12" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M30 30c8-2 16-10 30-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: Progressive rehearsal of race-day carbohydrate ingestion rates in training to improve absorption capacity and reduce gastrointestinal distress.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Apparent performance benefit from swilling a carbohydrate solution without swallowing, attributed to oral receptors and central drive rather than substrate delivery. Effects are small and most consistent when the athlete is fasted or glycogen-low.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

24.exam_focus: Matching a daily carbohydrate target (g/kg) and around-session fuelling plan to a described training day, and stating why train-low is restricted to easy sessions while competition is always fuelled high.

25.title: Hydration & electrolytes
25.key_concept: Hydration status is a performance variable, not a comfort variable.
