Sweat rate and sweat sodium concentration are highly individual and must be measured, not assumed — body-mass change across a controlled session is the practical field tool. Losses beyond roughly 2% of body mass are generally where thermoregulation, cardiac output and perceived effort start to suffer, with the cost rising as the deficit grows and as heat and humidity climb; the exact threshold is dose-dependent and debated in real-world settings, so treat 2% as a planning guideline rather than a cliff edge. The opposite error — drinking large volumes of plain hypotonic fluid — dilutes serum sodium and risks exercise-associated hyponatraemia. The coaching target is euhydration entering the race, drinking to a rehearsed plan with sodium during it, and deliberate rehydration after.
key_facts: Sweat rate (L/h) = (pre-BM − post-BM + fluid in − urine out) ÷ hours; 1 kg BM ≈ 1 L fluid.
Typical exercising sweat rates 0.5–2.0 L/h; large/hot/hard athletes can exceed 2.5 L/h.
Sweat sodium highly variable, ~20–80 mmol/L (≈0.5–1.8 g Na per litre); 'salty sweaters' sit at the top end.
Around 2% BM loss and beyond → ↓ plasma volume, ↑ HR at fixed work, ↑ RPE, ↑ core temp; effects are graded (worse as deficit grows) and magnified in heat/humidity.

Pre-event (ACSM-style staged loading): ~5–7 mL/kg at least 4 h before, plus a further ~3–5 mL/kg about 2 h out if urine is dark or absent; take it with sodium/food, aim for pale-yellow urine, then a 200–300 mL top-up near the start.

During: drink toward — not necessarily matching — sweat rate; commonly 0.4–0.8 L/h, and as a safety cap do not routinely exceed measured sweat rate. Typical commercial sports drinks carry only ~10–25 mmol/L Na (≈0.2–0.6 g/L); dedicated high-sodium formulations run ~30–50+ mmol/L and suit salty sweaters or hot halls.
Post: replace ~125–150% of the deficit over 2–4 h WITH sodium — sodium drives retention; plain water → diuresis.
EAH = serum Na <135 mmol/L; cause is fluid overload relative to sodium, not sodium deficiency. Red flags: nausea, headache, confusion, bloating, weight GAIN.
Indoor HYROX venues: high humidity, crowded, low airflow → ↑ sweat rate, ↓ evaporative cooling; do NOT plan from cool-gym training data.

Race window runs from roughly 55–60 min for elites to well over 2 h for slower age-group finishers: EAH risk is low but real in the slowest finishers who over-drink; hypohydration is the more common practical limiter.
25.training_link: Have your athlete do a naked pre/post weigh-in on two or three race-pace sessions — one in your normal gym, one deliberately in the hottest, stillest conditions you can find — logging fluid drunk to get a real L/h number rather than a guess. Build the race plan around that: fixed sodium-containing sips at specific roxzones (e.g. after the sled pull and after the row) rather than 'drink when thirsty', and rehearse it in every simulation so the gut is trained and the timing is automatic. Then check white salt marks on kit and any history of cramping or brain fog — those athletes get a higher-sodium drink and pre-load, not just more water. Note that the cramping link is suggestive rather than proven, so treat it as one input among several, not a diagnosis.

glossary.def: The normal, balanced state of body water — neither meaningfully depleted nor overloaded. The target state at the start line.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M32 8h16l-3 26a5 5 0 0 1-10 0Z" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 22h12" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Fluid lost per hour of exercise, estimated from body-mass change corrected for what was drunk and any urine passed.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M32 8h16l-3 26a5 5 0 0 1-10 0Z" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 22h12" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: How much sodium each litre of sweat carries. Largely individual and partly genetic, modestly reduced by heat acclimation, and the reason two athletes with identical sweat rates need different sodium plans.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M32 8h16l-3 26a5 5 0 0 1-10 0Z" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 22h12" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Serum sodium below 135 mmol/L during or shortly after exercise, usually from drinking more fluid than is being lost. Ranges from mild nausea to cerebral or pulmonary oedema.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The tendency to drink less than is being lost because thirst lags behind actual fluid deficit, especially during hard intermittent work.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M32 8h16l-3 26a5 5 0 0 1-10 0Z" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 22h12" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A body-water deficit relative to normal; expressed as a percentage of pre-exercise body mass lost.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M32 8h16l-3 26a5 5 0 0 1-10 0Z" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 22h12" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The proportion of an ingested fluid still retained some hours after drinking rather than urinated out — improved by sodium, by co-ingested food, and by drinking steadily rather than in large boluses.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M32 8h16l-3 26a5 5 0 0 1-10 0Z" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 22h12" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Adaptation to repeated heat exposure: plasma volume expands, sweating starts earlier and becomes somewhat more dilute, and core temp and HR fall at a given workload.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The HYROX transition area between each run and the following station — in practice the only realistic place to take on fluid mid-race.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

25.exam_focus: Calculating sweat rate from pre/post body mass and translating it into an individualised fluid-and-sodium plan, while correctly distinguishing dehydration from exercise-associated hyponatraemia.

26.title: Race-day nutrition & supplements
26.key_concept: A HYROX race (8 x 1 km runs alternating with 8 stations — SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump, Row, Farmers Carry, Sandbag Lunges, Wall Balls) is a continuous near-threshold effort lasting roughly 60 min for elites to well over 2 h for many age-groupers. Because of that, fuelling aims to have muscle glycogen full at the gun rather than relying on heavy mid-race feeding. Build a high-carbohydrate final 24-36 h (~7-12 g/kg/day, low fibre), then a low-fibre, low-fat, familiar meal ~3-4 h out (~1-3 g/kg CHO) plus an optional small top-up 30-60 min pre-start. Intra-race intake is constrained by grip, breathing and gut tolerance: under ~75 min, fluid or a CHO mouth rinse is usually enough; longer finishing times justify ~30-60 g/h if it has been gut-trained. Supplements with genuine evidence — caffeine, creatine, beta-alanine, nitrate, bicarbonate — are dose- and timing-dependent, vary a lot between individuals, must be rehearsed in advance, and nothing novel appears on race day.
key_facts: Carb-load final 24-36 h: ~7-12 g/kg/day, low fibre. Tops up muscle glycogen without gut load; no depletion phase needed. Expect ~1-2 kg of water-bound weight gain.
Pre-race meal ~3-4 h out: ~1-3 g/kg CHO, low fat, low fibre, low-moderate protein, familiar foods only.
Optional top-up 30-60 min pre-start: ~20-30 g easily digested CHO + sips of fluid. Reactive ('rebound') hypoglycaemia is uncommon, transient, and rarely impairs performance.

Intra-race: sub-75 min finishers → fluid and/or CHO mouth rinse is usually sufficient; longer finishing times → ~30-60 g/h if gut-trained. Practical intake windows are the roxzone and the runs, not the stations. Start euhydrated (~5-7 ml/kg fluid, 2-4 h pre). Sweat rate = (pre-weight − post-weight + fluid in − urine) ÷ hours.

Caffeine: 3-6 mg/kg, ~45-60 min pre (lower doses, or gum/mouth forms, work closer to the start). Well-supported for endurance and repeated high-intensity work, but response varies widely; higher doses raise HR, jitters, GI and sleep-disruption risk without adding benefit.

Creatine monohydrate: 3-5 g/day chronic, or ~20 g/day for 5-7 d to load. Benefits repeat-effort and strength qualities. Loading in race week does raise phosphocreatine, but it also adds ~1-2 kg body mass in a running-heavy race and has not been rehearsed — treat it as a base-phase project, not a race-week lever.

Beta-alanine: 3.2-6.4 g/day in split doses for 4+ weeks (commonly 4-12) raises muscle carnosine, an intracellular buffer for efforts of roughly 30 s to 10 min. Chronic only — there is no acute race-day dose. Split or sustained-release dosing limits paraesthesia.

Dietary nitrate (beetroot): commonly ~5-9 mmol NO3− (~310-560 mg) taken ~2-3 h pre; some studies use up to ~13 mmol. Modestly lowers the O2 cost of submaximal work; effects are smaller and less consistent in highly trained athletes. Avoid antibacterial mouthwash, which kills the oral bacteria that reduce nitrate.

Sodium bicarbonate: ~0.2-0.3 g/kg, ~60-180 min pre (time-to-peak varies a lot between individuals) to raise extracellular buffering. High GI-distress risk → split doses taken with a CHO-rich meal, or serial loading, and rehearse it before ever using it in competition.

Gut training: practise the exact race-day CHO rate and product in key sessions over 2-6+ weeks to improve intestinal transport capacity and gastric tolerance, reducing GI symptoms. Nothing new on race day — food, supplement, dose or brand.
26.training_link: Lock the race-day fuel plan 4-6 weeks out and rehearse it in every simulation — same wake time, same pre-race meal, same gel at the same roxzone, same caffeine dose. Weigh the athlete before and after a hard sim to get a real sweat rate instead of guessing. Schedule chronic supplements (creatine, beta-alanine) as base-block projects, not race-week fixes, and expect individual responses to differ. If you are trialling bicarbonate, test it in at least two hard sessions — and find that athlete's own timing — before it goes anywhere near a start line.

glossary.def: A short high-CHO, low-fibre phase (~24-36 h is enough for a sub-2 h event) that maximises muscle and liver glycogen before competition. Modern protocols need no depletion phase.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M32 8h16l-3 26a5 5 0 0 1-10 0Z" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 22h12" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Deliberate, progressive practice of race-day fuelling in training so the gut tolerates and absorbs the intended carbohydrate rate. Adaptation is trainable and largely product-specific.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Swilling a carbohydrate solution briefly without swallowing. Stimulates oral receptors linked to central drive and perceived effort; most useful in shorter efforts where absorption is not the limiter, and the effect appears smaller in a well-fed athlete.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Raising blood bicarbonate so H+ leaves the working muscle faster, delaying intramuscular acidosis in high-intensity efforts of roughly 1-10 minutes.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 30h52" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="14" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="30" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#ffb86b"/><rect x="46" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

glossary.def: Chronic beta-alanine intake that raises muscle carnosine, an intracellular buffer. The effect builds over weeks and washes out slowly; a single dose does nothing acutely.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Dietary nitrate is reduced by oral bacteria to nitrite and then to nitric oxide, which is associated with improved blood flow and contractile efficiency, with the largest effects reported in type II fibres.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Fluid lost per hour of exercise, estimated from body-mass change corrected for fluid drunk and urine passed. Used to individualise race-day drinking rather than drinking to a generic number.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M32 8h16l-3 26a5 5 0 0 1-10 0Z" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 22h12" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The HYROX transition area an athlete crosses between the running track and each station. Practically, the most reliable and repeatable place to take on fluid or a gel mid-race.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The principle that no food, drink, supplement, dose or brand is used in competition unless it has already been rehearsed successfully in training.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 30h52" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="14" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="30" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#ffb86b"/><rect x="46" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

26.exam_focus: Matching each supplement to its correct dose, timing and acute-vs-chronic classification, and applying pre-race meal timing, sweat-rate estimation and the gut-training/no-novelty principles to a specific HYROX athlete scenario.

27.title: Motor learning & skill acquisition
27.page_refs: Embedding Skills in Athletes for HYROX Performance
27.key_concept: Motor learning is the set of practice-driven processes that produce a relatively permanent change in the capability for skilled movement — distinct from performance, which is what you observe on the day and is confounded by fatigue, arousal and the feedback currently being given. Athletes are commonly described as passing through cognitive (large errors, heavy attentional demand, verbal-motor problem solving), associative (errors shrinking, refinement, self-detection emerging) and autonomous (largely automated, low attentional cost, more robust under load) stages; these are descriptive phases on a continuum, not sharp thresholds, and the autonomous stage requires extensive practice that many athletes never fully reach for complex skills. Transfer is governed by specificity: skills carry over to the extent practice matches the competition's coordination pattern, load, tempo and — critically for HYROX — its fatigue and decision context. Practice conditions that feel worse (variable, random, distributed, reduced-frequency feedback) tend to depress acute performance while improving retention and transfer. Fatigue degrades coordination and the athlete's own error detection, so new patterns are best taught fresh and stress-proofed later.
key_facts: Learning = durable capability change, inferred from delayed retention + transfer tests; performance = what you see today, contaminated by fatigue/arousal/feedback.
Fitts & Posner stages: cognitive → associative → autonomous; across stages automation ↑, attentional demand ↓, within-athlete movement variability ↓. Treat them as a continuum, not discrete levels.
Autonomous stage frees attention → the athlete can pace, count reps and read the roxzone instead of thinking about the movement itself.
Blocked/constant practice: ↑ acute performance, typically ↓ retention. Random/variable practice: ↓ acute, typically ↑ retention + transfer — the contextual interference effect.

The contextual interference benefit is moderated by skill level and task complexity: rank novices and very complex tasks often need blocked practice first, with randomisation introduced once a basic pattern exists.
Feedback: high-frequency or concurrent KP can create dependency on the external signal (the guidance hypothesis). Faded, bandwidth, summary and self-controlled feedback generally favour retention.
External focus cues ("drive the floor away", "send the ball to the target") tend to outperform internal body-part cues for both output and retention, though effect sizes vary by task and expertise.
Specificity of transfer: carryover scales with shared coordination pattern, velocity, load and physiological state — practising skills only when fresh under-prepares race execution.

Fatigue effects: ↓ proprioceptive acuity, ↓ force control, altered joint kinematics, ↓ ability to detect one's own errors → new motor programs are encoded poorly, and injury risk rises, under high fatigue.
Practical rule: acquire technique at low fatigue early in the session; stress-test an already-acquired skill under fatigue later.

Cognitive-stage athletes need a demonstration, a clear reference model and very few cues (a common coaching heuristic is one cue per set); autonomous athletes generally respond better to task constraints and environment design than to more verbal instruction.
27.training_link: Teach any new HYROX pattern — burpee broad jump rhythm, sandbag lunge stride, wall ball catch-to-squat timing — early in the session, before meaningful fatigue accumulates, using one external cue at a time and letting the athlete self-report errors before you correct them. Keep early reps blocked and low-volume until the basic pattern exists, then introduce variability and mixed ordering. Once the pattern is reliable, deliberately relocate it behind a hard run or a sled so you can see whether it survives race fatigue; that fatigued rehearsal is skill-proofing, not skill-teaching. If technique holds when fresh and collapses only under load, the limiter is capacity or pacing rather than motor learning, and your intervention should shift accordingly.

glossary.def: Practice-driven processes producing a relatively permanent improvement in the capability to produce a movement. Assessed by retention and transfer, not by a single good session.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="7" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 14h28M34 20h22M34 26h16" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Observable movement quality/output at one moment in time. It can rise or fall from fatigue, arousal or feedback without any underlying change in learning.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The learning benefit from mixing tasks or variants within a practice block rather than repeating one. It slows in-session performance but typically improves retention and transfer; the effect is smaller or reversed for true novices on complex tasks.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Prior practice on one task improving a target task, driven by shared coordination pattern, load, velocity and context.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.term: Knowledge of results (KR) / knowledge of performance (KP)
glossary.def: KR is feedback about the outcome (time, reps, metres); KP is feedback about how the movement was executed (technique).
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The explanation that frequent or concurrent feedback guides performance in the moment but blocks development of the athlete's own error-detection, so learning suffers once feedback is withdrawn.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A practitioner label (not a formal textbook term) for deliberately rehearsing an already-acquired skill in a pre-fatigued state so technique holds at race-relevant physiological cost.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M14 12v18M14 12h12" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M30 30c8-2 16-10 30-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: Directing attention to the movement's effect on the environment or implement rather than to body segments, which typically improves both output and retention.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The final described learning stage where execution is largely automatic, error rate is low, and spare attention is available for pacing, tactics and self-regulation. Reached only after extensive practice.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A delayed re-test after a practice block, conducted without feedback, used to separate genuine learning from temporary performance boosts.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: A test of the skill in a novel or race-relevant condition (different load, tempo or fatigue state) used to check whether the learning generalises beyond the practice context.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

27.exam_focus: Expect to be asked to justify when to coach technique versus when to load it — applying the learning-versus-performance distinction, the guidance hypothesis and fatigue's effect on skill acquisition to a specific HYROX station scenario.

28.title: Practice design — blocked, random & variable
28.page_refs: Embedding Skills in Athletes for HYROX Performance
28.key_concept: How you schedule practice matters as much as how much you do. Blocked practice (AAA BBB) builds fast within-session gains but weaker retention; random/interleaved practice (ABC BCA) feels worse in-session yet typically produces better retention and transfer — the contextual interference effect. Its mechanism is still debated: the two long-standing explanations are that interleaving forces the motor plan to be forgotten and reconstructed each trial, and that it invites richer inter-task comparison and elaboration. The effect is not universal — it is most reliable in relatively skilled learners on moderately complex tasks, and can shrink or reverse in true novices or on very complex skills, so match the difficulty of the schedule to the athlete's current competence. Constant practice fixes one parameter set; variable practice samples loads, speeds and grips, widening the generalised motor programme so novel race conditions are covered. Part practice suits low-organisation, high-complexity skills; whole practice suits high-organisation continuous skills. For HYROX, transfer demands practising stations pre-fatigued, in race order, with race-standard cues.
key_facts: Blocked = high acquisition, lower retention; random = depressed acquisition, better retention + transfer (contextual interference).
The contextual interference mechanism is contested — forgetting-and-reconstruction and elaboration/inter-task comparison are competing explanations, not settled fact.

Contextual interference is conditional, not automatic: strongest for competent learners on moderately complex tasks, weak or reversed in novices and on very complex skills — scale schedule difficulty to the athlete.
Performance during practice ≠ learning — judge by delayed retention/transfer tests, not session-day scores.
Learning progression: blocked → serial → random as competence rises; novices need some blocked exposure first.
Constant practice = one parameter (fixed load/pace); variable practice = many parameters → broader motor schema.

Vary the parameters that genuinely differ between venues and race days (sled load, flooring friction under the sled, sandbag shape and placement, rope thickness, footwear/surface), not the movement standard itself — standards such as wall-ball target height are fixed by division and must be trained at spec, never varied.
Part practice fits low-organisation/high-complexity skills (sled pull hand-over-hand); whole practice fits continuous high-organisation ones (SkiErg, row, run).
Progressive part / whole-part-whole beats isolated drilling that never rejoins the full skill.
Specificity: transfer ↑ when practice matches race context — fatigue state, roxzone entry, footwear, surface, noise.
Fatigued practice must be technique-gated: stop the set when the movement standard breaks, or you groove the fault.
Random ≠ chaotic — session order is planned; only the athlete's expectancy is randomised. Short blocked blocks still repair a named fault.
28.training_link: Stop letting your athletes drill wall balls fresh in tidy sets of 20 — that is blocked, constant, unfatigued practice, and it flatters them. Once the standard is clean, interleave: 400 m run → 15 wall balls → 100 m sandbag lunges → 200 m farmers carry, rotated in an order they cannot predict, with sled loads varied around race spec and the wall-ball target held at division height. Keep short blocked corrections in the warm-up for one named fault, then hand the skill back to a fatigued, race-ordered environment and cut the set the moment depth or catch position degrades. For a genuine novice, resist the urge to interleave immediately — build a repeatable pattern in blocks first, or the added schedule difficulty just buys you worse reps.

glossary.def: The learning benefit that arises when practice trials are interleaved rather than repeated in blocks. It typically slows acquisition but improves long-term retention and transfer, most reliably in learners who already have a workable movement pattern.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: All repetitions of one task completed before moving to the next. Produces rapid, often misleading within-session improvement.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="24" width="10" height="10" fill="#5ec8ff"/><rect x="24" y="18" width="10" height="16" fill="#5ec8ff" opacity=".8"/><rect x="38" y="12" width="10" height="22" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="52" y="20" width="10" height="14" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Tasks rotated unpredictably so the athlete must rebuild the motor plan each trial. Lower session performance, better retention.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="7" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 14h28M34 20h22M34 26h16" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Repeating one skill class while varying its parameters — load, tempo, distance, implement — to widen the generalised motor programme.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="7" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 14h28M34 20h22M34 26h16" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A stored movement pattern whose invariant structure (order of elements, relative timing, relative force) is fixed but whose parameters (overall force, overall duration, amplitude) are scaled to the demand at hand.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Breaking a skill into components trained separately, then reintegrated. Best for skills with distinct, weakly interdependent parts.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="7" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 14h28M34 20h22M34 26h16" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Rehearsing the skill in full. Preferred for continuous, highly organised actions where segmenting destroys the rhythm.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="7" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 14h28M34 20h22M34 26h16" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The degree to which practised capability carries into a different context — for HYROX, into deep fatigue on competition equipment.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A delayed re-test after a rest interval, used to measure learning rather than temporary practice-day performance.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

28.exam_focus: Recognising that blocked/constant practice inflates session performance while random/variable practice under race-like fatigue drives retention and transfer — knowing the boundary conditions that limit contextual interference — and applying that to schedule HYROX station work correctly.

29.title: Technical progressions & regressions
29.page_refs: Embedding Skills in Athletes for HYROX Performance
29.key_concept: A progression is a ladder of movement variants that share the target motor pattern but differ in load, range, speed, stability, or complexity. The coach's job is picking the entry rung — the hardest version the athlete can own with acceptable technique for the intended work duration — then advancing on observable criteria rather than on the calendar alone. Regression is the same ladder used downward: when fatigue degrades a station pattern mid-set, drop a rung (lighter load, shorter range, smaller set size) rather than accumulate reps in broken positions. Repeatedly practising a degraded version of a pattern is poor motor-learning practice, and form breakdown under fatigue is generally regarded as an injury-risk factor; in HYROX it also has a direct time cost, since a judge can no-rep sub-standard reps and the athlete must repeat them.
key_facts: Entry point = hardest variant executed to standard for the full intended work duration, not for one clean rep.

A workable ordering of progression variables, from gentler to more aggressive: stability → range of motion → load → velocity/density → volume → complexity. This is a practical coaching sequence, not a validated scientific hierarchy — the point is to move one variable at a time.

Progress on observable criteria rather than dates. A common working rule of thumb: standard met on roughly 90%+ of reps across 2–3 consecutive sessions, with RPE trending down at a fixed load. The exact percentage is a coaching convention, not a research-derived cut-off — set it explicitly and apply it consistently.

Fatigue-resistance criterion is HYROX-specific: technique must hold at race intensity and after a 1 km run, not only when fresh. Race intensity for most athletes sits around threshold, but the exact zone varies with fitness and finish time — test it, don't assume it.
Regress in-set, don't grind: 2–3 consecutive reps off-standard → cut the set, shed load/range, or shorten the set.

Wall ball ladder: box squat to target → squat + med-ball press (no throw) → lighter ball to target height → race ball at target height → sets of 10+ under fatigue. Wall balls are the eighth and final station (100 reps), so fatigue tolerance matters more here than anywhere else.
Burpee broad jump ladder: step-back burpee + step forward → burpee + short 2-foot hop → full burpee broad jump → pacing it over the full 80 m.
Sandbag lunge ladder: split squat → bodyweight walking lunge (knee touch) → light front-rack/back sandbag → race bag over the full 100 m.

Sled ladder: load is the main regression dial — cut sled weight in training to keep hip angle, stride length and continuous drive intact, then rebuild load. Note that race-day sled loads are fixed by division, so the regression is a training tool, not a race option.
Ski/Row ladder: technique at low damper/low stroke rate → rate-controlled intervals → race pace → race pace with elevated HR.
Standards drive the rungs: only a rep that would count at the judging standard counts as a rep in training.

Station order is fixed (SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump, Row, Farmers Carry, Sandbag Lunges, Wall Balls) with a 1 km run before each — so every station must be rehearsed pre-fatigued, and the later the station sits in the order, the more fatigue-resistant its progression criterion should be.
29.training_link: Pick each athlete's entry rung by watching them under fatigue, not fresh — run them 800 m first, then test the station variant. Write the progression criterion on the whiteboard before the block starts (e.g. "3 x 15 wall balls to standard at race ball, post-run, two sessions running") so advancing is a decision the athlete can see coming. Coach a named regression cue during sessions — "lighter ball", "sets of 8", "knee touch only" — so dropping a rung reads as executing the plan, not failing it. Weight the fatigue testing toward the back half of the station order, where accumulated fatigue is greatest.

glossary.def: An ordered sequence of movement variants that increase demand toward a full station movement while preserving the same underlying pattern.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A deliberately easier variant used as an entry point for a novice or as a mid-set fallback when fatigue starts to break technique.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The rung of the ladder an athlete starts on — the most demanding variant they can perform to standard for the whole intended work bout.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A pre-set, observable pass/fail rule (rep quality, range, tempo, RPE) that must be met before advancing a rung.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The point in a set where the movement standard is lost, distinct from muscular failure; the trigger to regress rather than continue.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Ability to hold the movement standard when pre-fatigued — after running, at race intensity. Fresh competence is necessary but not sufficient; this is the version of skill that has to survive on race day.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Changing only one demand (load OR range OR speed OR volume) per progression step, so cause and effect stay readable.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 30h52" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="14" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="30" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#ffb86b"/><rect x="46" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

glossary.def: The race-day cost of drilling sub-standard reps: a judge can reject them, forcing the athlete to repeat reps and lose time at the station.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The transition area athletes pass through between the running track and each station; time spent there counts toward the total, so inefficient technique upstream shows up as slower, longer transitions.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

29.exam_focus: Given an athlete breaking down on a specific station, select the correct entry-point or in-set regression and justify it with an objective progression criterion rather than a time frame.

30.title: Gait cycle & running mechanics
30.page_refs: Running Biomechanics and Technique for HYROX Performance
30.key_concept: Running gait is a cyclic alternation of stance and swing for each limb, with a flight phase separating single-leg supports — there is no double support, unlike walking. Stance runs initial contact → absorption/loading → midstance → propulsion → toe-off; swing runs toe-off → follow-through → forward swing → pre-contact. Elastic energy stored in the Achilles–triceps surae and plantar fascia during eccentric loading is partly reused via the stretch-shortening cycle, which lowers the metabolic cost of each stride. Ground contact time, vertical oscillation, cadence, step length and contact position relative to the centre of mass are the observable levers. In HYROX these tend to degrade under station-induced fatigue, so a coach should assess mechanics late in a session, not only when fresh.
key_facts: Gait cycle = stance + swing; running has a flight phase and no double support. Stance is roughly 30-40% of the cycle at moderate running speeds and falls toward ~20% at sprint speeds (speed-dependent, not a fixed value).
Stance sub-phases in order: initial contact → absorption/loading → midstance → propulsion → toe-off; the limb then swings through to the next contact.

Ground contact time is strongly speed-dependent. Rough guide at typical training/race paces: ~250-300 ms recreational, ~180-220 ms well-trained, under ~180 ms elite. Compare an athlete to themselves at matched pace, not to a table.

At a given speed, shorter ground contact tends to accompany better running economy. This is an association reported in the literature, not a proven cause — deliberately forcing shorter contacts does not reliably improve economy.
Vertical oscillation commonly falls around ~6-12 cm. Some is unavoidable (it creates flight time); excess adds work with no horizontal return.
Cadence for trained distance runners at race pace commonly sits around 165-185 steps/min, but it is individual and rises with speed. '180 spm' is a rule of thumb, not a target.
SSC = eccentric stretch → brief amortisation (coupling) → concentric shortening; elastic return falls off if the amortisation time is prolonged.
Speed = step length × step rate (equivalently stride length × stride rate, where one stride = two steps).
Under fatigue, step length typically shortens before cadence drops meaningfully — so pace loss late in a race is usually a step-length problem.
Overstriding = contact well ahead of the COM → larger braking impulse, higher loading, longer ground contact.
Coach checkpoints visible on video: contact position vs COM, pelvic drop in single-leg stance, trunk lean originating from the ankle vs hip flexion, arm/shoulder tension, foot crossover.
Foot-strike pattern alone is a weak predictor of economy or injury risk; contact position relative to the COM is the more meaningful variable. Assess fatigued gait, not just fresh gait.
30.training_link: Film your HYROX athlete twice — fresh, and immediately after a station such as the sandbag lunges (station 7, straight into the last run) or the sled push (station 2) — because the mechanics that break under fatigue are the ones that cost race time. Score the same checkpoints each time: contact position relative to the hip, pelvic drop, trunk lean, and cadence. Watch the size of the change rather than an absolute number: if cadence and step length fall away sharply over the later run legs while effort is unchanged, treat it as a durability problem to train rather than a technique flaw to cue. Program plyometrics and short hills to protect SSC quality, and rehearse the first 100 m out of every station so the athlete deliberately reloads the running pattern instead of shuffling.

glossary.def: The portion of the gait cycle for one limb from initial contact to toe-off, when the foot is loading the ground. It contains both the braking and the propulsive impulse.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The portion for a given limb from toe-off to its next initial contact, when that foot is off the ground (the body itself is airborne only during the flight phases). Largely driven by momentum and reflexive action rather than heavy voluntary effort.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Milliseconds the foot spends on the ground per step. At a matched speed, shorter contacts generally accompany stiffer, more elastic, more economical mechanics.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The up-and-down displacement of the centre of mass each stride. Some is required to create flight time; excess costs energy with no horizontal return.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Rapid eccentric loading of a muscle-tendon unit immediately followed by concentric action, reusing stored elastic energy and benefiting from reflex contributions. The benefit shrinks if the eccentric-to-concentric transition is slow.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The brief transition between the eccentric and concentric actions, conventionally described as near-isometric. Prolonging it lets stored elastic energy dissipate as heat.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Landing with the foot markedly ahead of the centre of mass, producing a larger braking impulse and longer ground contact. Usually addressed by nudging cadence up rather than by cueing the foot directly.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Steps per minute, counting both feet. Stride rate is half of this, since one stride = two steps. Cadence x step length determines speed; small cadence increases shorten the step and pull contact back under the COM.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: The spring-like resistance of the whole limb to compression during stance. More stiffness supports shorter contacts and better elastic return, but there is an individual optimum — very high stiffness raises impact loading, and tolerance has to be built gradually.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

30.exam_focus: Identifying gait-cycle phases and the SSC mechanism, then applying observable checkpoints (contact position, ground contact time, cadence, step length, vertical oscillation) to diagnose fatigue-driven mechanical breakdown in a HYROX athlete's later run legs.

31.title: Cadence, stride length & running economy
31.page_refs: Running Biomechanics and Technique for HYROX Performance
31.key_concept: Speed = cadence x stride length, so any pace can be produced by many combinations of the two. Most self-selected patterns sit close to the metabolically optimal combination for that individual, but fatigued or undertrained runners tend to drift toward long, low-cadence strides: the foot lands well ahead of the centre of mass with an extended knee, creating a larger horizontal braking impulse, longer ground-contact time and greater vertical oscillation. Raising cadence roughly 5-10% shortens the stride, brings footstrike closer under the hips, reduces braking and shifts load away from the knee and hip toward the ankle, calf and Achilles. Cadence cueing redistributes load; economy itself is improved mainly through heavy strength and plyometric training (tendon and leg-spring stiffness), not by a cue alone.
key_facts: Speed = cadence x stride length; cadence in steps/min (spm), stride length taken here as distance per step.
Typical observed range: recreational runners ~150-170 spm, well-trained/elite ~175-190+; '180 for everyone' is a myth — optimal cadence varies with speed, leg length and stature.
As pace increases, speed is gained mainly by lengthening the stride at low-to-moderate speeds; cadence becomes the dominant contributor only as the runner approaches near-maximal sprint speeds.
Overstriding = footstrike far ahead of COM with an extended knee → larger braking impulse, longer contact time, higher impact loading rate, poorer economy.
Cadence increased ~5-10% at a fixed pace → shorter stride, less vertical oscillation of the COM, lower patellofemoral and hip load; higher load per minute at the ankle/Achilles/calf.
Reducing cadence (longer stride) shifts load the other way — more knee and hip, less Achilles — which can be used deliberately when managing site-specific injury.
Running economy = the oxygen or energy cost of running at a given submaximal speed; among athletes matched for VO2max and lactate threshold, the more economical runner is generally faster.

Heavy resistance training (commonly ~80%+ 1RM) combined with plyometrics improves running economy in most trials by roughly 2-8% over about 6-14 weeks, attributed largely to greater tendon/leg stiffness and shorter ground-contact time, and typically without meaningful gains in body mass.
Shoe mass matters: economy cost is often estimated at roughly 1% per extra 100 g per shoe; modern carbon-plated 'super' shoes have been shown to improve economy by a few percent in lab testing.

Fatigue commonly degrades running form — cadence tends to fall while contact time and vertical oscillation rise (individual responses vary). HYROX running is nearly always performed pre-fatigued, so form under fatigue has to be trained, not assumed.
31.training_link: Give your athlete a re-entry cadence cue for the first 100-150 m out of every roxzone — a metronome or a counted 3-step rhythm — because cadence and posture are typically the first things to degrade after heavy stations such as the sled push and sandbag lunges, and a long, braking stride there costs seconds on each of the eight 1 km runs. Build the underlying economy separately: two heavy lower-body sessions per week (squat, deadlift, split squat in the ~80%+ 1RM range, low reps) plus short plyometrics performed on fresh legs. Reserve compromised-running work (station into 400-1000 m at race pace) for testing whether that form holds under fatigue. Progress cadence changes gradually — a 5-10% increase adds load to the Achilles and calf, so build it over weeks rather than in a single session, and screen for existing Achilles symptoms first.

glossary.def: Step frequency, usually expressed as steps per minute counting both legs. Halve it to get strides per minute, since one stride = two steps.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: The backward (decelerating) horizontal force applied over the early part of stance. It grows when the foot lands far ahead of the centre of mass.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 30h44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M30 30l0-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="26,34 34,34 30,28" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: The oxygen or energy cost of running at a fixed submaximal speed. Lower cost at the same pace means better economy.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: The ratio of peak force to how much the leg-spring compresses during stance. Higher stiffness means less compression for a given load, and is associated with shorter ground contact and better elastic energy return.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Time the foot spends on the ground each step. At a given pace, shorter GCT tends to accompany higher cadence and is often associated with better economy, though it is not a guarantee of it.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Up-and-down travel of the centre of mass per stride. Excess oscillation represents energy spent moving upward rather than forward.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Landing with the foot notably ahead of the hips and a relatively straight knee, producing a braking spike and, in most runners, a harder heel-first collision.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Running performed on pre-fatigued muscles immediately after a strength- or grip-heavy task — the characteristic running condition in HYROX.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: The transition between a run and a station. That transition time counts toward the total race time, and it is where cadence and posture have to be re-established.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

31.exam_focus: Expect to be asked how a 5-10% cadence increase redistributes load (knee and hip down, ankle and Achilles up) and to justify why running economy for HYROX is developed through heavy strength plus compromised-running practice rather than by cueing an arbitrary 180 spm.

32.title: Running drills & technique correction
32.page_refs: Running Biomechanics and Technique for HYROX Performance
32.key_concept: Drills are not warm-up filler — each isolates one element of the gait cycle so the pattern can be rehearsed at low speed, then expressed at race pace. A-skip rehearses hip flexion, dorsiflexion and cyclical ground contact; B-skip adds active knee extension then a pawing recovery; dribbles bias fast, low-amplitude contacts under the hips; strides restore speed-specific coordination at very low fatigue cost. Correction is a separate skill: identify the primary fault, cue the one change that cascades downstream, and hold it for weeks. Keep it to one or two cues — piling on verbal instruction splits attention and slows motor learning, especially on fatigued HYROX legs leaving the roxzone.
key_facts: Drill purpose = isolate → rehearse → transfer. A drill that never gets expressed in a stride or a run rep is wasted volume.
A-skip → hip flexion + dorsiflexed foot + stiff, brief ground contact under the COM. Cue: "tall, toes up, punch the ground."
B-skip = A-skip + active knee extension then a backward paw → rehearses hamstring pre-activation and shin deceleration, discouraging over-reaching/braking.
Dribbles (ankling → low knee) → cadence, elastic ankle stiffness, contact under the hips. A strong pre-run choice for over-striders.
Strides = 15–30 s at roughly mile-to-5 k effort, full recovery → speed-specific coordination at a small enough metabolic cost that it does not compromise the session.

Over-striding = foot lands well ahead of COM → braking impulse ↑, contact time ↑, knee/tibial load ↑. Fix with posture + a ~5% cadence nudge (most trained runners sit ~165–185 spm, rising with speed) — never impose a fixed number, never coach the foot.

Foot strike is largely an OUTPUT: fix posture and contact position and the strike tends to self-select. Forcing a forefoot landing shifts load from the knee to the ankle/Achilles — a trade, not an upgrade, and prospective injury evidence does not favour either pattern outright.
Arms drive rhythm and counter-rotate the trunk: relaxed hands, ~80–100° elbow, motion from the shoulder, minimal midline cross.
Rule of one: one fault, one cue, held for several weeks (roughly 2–6) before adding another.
Drills for SKILL ACQUISITION go post-warm-up while fresh. Deliberately fatigued rehearsal is a separate, later step for TRANSFER — not the place to teach a new pattern.
In HYROX, the fault most worth fixing is posture collapse in the first 100–200 m out of the roxzone (hips back, trunk flexed, cadence dead).
32.training_link: Slot 8–10 minutes of drills — dribbles → A-skip → B-skip → 3–4 strides — after your athlete's warm-up and before compromised-run work, never at the end when they're cooked. Film them at 30 s and again at the last 200 m of a run after the sled push: the fault that only appears fatigued is the one costing them real time on race day, and it's almost always trunk collapse plus a dead cadence out of the roxzone. Give one cue for that block (e.g. "ribs down, quick feet") and re-film in three weeks rather than stacking a second correction on top.

glossary.def: A rhythmic skipping drill emphasising a high, flexed hip with a dorsiflexed foot and a short, stiff ground contact directly beneath the body. Rehearses the front-side mechanics of the swing phase.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M14 12v18M14 12h12" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M30 30c8-2 16-10 30-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: An A-skip with an added active knee extension followed by a backward sweep of the foot. Rehearses the hamstrings decelerating the shin and pulling the ground back rather than landing in front of the body.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M14 12v18M14 12h12" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M30 30c8-2 16-10 30-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: Very low-amplitude running-on-the-spot-to-forward drill driven almost entirely by the ankle. Builds elastic ankle stiffness, quick contacts and higher cadence.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A short, controlled acceleration of roughly 15–30 seconds at fast-but-relaxed effort with full recovery, used to rehearse fast mechanics without accumulating meaningful fatigue.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Landing with the foot noticeably ahead of the centre of mass, producing a braking force and a longer, higher-load ground contact.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The backward-directed portion of the horizontal ground reaction force during early stance. Larger with over-striding; it costs speed and raises tissue load.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 30h44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M30 30l0-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="26,34 34,34 30,28" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Step frequency in steps per minute (both legs). For a fixed pace, raising cadence shortens stride length and moves the landing closer to the body.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: A coaching constraint: correct a single dominant fault with a single cue and hold it long enough for the motor pattern to consolidate before adding another.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 30h52" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="14" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="30" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#ffb86b"/><rect x="46" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

glossary.def: Changing the task or environment (metronome, hill, marker spacing) so the desired mechanics emerge, rather than telling the athlete which body part to move.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="7" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 14h28M34 20h22M34 26h16" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Directing the athlete's attention to the effect of the movement or the environment rather than to their own body segments. Generally produces better retention and transfer than internal, body-part cueing.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

32.exam_focus: Matching each drill to the specific gait-cycle element it trains, and demonstrating a disciplined correction process — one prioritised fault, one cue, transfer into running — rather than listing every technique flaw you can see.

33.title: Running technique under fatigue
33.page_refs: Running Biomechanics and Technique for HYROX Performance
33.key_concept: HYROX running is never fresh running. Every station leaves its own mechanical debt: the sled push loads the knee extensors and calves in a sustained forward-lean, short-lever drive; the sled pull is a hand-over-hand upper-back and grip effort over a braced, largely isometric lower body; sandbag lunges load the quads, glutes and erectors heavily through range; wall balls and burpee broad jumps drain the same triple-extension chain. The first strides out of the roxzone commonly show reduced cadence, longer ground contact, more trunk flexion, and overstriding with a braking heel strike. Coaching the transition means restoring posture and cadence before restoring speed, and deliberately rehearsing compromised running so the degraded pattern is already familiar and self-correcting on race day.
key_facts: Typical fatigue signature out of a station: ↓ cadence, ↑ ground contact time, ↑ trunk flexion, often ↑ pelvic drop → overstride + heel braking. Magnitude varies widely between athletes.
Sled push = high knee-extensor + plantarflexor load in a sustained forward lean → the athlete tends to carry that lean and a short choppy stride into the run; cue tall posture first.

Sled pull = predominantly lats, upper back and grip, with the legs braced and largely isometric → less direct corruption of stride mechanics than the push, but grip and postural fatigue still degrade arm carriage and trunk position.

Sandbag lunges (100 m) load the quads, glutes and erectors hard through a long range — plausibly one of the most disruptive stations for subsequent run mechanics, though which station hurts most is individual and should be measured, not assumed.

Cadence is the fastest lever: hold near the athlete's own habitual cadence even as pace drops — this shortens stride, cuts braking, and demands less peak force from fatigued legs. Habitual cadence is highly individual and rises with speed; the commonly cited '180 spm' is a rough average, not a target.

The first 100-200 m out of the roxzone is best treated as a re-patterning window rather than a passing window; a controlled slightly-slower opening often beats surging, though the optimal amount varies by athlete and station.

Early-run heaviness is multifactorial — local metabolite accumulation, residual muscle fatigue, and the demands of redistributing blood flow between working muscle groups all plausibly contribute; mechanics typically settle once cadence and breathing stabilise.
Roxzone time counts toward the finishing time; sloppy transitions add up meaningfully across the race — walk with purpose rather than stagger-then-sprint.

Compromised running is trainable. Both general aerobic and strength-endurance work and specific station→run rehearsal contribute; the specific pairings are worth training in race order, but generic fatigued running is not wasted.
Common technique fault chain: quad fatigue → ↓ knee flexion at swing → overstride → ↑ braking impulse → ↑ energy cost → further fatigue.

Monitor cadence, GCT and heart-rate drift per run leg. A meaningful cadence decline from the early to the late run legs is a useful practical flag for pacing or durability problems — treat any specific percentage as a working coaching heuristic, not an established cutoff.
33.training_link: Program your athlete's transitions as skill work, not just conditioning: after every sled or lunge set in the build phase, send them straight into 200-400 m at target race pace and score the first 100 m on posture and cadence, not on split. Give them one fixed cue stack — stand tall, exhale hard, quick feet, then lengthen — and drill it until it fires automatically. In race-simulation sessions, use a metronome or cadence alert and hold habitual cadence out of each roxzone; review per-leg cadence and GCT afterwards to find which station consistently breaks that individual's form, then bias practice toward that specific pairing rather than assuming which station is worst.

glossary.def: Running performed under pre-existing local muscular fatigue from a preceding non-running task. In HYROX it is the default running state, not a special case.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: The transition area between run and station. Time spent there counts toward the finishing time, so it is coached as an active, deliberately paced segment.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Duration each foot spends on the ground per stride. It commonly lengthens under fatigue, and shorter contact times are generally associated with better running economy — an association rather than a simple lever to pull.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The spring-like resistance of the lower limb to compression on landing. Fatigue can alter it, but the research is genuinely mixed — decreases, increases and no change have all been reported — so treat it as a concept to understand rather than a metric to chase.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The backward force generated when the foot lands ahead of the centre of mass. Rises with overstriding and wastes forward momentum.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 30h44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M30 30l0-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="26,34 34,34 30,28" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Steps per minute. Holding cadence while allowing stride length to shorten is the simplest way to preserve mechanics as pace drops.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: The trained ability to restore acceptable running mechanics quickly after a specific station. Partly task-specific, so it benefits from rehearsing the actual pairing.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: A short, fixed sequence of coaching cues an athlete runs through on leaving the roxzone, e.g. posture → breathe → cadence → reach.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="7" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 14h28M34 20h22M34 26h16" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The ability to retain mechanical and physiological efficiency deep into accumulated fatigue, rather than peak fresh capacity.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

33.exam_focus: Identifying the specific mechanical faults each station imposes on the subsequent run and prescribing the correct transition cues and compromised-running training to correct them.

34.title: SkiErg technique & programming
34.key_concept: The SkiErg is station 1 — entered on fresh legs but with HR already elevated from run 1, so it sets the tone for the whole race. Power comes from a sequenced chain: tall start with loaded lats, then hip hinge and lat/tricep drive together, trunk compressing over the hips, finishing with a short abdominal/hip snap and a relaxed recovery back to full stretch. The hinge and trunk contribute substantially more force than elbow flexion alone; athletes who pull mainly with the arms tend to fade. On a Concept2 machine, displayed power rises with roughly the cube of pace, so small split improvements demand disproportionately large watt increases. Manage damper/drag, stroke rate and stroke length together, and exit the machine with HR and grip intact for the sleds.
key_facts: Station order: Ski is #1 of 8 → run 1 → SkiErg 1000 m. Fatigue arriving here is largely systemic (cardiovascular) rather than local, though upper-body and grip fatigue accumulate during the station itself.
Sequence: hinge + lat drive together → trunk compression → short abs/hip finish → relaxed recovery back to full overhead reach.
Concept2 relation: watts ≈ 2.80 / t³, where t = seconds per metre. Power therefore scales with roughly the cube of velocity, so pace gains are expensive in watts.
Damper (1–10) ≠ drag factor. The damper is an airflow lever; drag factor is the machine-measured flywheel deceleration and is the value that makes resistance comparable across units.

Mid-range damper/drag settings are commonly used, but no single optimum is established — high damper raises per-stroke load and forearm/lat fatigue, low damper tends to raise stroke rate and cardiac cost. Test both and individualise.
Ski stroke rates in racing are generally higher than rowing rates (rowing typically sits in the 20s–low 30s). Exact ski rates vary widely by athlete; rate alone is not a quality marker.
Power = stroke rate × work per stroke. Raising rate only helps if work per stroke does not fall proportionally more — a shortened stroke at high rate can leave output unchanged or lower.
Common faults: squatting instead of hinging, early elbow bend, pulling the handles back well past the hips, yanking the handles apart, incomplete overhead reach on recovery, over-gripping.
Pacing: hold target 1000 m split, or roughly 1–3 s/500 m slower than a fresh-tested 1000 m as a practical starting point; the ski should not be a personal-best attempt.
Exit cost matters: forearm and grip fatigue carry straight into sled push and, more so, sled pull — easing the last 100–150 m is a reasonable tactic if grip is loading up.
Interval formats that transfer: 8–10 × 250 m at goal pace, 4–6 × 500 m off short rest, 3 × 1000 m, and run→ski→run compromised-state blocks.
34.training_link: Test your athlete's fresh 1000 m ski, then set a race target modestly slower (about 1–3 s/500 m is a workable starting point) and rehearse it off a run at goal 1 km pace rather than standing rested at the machine. Watch the first 200 m specifically — this is where athletes most often go out several seconds per 500 m too fast on adrenaline and pay for it on the sleds. Coach the exit as part of the station: ease the last 150 m, shake the forearms out in the roxzone, and cue hinge-and-lat drive rather than arm pulling whenever the split drifts while stroke rate climbs.

glossary.def: A machine-measured number reflecting how quickly the flywheel decelerates between strokes. It standardises resistance feel across different ergs, unlike the damper number alone.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="20" width="22" height="12" rx="2" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".75"/><path d="M36 26h26M56 20l6 6-6 6" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The 1–10 lever that changes airflow into the flywheel cage. It influences drag factor but is not itself a unit of resistance.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Strokes completed per minute. Total power equals stroke rate multiplied by work done per stroke, so rate alone says nothing about output.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M14 12v18M14 12h12" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M30 30c8-2 16-10 30-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: Initiating the pull with shoulder extension driven by the latissimus dorsi and surrounding back musculature rather than with elbow flexion.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Time to cover a reference distance at the current pace — conventionally per 500 m on Concept2 machines.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: An interval performed immediately after another modality (e.g. ski straight off a run) to train the transition and pacing under pre-existing fatigue.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The transition area between runs and stations; time spent there counts toward total race time.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The distance the handles travel from the fully stretched overhead position to the finish. Shortening it drops work per stroke even if rate stays high.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M14 12v18M14 12h12" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M30 30c8-2 16-10 30-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>

34.exam_focus: Expect to be tested on correct stroke sequencing and fault identification, and on choosing a race-appropriate 1000 m ski pace that protects performance on the subsequent sled stations.

35.title: Rowing technique & programming
35.key_concept: Rowing is a cyclical leg-dominant push, not a pull. Each stroke runs catch → drive → finish → recovery, with force sequenced legs → hips/trunk → arms on the drive and reversed (arms → body → legs) on the recovery. Power comes from the horizontal leg drive against the footstretcher; the arms only finish what the legs started. On an ergometer, power rises roughly with the cube of speed, so a small split improvement costs a large power increase — split discipline matters more than surging. Drag factor (not damper number) is the measure of the resistance the flywheel actually applies. In HYROX the 1000 m row lands at station 5 on pre-fatigued legs and hips, so technique must survive fatigue, not just look clean fresh.
key_facts: Sequence: catch → drive → finish → recovery. Drive = legs → hips/trunk → arms; recovery = arms → body → legs.
Legs contribute the largest share of stroke power, the hips/trunk the next largest, the arms the smallest — coach the leg drive first.
Drive:recovery ratio ≈ 1:2 at low stroke rates, compressing toward ~1:1 as rate climbs.
