Damper setting ≠ resistance. Damper controls airflow into the flywheel cage; drag factor is the machine-measured value (shown in the Concept2 monitor menu) and is what should be matched between machines. A commonly used work range is ≈ 100–140, but it is individualised.
↑ drag → heavier stroke, more strength/leg-endurance cost; ↓ drag → faster catch and lighter stroke, so pace is held with more rate and aerobic cost.
Pace unit = time per 500 m ("split"). 1000 m time = split × 2.
Concept2 power estimate: watts ≈ 2.80 × (500 ÷ split_seconds)³ — because power scales with the cube of speed, a ~1% pace gain needs ~3% more power.
Most HYROX athletes row the 1000 m efficiently at roughly 24–30 spm: relatively low rate, long powerful strokes, protecting the legs for the next run. Optimal rate is individual.
Common faults: opening the back early (shooting the slide), early arm bend, over-compression at the catch, rushing the slide, heels never loading, excessive layback.

Race context: the row is station 5 of 8, immediately after burpee broad jumps and before a 1 km run and the farmers carry — hip flexors, shoulders and grip are already taxed, so a legs-driven, lower-rate stroke is usually cheaper than a rate-driven one.

Come off the erg controlled. Sprinting the final 200 m adds peripheral fatigue and blood lactate for a small split gain; in practice most athletes lose more on the following run than they save on the erg, though this is a coaching heuristic rather than a well-quantified finding.
35.training_link: Set your athlete's drag factor once, then keep it fixed across sessions so their split data actually means something — chasing a new damper number every race is why erg pacing feels random. Rehearse the row exactly as it appears in the race: burpee broad jumps straight into 1000 m at target split, then out onto a 1 km run, so they learn what a legs-first, ~26 spm stroke feels like on tired hip flexors. Give them one number to hold, not a feeling, and a standing rule not to sprint the last 200 m.

glossary.def: The front end of the stroke where the shins are near vertical and the chain loads. The point at which force application begins.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The propulsive phase, from catch to finish, driven by leg extension, then hip/trunk opening, then arm draw.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: End of the drive: legs flat, trunk leaning slightly back, handle drawn to the lower ribs. Excess layback costs time and loads the lumbar spine.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The unloaded return to the catch — arms away, body over, then legs compress. Should be slower than the drive.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A machine-calculated number describing how fast the flywheel decelerates between strokes, i.e. the real resistance per stroke. Depends on damper position, airflow through the flywheel cage, air density and how clean the machine is.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="20" width="22" height="12" rx="2" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".75"/><path d="M36 26h26M56 20l6 6-6 6" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Projected time to cover 500 m at the current pace. The primary pacing unit on a rowing ergometer.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Strokes taken per minute. Not the same thing as pace — the same split can be produced at different rates with different power per stroke.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M14 12v18M14 12h12" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M30 30c8-2 16-10 30-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: Fault where the legs extend but the handle barely moves, because the hips open early and the trunk collapses — force leaks instead of reaching the chain.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Recovery performed too fast, throwing the athlete into the catch, checking the flywheel and raising metabolic cost for no pace gain.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

35.exam_focus: Correctly sequencing the drive/recovery phases and diagnosing a technical fault, plus interpreting drag factor, stroke rate and 500 m split when prescribing a fatigue-realistic 1000 m row.

36.title: Bike, cross-training & off-feet volume
36.key_concept: Off-feet conditioning buys aerobic adaptation without the ground-contact loading that drives most running injuries. The transfer is uneven, and knowing which half transfers is the whole lesson: CENTRAL adaptations — stroke volume, plasma/blood volume, cardiac output — are properties of the heart and blood, so they carry across modalities. PERIPHERAL adaptations — mitochondrial density, capillarisation, oxidative enzymes — occur in the muscle fibres actually recruited, so they transfer only as far as the muscle groups overlap. That is why bike and erg work supplements running rather than replacing it. Use off-feet volume to add Zone 2 without adding impact, to bridge return-to-run, to protect high-bodyweight or high-injury-risk athletes, and to rehearse the HYROX machines. Match intensity across modalities by internal load (HR, RPE, ventilatory thresholds), never by transferring pace or watt figures.
key_facts: Central adaptations (stroke volume, plasma/blood volume, cardiac output) are heart- and blood-level, so they transfer broadly across modalities.

Peripheral adaptations (mitochondrial density, capillary density, oxidative enzymes) are LOCAL to the muscle fibres trained — cycling transfers to running only insofar as the musculature overlaps. This is the main ceiling on cross-training transfer.
Peak vertical ground reaction force in running is roughly 2–3× bodyweight per step at typical distance-running speeds; cycling and erg work involve essentially no impact and little eccentric loading.

Off-feet is a load-management tool, not a running substitute — running economy and gait-specific impact tolerance need running. (Heavy resistance training also builds tendon stiffness; running is not the only route to that one.)
General finding in the cross-training literature: off-feet work maintains VO2max well during a running layoff, but is clearly inferior to running for IMPROVING running performance.

Best HYROX-specific off-feet: SkiErg and Concept2 row (double as skill practice — they are race stations 1 and 5), bike/BikeErg (highest volume tolerance, lowest soreness), elliptical, deep-water run, incline walk (low impact, high aerobic).
Match by internal load: HR zones, RPE, talk test, or %threshold — never transfer a running pace or a bike FTP watt figure directly.

HRmax is typically ~5–10 bpm lower in cycling than running (smaller active muscle mass, seated position). Rowing recruits large muscle mass and usually sits much closer to running HRmax — only a few bpm below, sometimes equal. Do not lump rowing in with cycling; set zones per modality from a modality-specific test.
Return-to-run: hold aerobic fitness off-feet, reintroduce running via walk/run intervals, increase running gradually, and taper off-feet volume down as run volume comes up.

The '10% per week' rule is a coaching convention, not an evidence-backed threshold — a randomised trial of a graded 10%/wk program found no reduction in running injury rates. Use it as a default starting heuristic, governed by symptoms, not as a safety guarantee.
High-bodyweight / masters / high-injury-history athlete: shift a larger share of Zone 2 off-feet; keep enough running to preserve race-specific tolerance for 8 × 1 km.
Common coaching split (convention, not research): ~60–80% of aerobic volume on feet for a healthy HYROX athlete; can invert during injury or heavy strength blocks — depends on history and race date.
Rowing/SkiErg add posterior-chain and lat/trunk fatigue → they are not 'free' recovery volume; the bike is the cleanest true-recovery modality.
36.training_link: For a heavier or injury-prone HYROX athlete, keep the running you can tolerate for race specificity and move the extra Zone 2 onto the bike or SkiErg — you raise weekly aerobic minutes without adding several thousand more ground contacts. Set separate HR zones per modality on their watch, and test rather than assume: their bike zones will likely sit below their running zones, while their rowing zones may be nearly identical to running. In return-to-run, add running back gradually (the 10%/wk convention is a reasonable starting default, but let symptoms govern it) and pull off-feet minutes down in step, so total aerobic load stays flat rather than spiking.

glossary.def: Aerobic work performed without running ground contacts — bike, erg, elliptical, deep-water run. Delivers cardiovascular stimulus while sparing impact-loaded tissue.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M14 12v18M14 12h12" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M30 30c8-2 16-10 30-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: The mechanical/eccentric loading a session imposes on bone, tendon and muscle, separate from its metabolic cost. Running is high; ergs and cycling are near zero.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Change at the heart/blood level — stroke volume, plasma and total blood volume, maximal cardiac output. Serves any working muscle, so it transfers across modalities.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Change within the trained muscle — mitochondrial density, capillarisation, oxidative enzyme activity, arteriovenous O2 difference. Localised to the fibres recruited, so transfer between modalities is partial.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The proportion of a fitness gain in one modality that shows up in another. High for central adaptations, partial for peripheral ones (scales with muscle-group overlap), low for modality-specific skill and neuromuscular qualities.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The athlete's physiological response to work — HR, RPE, lactate, breathing rate. The valid currency for equating intensity across different modalities.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Peak heart rate differs by exercise mode because of active muscle mass and body position. Running is typically highest, cycling ~5–10 bpm lower, rowing usually close to running. Test per modality rather than assuming a single HRmax.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Staged reintroduction of running after injury or layoff, usually walk/run intervals with conservative, symptom-governed weekly increases, with off-feet volume holding aerobic fitness meanwhile.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Total low-to-moderate intensity endurance minutes per week; the primary driver of aerobic base, though the modality determines where the peripheral adaptations land.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="22" cy="20" r="8" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M34 20h16M44 14l6 6-6 6" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="60" cy="20" r="5" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

glossary.def: Suspended running in a pool with a flotation belt; replicates the running motion with essentially no impact. Useful in early return-to-run and well supported for maintaining aerobic fitness during a layoff.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

36.exam_focus: Prescribing off-feet volume to manage impact load — distinguishing central (transferable) from peripheral (muscle-local) adaptation, choosing the modality, equating intensity by internal load rather than pace/watts, and tapering off-feet minutes as running is reintroduced.

37.title: Strength & power for HYROX
37.key_concept: HYROX rewards a strength floor more than a strength ceiling. Station loads are fixed and absolute, so what matters is the fraction of an athlete's maximal capacity each rep demands: once someone can handle the race loads with room to spare, further 1RM gains buy progressively less race time and the payoff shifts to strength-endurance and to holding force output under accumulating fatigue. The sleds are the exception — pushing and pulling a heavily loaded sled can sit close to an underpowered athlete's maximal horizontal force, so max strength still gates that station. In a concurrent build, most athletes hold this with two low-volume, high-intent lifting sessions a week — heavy low-rep work plus loaded carries and compromised-position practice — sequenced so lifting fatigue does not land on key running sessions. Note that specific strength 'floors' below are coaching heuristics for programming decisions, not validated cut-offs.
key_facts: Three qualities sit on a continuum: maximal strength (force ceiling) → strength-endurance (repeat submaximal force with little decay) → rate of force development (produce force fast). HYROX loads the middle of that continuum hardest.
Relative strength drives the experience of the race: because loads are absolute and fixed, a lighter or weaker athlete works at a higher percentage of their maximum on every rep of the same station.

Sled push and sled pull are the most strength-dependent stations. Sled friction means force must be produced against a load that does not accelerate away, so for underpowered athletes — especially in Pro divisions, where sled loads are heavier — the effort can approach maximal.

Working strength floor used by many coaches for competitive Open athletes: roughly a bodyweight back squat progressing toward ~1.5x, a deadlift around ~1.5-2x bodyweight, and the ability to carry the division's farmers load unbroken for the full 200 m. Treat these as rules of thumb for triage, not as tested standards — no published data establishes a HYROX strength cut-off.

Interference effect: concurrent endurance training can attenuate strength, power and hypertrophy adaptation. The attenuation is most consistent for explosive/power qualities and hypertrophy, and least consistent for maximal strength, which many concurrent-training studies show develops nearly normally.

Mechanism is not settled. The AMPK-mTOR 'molecular switch' is a proposed explanation but is now regarded as an oversimplification; residual fatigue, glycogen depletion and compromised session quality likely explain much of the real-world effect. Present it as a working model, not established fact.

Interference magnitude scales with endurance volume, endurance intensity, and how close the two sessions sit in time; running appears to interfere more than cycling, plausibly because of its eccentric loading.

Practical mitigation: separate conflicting sessions where possible (a common guideline is at least ~6 h, ideally different days), put lifting after hard runs or on easy days rather than before key run sessions, and keep lifting volume low with high intent.

Maintenance is cheap. In trained athletes, reduced-volume training that holds intensity (heavy loads, roughly 2-4 working sets, 1-5 reps, once or twice weekly) preserves existing maximal strength for several weeks to a few months while endurance volume climbs.

The high-rep stations — wall balls, sandbag lunges, burpee broad jumps — are limited mainly by local muscular endurance, eccentric tolerance and pacing, so they respond far more to specific repeated-effort practice than to a bigger squat.

Wall balls close the race and sandbag lunges precede them, so the quads and glutes are already heavily pre-fatigued when they arrive. Under the current rulebook every individual division does 100 reps (earlier seasons set women's Open at 75; doubles split the work) — check the current rules for the athlete's division rather than assuming.

Loaded carries and controlled eccentric work build the grip and trunk tolerance the farmers carry and sandbag demand; failing grip mid-carry forces drops and re-grips, which costs time directly on the station.

Peaking: taper lifting volume roughly two weeks out while retaining load/intensity, and pull heavy eccentric work about 10 days out so residual soreness has cleared by race day. These timelines are practical conventions, individualised by how an athlete recovers.
37.training_link: Triage relative strength before you write a strength block. If an athlete cannot move their division's sled at a steady walk, or their squat and deadlift sit well below the working floor, force capacity is a genuine limiter and a dedicated strength emphasis is justified. Once they clear it, drop to roughly two 40-minute sessions a week — heavy hinge and squat in low reps, plus loaded carries and unilateral work — placed after the hard interval day so run quality stays clean. Spend the reclaimed time on compromised work: wall balls and sandbag lunges straight off a 1 km run. Then retest what you actually sold them: sled time and station splits under fatigue, not the 1RM.

glossary.def: Force capacity expressed per unit bodyweight. It is the decisive framing when race loads are fixed and absolute, because it sets how large a fraction of maximum each rep costs.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The ability to repeat submaximal force output with minimal decay across many reps. Trained with moderate loads, high total rep counts and short or incomplete recoveries.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: How quickly force rises from the onset of contraction. Relevant in HYROX to sled acceleration off the start, burpee broad jump take-off, and the drive out of the bottom of a wall ball.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 30h44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M30 30l0-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="26,34 34,34 30,28" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Attenuation of strength, power or hypertrophy adaptation when high endurance loads are trained concurrently. Best supported for power and hypertrophy; mechanisms are debated and likely include both molecular signalling and simple accumulated fatigue.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A coaching shorthand for the strength level above which race performance is limited by fatigue resistance rather than by force capacity. Useful for deciding where to spend training time; not a validated threshold.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The minimal weekly stimulus — typically a small number of heavy, low-volume sets with intensity preserved — that holds an existing strength level while endurance volume rises.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Force directed against the ground in the direction of travel. It is the dominant demand in sled push and pull and in the acceleration phase of running; in steady-state running, vertical force dominates and horizontal force mainly offsets braking.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 30h44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M30 30l0-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="26,34 34,34 30,28" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Deliberately performing a lift or station immediately after a run or metabolic bout, to rehearse technique and force output under race-like fatigue.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The transition corridor between each run and each station. Named here only to be clear that it is a transition-time variable, distinct from the strength qualities this lesson covers.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

37.exam_focus: Recognising that HYROX demands a strength floor plus well-developed strength-endurance rather than a maximal-strength ceiling, correctly bounding the certainty of interference-effect claims, and applying concurrent-training sequencing — maintenance dosing, session separation, taper timing — so that lifting does not degrade running quality.

38.title: Injury risk screening & prehab
38.key_concept: A HYROX race is 8 x 1 km of running alternating with 8 stations in a fixed order (SkiErg, sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jump, row, farmers carry, sandbag lunges, wall balls), so the same tissues get loaded repeatedly while already fatigued: the calf-Achilles complex (running on tired legs, driving the sled), the single-leg system (lunges, sled push, the turns on a looped run course), the trunk (carries, hinge-loaded sled pull) and the shoulder-scapula unit (SkiErg, wall balls). Screening should therefore lean capacity-and-control first rather than passive-flexibility first — how many quality heel raises, how long a side bridge holds, how controlled a single-leg step-down looks after work, not how far a joint bends. Treat any asymmetry as a ratio against the athlete's own opposite side, confirm it repeats before acting on it, then prescribe low-dose, targeted prehab placed so it does not compete with the key run or strength stimulus. Note that no screening test has strong prospective evidence for predicting injury; these tools are for finding capacity gaps worth training, not for forecasting who gets hurt.
key_facts: Screen capacity and control under fatigue rather than passive ROM alone — the failures HYROX exposes are usually endurance and control failures.

Calf/Achilles: single-leg heel raise to failure, knee straight (biases gastrocnemius) and knee bent (biases soleus); roughly 20-25 clean reps is a commonly cited healthy-adult reference, but norms shift a lot with age, sex and protocol (tempo, incline, range), so compare to the athlete's other side first.

At endurance running speeds the soleus is the single largest contributor to propulsion and vertical support, so test bent-knee raises separately — a straight-knee-only screen can miss the tissue doing most of the work.

Limb Symmetry Index = (weaker or involved limb / stronger or uninvolved limb) x 100. The familiar >=90% cut-off comes from post-injury return-to-sport criteria; borrowed for healthy screening it is a rough flag, not a validated pass mark.
Single-leg control: step-down / single-leg squat — watch pelvic drop, dynamic valgus and trunk lean. Score the quality you see; do not over-read a single trial.

Y-balance anterior reach asymmetry of about 4 cm is a widely used flag, but it traces back to a small number of studies in specific populations (notably high-school basketball) and later reviews found weak predictive value, so treat it as a prompt to look closer, not a diagnosis.

Trunk endurance (McGill's guidance): right vs left side bridge should be close, roughly within about 5%; flexor endurance should not exceed extensor endurance. The relationship between holds is more informative than any one raw time.

Shoulder: near-full overhead flexion (about 170-180 degrees) with the ribs down, plus scapular upward rotation and posterior-cuff endurance. Restriction here typically shows up as lumbar extension in wall balls and a short catch on the SkiErg.
One-off asymmetry is not a deficit. Retest on at least two occasions, rested and fatigued; the fatigued retest exposes what race pace exposes.
Practical prehab dose: 2-3x/wk, 5-15 min, 2-4 sets — enough to load the tissue, small enough not to blunt the next quality session.

Heavy tendon-focused work (heavy slow calf raises, long isometrics) is typically run on alternate days, around 2-3 sessions a week; stack it after easy runs or lower-body strength rather than before an interval session.
38.training_link: Screen at block start and again mid-block, and always re-test the flagged item after a hard run session — a calf that holds 24 raises fresh and 14 tired is your real number. Prescribe prehab as tail-work on sessions that already exist: bent-knee heel raises after lower-body strength, side bridges and loaded carries after an easy run, cuff and overhead-position work before SkiErg or wall-ball sessions. As a practical rule of thumb keep total weekly prehab modest — on the order of half an hour or so — and trim it in race week rather than letting it eat into taper freshness.

glossary.def: One limb's score expressed as a percentage of the other. In rehab it is involved over uninvolved; in healthy screening it is simply weaker over stronger. A within-athlete normalisation used to flag side-to-side capacity gaps.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The relationship between flexor, extensor and lateral (side-bridge) hold times. McGill proposed these ratios as a way to spot lopsided trunk endurance; they are a practical guide rather than a validated injury predictor.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Knee collapsing inward relative to hip and foot during a single-leg task, commonly associated with hip abductor/external rotator fatigue or poor foot control.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Tendon-loading protocol using heavy loads with deliberately slow concentric and eccentric tempo, one of the better-supported tools for building Achilles and patellar tendon capacity.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Targeted low-dose training aimed at the specific tissue or control deficit a screen exposed, done to build capacity before a problem appears rather than to rehabilitate one.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M30 8v12l14 14" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="30" cy="20" r="3.5" fill="#e0556b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Rotation of the scapula that lets the arm reach true overhead without lumbar compensation. Limited rotation shifts range demand onto the spine and the shoulder joint itself.

glossary.def: Repeating a control or capacity test immediately after a hard bout, revealing the movement quality an athlete actually holds at race intensity.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The smallest test difference that exceeds measurement error. Below it, a side-to-side or session-to-session change should be read as noise, not signal.

38.exam_focus: Choosing the right capacity or control screen for a specific HYROX failure site, interpreting asymmetry (LSI, side-bridge ratio) with appropriate caution about measurement error and weak predictive validity, and converting a finding into a prehab dose that does not add meaningful fatigue.

39.title: Load management & managing niggles
39.key_concept: Load management is keeping applied load under tissue capacity while still driving adaptation. Most HYROX breakdowns are not accidents — they are accumulated: 8 km of fatigued running plus burpee broad jumps, sandbag lunges and wall balls loads the same lower limb repeatedly. The coach's job is triage, not diagnosis. Classify what the athlete reports as soreness (diffuse, symmetrical, eases with warm-up, settling over a few days), a niggle (local, reproducible, low-grade, no loss of quality) or an injury (sharp, night/rest pain, swelling, altered mechanics, function lost). Then apply traffic-light rules: modify the stimulus, keep the intent, substitute off-feet, and progress running volume gradually rather than stopping everything.
key_facts: DOMS: onset ~12–24 h, peaks ~24–72 h, and usually resolves within 5–7 days; unaccustomed eccentric-heavy work (lunges, downhill running, burpee broad jump landings) drives it most. Soreness still worsening after a week is a flag to reassess, not to push.
Soreness = diffuse + bilateral + eases with warm-up. Niggle = focal + reproducible on a specific movement. Injury = sharp/night pain, swelling, giving way, or gait change.
24-hour response rule: symptoms may rise during a session but should return to baseline by the next morning, or the load was too high.

Pain-monitoring model (Silbernagel et al., 2007, developed for Achilles tendinopathy and since applied more broadly to tendon rehab): pain up to ~5/10 during activity is acceptable provided it does not keep climbing week to week and the morning-after score returns toward baseline. It is a tendon-loading guide, not a rule for bone or acute injury.

Traffic-light bands used in this lesson are deliberately more conservative in-session than the tendon model: GREEN (0–2/10, no function loss) → train as planned, monitor. AMBER (3–5/10, technique intact) → modify volume/intensity/range/impact, keep the session intent. RED (>5/10, limp, swelling, night pain, focal bone pain) → stop the aggravating stimulus, refer.
Focal, point-tender bone pain that worsens with each impact and hurts on single-leg hopping = suspected bone stress injury → RED, no traffic-light trial, medical referral.

Off-feet substitutions preserve aerobic dose with ↓ ground-reaction load: SkiErg, Row, bike/AirBike, pool run, incline walk (reduced-impact rather than truly zero-impact). Match duration + intensity zone, not distance.

Eccentric demand is not evenly spread across the stations. Highest: sandbag lunges, burpee broad jump landings, wall ball catch/descent, and long or compromised running. Lowest: sled push and sled pull, which are near-purely concentric — they are often the lower-body work you can keep in a modified week rather than the first thing to cut.

A common rule of thumb is to progress weekly running volume by roughly 5–10 % with a down-week every 3–4 weeks. Note the '10 % rule' is a convention, not a well-evidenced threshold — trials have not shown it reduces injury — so treat it as a starting point and let symptoms, training age and history set the real number.

Acute:chronic workload ratio ~0.8–1.3 is the commonly cited 'sweet spot'; ratios ≳1.5 flag a spike. Treat as a rough monitoring heuristic, not a law — the model has been substantially criticised on methodological grounds.
Modify one variable at a time (volume → intensity → impact → range) so you can tell what actually helped; never take the session away without giving something back.
39.training_link: When an athlete messages you 'my shin's been a bit sore since the race sim', don't guess — ask where exactly, what it scores out of 10, whether it hurts in the morning, and whether it changes their gait. If it's diffuse calf soreness at 2/10 you keep the session; if it's a pinpoint spot on the tibia that worsens with each stride, you stop running that week and rebuild the aerobic dose on the SkiErg, row and bike at the same durations and zones — and refer, because focal bone pain is outside a coach's scope to manage. Keep the strength work and the upper-body stations training as normal, then reintroduce running as short, frequent, easy blocks before touching compromised running or burpee broad jumps again.

glossary.def: The load a structure can currently absorb and recover from without symptoms. It rises with consistent, progressive exposure and falls with detraining, illness or poor sleep.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M30 8v12l14 14" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="30" cy="20" r="3.5" fill="#e0556b"/></svg>

glossary.def: A low-grade, localised, reproducible complaint that does not yet limit performance or alter technique. It is a warning signal, not an injury — the window where modification still works.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M30 8v12l14 14" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><circle cx="30" cy="20" r="3.5" fill="#e0556b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Delayed-onset muscle soreness: diffuse muscular discomfort appearing within a day of unaccustomed or eccentric-heavy work, peaking around 24–72 h, easing with warm-up and typically clearing inside a week.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A monitoring standard where a session is judged acceptable if any symptom provoked returns to its pre-session baseline by the next morning.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 30h52" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="14" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="30" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#ffb86b"/><rect x="46" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

glossary.def: A green/amber/red decision framework that converts an athlete's reported symptoms into a preset training action, so decisions are consistent rather than mood-driven.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Aerobic training with little or no ground impact — erg, bike, pool, incline walk — used to keep the aerobic stimulus while unloading bone and tendon.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M14 12v18M14 12h12" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M30 30c8-2 16-10 30-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: Short-term load (typically a 7-day acute window) divided by the rolling average of recent weeks (typically 28 days). Used as a rough flag for load spikes rather than a validated injury predictor.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Running performed under pre-existing station fatigue, as in HYROX. It carries different mechanical and metabolic cost than fresh running and must be progressed as its own load.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: A planned reduction in volume — with intensity usually held rather than cut — for a week or so, allowing accumulated fatigue to dissipate and adaptation to surface.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

39.exam_focus: Correctly triaging a described symptom into soreness / niggle / injury and selecting the matching traffic-light action — including recognising the red-flag presentations that require referral rather than modification, and knowing which load-management numbers are firm versus rules of thumb.

40.title: Periodization models
40.key_concept: Periodization = planned manipulation of volume, intensity and specificity across time so fitness peaks on race day, not in training. Linear/traditional progresses from high-volume/low-intensity work early to low-volume/high-intensity work near competition. Block (ATR) concentrates 2-4 week loads onto a few compatible qualities and relies on residual training effects to hold the rest. Undulating (weekly or daily) rotates stimuli inside the microcycle. Conjugate develops several qualities simultaneously with one emphasized. HYROX is unforgiving of single-quality plans: the athlete needs aerobic power, strength-endurance, grip and running economy concurrently. The common coaching answer for hybrids is a block-undulating blend — a concentrated emphasis block plus maintenance dosing (commonly 1-2 quality sessions/week) on everything not being emphasized. Note this blend is a practical convention among hybrid coaches, not a model with its own dedicated evidence base.
key_facts: Hierarchy: macrocycle (season / race build, ~3-12 mo) → mesocycle (block, ~3-6 wk) → microcycle (~7 d) → session.

Volume and intensity are inversely coupled in practice — you generally raise one and let the other fall. Training load is usually estimated as volume x intensity (e.g. sets x reps x load, or session RPE x duration); there is no single agreed formula, and density/frequency modify tolerance rather than entering a fixed equation.
Linear: simple, well suited to novices and single-peak sports; weaker for HYROX because qualities left out of the current phase drift down while one is developed.
Block/ATR (Verkhoshansky's block concept, formalised as ATR by Issurin): Accumulation (volume, general) → Transmutation (event-specific, high load) → Realization (unload, race-speed) → race.

Issurin's residual training effect estimates: aerobic endurance ~30±5 d, max strength ~30±5 d, anaerobic glycolytic endurance ~18±4 d, strength-endurance ~15±5 d, max speed ~5±3 d. Treat these as planning heuristics from a model, not precisely measured constants — they vary with training age and prior exposure.

Undulating (DUP): intensity and rep-scheme vary session-to-session, so many qualities get touched each week; costs more planning complexity. Meta-analyses comparing DUP with linear periodization show broadly similar outcomes, so its appeal for hybrids is logistical (fits concurrent qualities) rather than proven superiority.

Conjugate: Verkhoshansky's conjugate sequencing = coupling concentrated loads with retained development of other traits. The Westside variant (Simmons) is the familiar weekly max-effort + dynamic-effort + repeated-effort template with main-lift rotation roughly every 1-3 wk to limit accommodation. The two are related but not the same system.

Concurrent-training interference is real but modest and manageable for most athletes: allow at least ~3 h between a hard endurance session and heavy lower-body lifting, ideally 6-24 h when both are high load; keep hard days hard and easy days easy. Interference is largest when endurance volume is high and the endurance work precedes the lifting.

Maintenance is much cheaper than development — reducing volume by roughly two-thirds while holding intensity and keeping frequency reasonably high preserves endurance and strength adaptations for several weeks.
Unloading: 2:1 or 3:1 build:deload suits most amateurs (volume ↓ ~40-50%); race taper ~8-14 d with volume ↓ ~40-60% — intensity and session frequency held in both.

Monitoring tells you a block ran too long or too dense: performance stalls or reverses at fixed submaximal loads/paces, session RPE climbs for identical work, sleep degrades, and resting HR rises / HRV trends down. Trend direction over days matters far more than any single day's reading.
40.training_link: For a 16-week HYROX build, run block-undulating: weeks 1-6 accumulation (aerobic volume, heavy sled and pulling strength, high-rep wall ball tolerance), weeks 7-12 transmutation (compromised-run intervals, race-pace station-run couplets, sled at race load), weeks 13-16 realization — the last ~10 days of which are the taper, with the race at the end of week 16. Keep every non-emphasized quality alive with 1-2 maintenance touches per week; strength-endurance carries a shorter residual (~15 d) than aerobic fitness or max strength, so grip and lunge tolerance are the first things to fade and they cost you the back half of the race. Deload every third or fourth week by cutting volume ~40-50% while holding your key intensities.

glossary.def: The full training plan for one competitive season or race build, ending at a target event. Contains all mesocycles.

glossary.def: A 3-6 week chunk of training with one dominant aim, e.g. aerobic base or compromised-running specificity.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="24" width="10" height="10" fill="#5ec8ff"/><rect x="24" y="18" width="10" height="16" fill="#5ec8ff" opacity=".8"/><rect x="38" y="12" width="10" height="22" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="52" y="20" width="10" height="14" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: How long an adaptation persists after its targeted training stops. Long residuals (aerobic, max strength) can be maintained cheaply; short ones (speed) must stay in the plan year-round.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Sequenced Accumulation → Transmutation → Realization blocks; general fitness is built, converted to event-specific capacity, then sharpened for competition.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="24" width="10" height="10" fill="#5ec8ff"/><rect x="24" y="18" width="10" height="16" fill="#5ec8ff" opacity=".8"/><rect x="38" y="12" width="10" height="22" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="52" y="20" width="10" height="14" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Rotating intensity and volume across sessions within a week rather than across months, so several qualities are touched repeatedly.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="24" width="10" height="10" fill="#5ec8ff"/><rect x="24" y="18" width="10" height="16" fill="#5ec8ff" opacity=".8"/><rect x="38" y="12" width="10" height="22" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="52" y="20" width="10" height="14" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Developing multiple qualities at once with a shifting emphasis and frequent exercise rotation, keeping every trait above a working floor.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The declining training response to a stimulus that is repeated unchanged for too long; countered by varying exercise selection, loading or organisation.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Attenuated strength or hypertrophy adaptation when high endurance loads are trained too close to resistance work; mitigated by session spacing, ordering and sensible intensity distribution.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Planned pre-race reduction in volume with intensity and frequency maintained, allowing fatigue to dissipate faster than fitness.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="24" width="10" height="10" fill="#5ec8ff"/><rect x="24" y="18" width="10" height="16" fill="#5ec8ff" opacity=".8"/><rect x="38" y="12" width="10" height="22" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="52" y="20" width="10" height="14" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Running performed immediately after a station under residual fatigue — the specific quality HYROX plans must periodize toward, since the race alternates 8x1 km runs with the 8 stations.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

40.exam_focus: Selecting and justifying the right periodization model for a hybrid athlete with multiple concurrent qualities — typically by sequencing ATR blocks, applying residual training effects to decide maintenance dosing, and structuring the taper.

41.title: Annual plan & race calendar
41.key_concept: An annual plan is built backwards from one dated A-race. Fix the race, count back the weeks, then fill the calendar with phases: preparation (general → specific), competition (peak, taper, race), transition (unloading, restoration). General prep builds the raw material — aerobic base, strength, tissue tolerance, technique on all eight stations. Specific prep converts it, compressing work density and adding compromised running so the athlete rehearses race physiology, not just its parts. Volume generally falls as specificity and intensity rise. B and C races are training stimuli and dress rehearsals, deliberately not tapered for. Sequencing is the variable coaches most often get wrong: each phase must leave the athlete able to absorb the next, and a well-ordered plan at moderate intensity will usually beat a harder but incoherent one.
key_facts: Plan backwards: fix A-race date → count weeks → assign phases → then write sessions.
Phases: preparation (general + specific) → competition (peak/taper/race) → transition.
A race = full taper + peak, 1–2 per year; B = tested but trained through; C = practice/skill exposure, no unload.
Race-specific block to a target race is typically 16–24 weeks; 8–12 only for an already-trained athlete.

Fixed HYROX order (8x1km runs alternating with 8 stations): SkiErg → Sled Push → Sled Pull → Burpee Broad Jump → Row → Farmers Carry → Sandbag Lunges → Wall Balls. The order is fixed, so plan position dictates fatigue state.
General prep ↑ volume, ↓ intensity, wide movement base; specific prep ↓ volume, ↑ race-pace + compromised work.
Compromised (run→station→run) training introduced meaningfully ~8–12 wk out; sharpened in final 4–6 wk.
Full-distance/near-full simulations: sparingly, roughly every 3–4 wk in specific prep, last one ≥2 wk pre-race.

Taper ~7–14 days: volume ↓ roughly 40–60%, intensity and race-pace touches retained, frequency held. These are common ranges from taper research, not a universal prescription — individual responses vary.
Transition 1–3 wk after A-race: unstructured, low load — restores tissue + motivation, not detraining.
Loading pattern commonly 2–3 build weeks : 1 deload; deload = ↓ volume first, keep some intensity. The ratio is a practical convention, not a validated constant.
Race-order specificity matters: wall balls and sandbag lunges are trained pre-fatigued, not fresh.
41.training_link: Start every athlete's plan by writing the A-race date at the right-hand end of a week-by-week grid and filling leftward — you will immediately see whether you have 20 weeks or 9, and the honest answer changes what you can build. Hold general strength and aerobic base work early; do not let an athlete's enthusiasm for full simulations pull race-specific compromised work forward past ~12 weeks out, or they risk arriving flat. Register B and C races on the same grid and tell the athlete explicitly which ones they are not tapering for, so a mid-block result is never read as a failure.

glossary.def: The largest planning unit. In classical (NSCA/Bompa) terminology this is usually the full training year; in common race-prep usage it is loosely applied to the whole multi-month block leading to one target race. Either way it contains the full phase sequence from general preparation through transition, and is subdivided into mesocycles (typically ~2–6 wk) and microcycles (typically ~1 wk).

glossary.def: Priority tiers. A = the peaked goal race; B = competitive but trained through with minimal unload; C = low-stakes exposure used as a hard training day or skill rehearsal.
