glossary.def: Early phase building broad capacities — aerobic base, strength, work tolerance, technique — with limited resemblance to race demands.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Later phase where sessions increasingly mirror race order, pace, load and fatigue state, converting general fitness into race performance.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Running performed with pre-existing station fatigue (or stations performed after running), rehearsing the neuromuscular and metabolic state of the actual race.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Planned reduction in training load before an A-race, cutting volume while largely preserving intensity and frequency, to shed accumulated fatigue while retaining fitness.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="24" width="10" height="10" fill="#5ec8ff"/><rect x="24" y="18" width="10" height="16" fill="#5ec8ff" opacity=".8"/><rect x="38" y="12" width="10" height="22" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="52" y="20" width="10" height="14" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Deliberate low-load period after a peak race for physical and psychological restoration before the next macrocycle begins.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 30h52" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="14" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="30" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#ffb86b"/><rect x="46" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

glossary.def: The transition area an athlete crosses between the running lane and the station. In HYROX results, roxzone time is reported as the total accumulated transition time across the whole race — every run→station and station→run movement, not a single crossing. It is a trainable skill (approach, setup, exit) and commonly accounts for several minutes of finish time.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Constructing the calendar from the race date backwards so every week has a defined purpose relative to the peak. Do not confuse this with reverse periodization, which is a distinct and unrelated concept describing a model that begins with low-volume/high-intensity work and progresses toward higher volume — the opposite of the traditional model.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="24" width="10" height="10" fill="#5ec8ff"/><rect x="24" y="18" width="10" height="16" fill="#5ec8ff" opacity=".8"/><rect x="38" y="12" width="10" height="22" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="52" y="20" width="10" height="14" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

41.exam_focus: Expect to be asked to lay out a phase sequence backwards from a given race date and justify when race-specific compromised work and A/B/C race priorities enter the calendar.

42.title: Concurrent training & the interference effect
42.key_concept: Concurrent training means developing endurance and strength/hypertrophy in the same block — unavoidable in HYROX. Interference is the blunting of adaptation when both are trained close together, and it appears to be asymmetric: endurance is seldom harmed, while strength and especially power adaptations are the ones that suffer. The classic molecular story is AMPK (energy-stress, endurance) restraining mTORC1 (growth, resistance work), but that acute signalling account is contested in humans and explains far less than residual fatigue, glycogen depletion, muscle damage and total training load. Coaches manage interference with sequencing, separation, modality choice and dose — not by abandoning one quality. HYROX athletes need both, so interference is minimised, never eliminated.
key_facts: Interference is asymmetric → endurance largely unaffected; strength, power and hypertrophy are what get blunted.

Meta-analytic evidence points to explosive/rate-of-force qualities being most fragile, with hypertrophy and maximal strength affected to a smaller degree; treat the exact ranking as a tendency, not a settled hierarchy.

Molecular sketch: endurance ↑AMPK/PGC-1α (mitochondrial, oxidative) vs resistance ↑mTORC1/p70S6K (myofibrillar protein synthesis); AMPK activation can restrain mTORC1 signalling acutely, though human data on this are inconsistent.
Signalling windows are hours; performance interference is chronic and mostly a fatigue/energy-availability problem.

Separation rule of thumb: ≥6 h between opposing sessions is the common coaching recommendation; ≥24 h or a separate day is safer for key strength work. This is practical convention, not a precisely validated threshold.
Running appears to interfere with lower-body strength more than cycling/rowing/ski — eccentric loading and muscle damage are the likely drivers.

Interference tends to scale with endurance dose: greater frequency and duration are associated with larger decrements, so a short HIIT block before lifting is generally less compromising than a long threshold or steady run.
Under-fuelling amplifies interference: low glycogen ↑AMPK signalling, ↓training quality and ↑catabolic drive.
Practical weekly ordering: hard strength/power early in the week or on separate days from long runs; place low-intensity aerobic work adjacent to lifting instead.
Concurrent-trained beginners often still gain both qualities; interference bites hardest in trained athletes near their adaptive ceiling, where recovery capacity is the limiting resource.
42.training_link: Protect the fragile qualities: put your heavy squat/deadlift or power work on its own day, or at minimum 6+ hours from a hard run, and never straight after a long threshold session. Use ski, row and bike for aerobic volume on your lifting days so the legs stay fresh, and reserve running-heavy days for compromised-running and station work. Keep carbohydrate intake up around double days — an under-fuelled athlete collects the interference without the adaptation.

glossary.def: The reduced rate of strength, power or hypertrophy adaptation that occurs when endurance training is performed concurrently with resistance training.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Training two or more competing fitness qualities — typically endurance and strength — within the same programme or block.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A signalling complex that drives muscle protein synthesis and growth; upregulated by resistance loading and amino-acid/energy availability.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: An energy-sensing kinase activated when cellular energy runs low, as in endurance work; it promotes oxidative adaptation and can acutely restrain growth signalling.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A transcriptional co-activator central to mitochondrial biogenesis, upregulated by endurance stimuli; an important regulator of aerobic adaptation rather than its sole cause.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The number of hours placed between two opposing training sessions to allow fatigue, substrate and signalling recovery before the second stimulus.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Carry-over neuromuscular and metabolic fatigue from a prior session that lowers the quality of the next one — the practical driver of most interference.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The principle that interference depends on the endurance mode used; non-impact modes (bike, ski, row) appear to transfer less muscle damage to lifting than running.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

42.exam_focus: Expect to be asked which quality interference blunts most, why fatigue rather than kinase signalling explains most of it, and how to sequence and separate strength and endurance sessions across a HYROX week.

43.title: Tapering & peaking
43.key_concept: A taper is a planned, progressive drop in training load in the final 1-3 weeks so accumulated fatigue dissipates faster than fitness decays, revealing adaptation that was masked by fatigue. The lever that matters is volume: cut it substantially while holding intensity and session frequency near normal. Intensity is what preserves neuromuscular qualities, running economy and station-specific pacing; volume is what carries most of the fatigue cost. Gains are real but modest — low single-digit percentages on average — and are largest in athletes carrying genuine accumulated fatigue, close to nothing in athletes who were undertrained going in. In HYROX the taper must also rehearse compromised running, station technique and race-week logistics without adding residual fatigue.
key_facts: Taper = ↓volume, → intensity, → frequency. Intensity is the last thing to cut, not the first.
Typical duration 7-21 days; ~2 weeks suits most trained HYROX athletes. Bigger training loads / longer builds → longer taper.
Volume cut ~40-60% from peak week, applied progressively; frequency held at ~80%+ of normal to protect feel and skill.
Two-week progressive template: taper week 1 ≈ 60-70% of peak volume, race week ≈ 40-50% of peak, session count unchanged.

Realistic gain ~1-3% in endurance performance from a well-executed taper; pooled estimates cluster near ~2%, with individual outcomes ranging roughly 0-6% depending on prior fatigue, training status and adherence.

Progressive/exponential taper (steady decay) appears to outperform a step taper (single abrupt drop) in most pooled data, though the margin is modest and the evidence is directional rather than settled.

Reported mechanisms: glycogen restoration and supercompensation, normalisation of hormonal and haematological markers, ↓ muscle damage markers, ↑ neuromuscular force and rate of force development, ↑ mood and perceived readiness. These are associations observed alongside taper, not a single proven pathway.
Over-taper risk: >3 weeks of low load, or losing intensity → detraining, flat legs, degraded high-intensity tolerance, loss of station rhythm.

Strength in taper: keep heavy sled/pull patterns at high intent but very low volume (few sets, submaximal reps, no failure); stop heavy eccentrics ~7-10 days out. This is a practical coaching heuristic, not a precisely evidenced cut-off.

Race week: last genuinely demanding session ~5-7 days out. Short race-pace touches (a few hundred metres of running, small station doses) may continue into the final 72 h — they are priming, not training.

Carbohydrate emphasis rises for the final 1-2 days while volume is minimal. HYROX is a ~60-90 min event, so a modest top-up is sufficient — full marathon-style multi-day loading is not required. Body mass may rise ~1-2 kg from stored glycogen and its associated water; this is expected, not fat gain.
43.training_link: Set your athlete's last genuine race-simulation block 10-14 days out, then cut weekly volume roughly in half across the two taper weeks while keeping the same number of sessions and the same paces. In race week, give them two short compromised-run pieces (e.g. 3 x 400 m at race pace off 15-20 wall balls or a short, light sled) plus a light technical touch on sled push, ski and lunge to keep the pattern alive. Expect them to feel sluggish or twitchy mid-taper — brief them in advance so they don't panic and add work back in.

glossary.def: A structured reduction in training load before competition designed to remove fatigue while retaining fitness. Usually 1-3 weeks and volume-led.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="24" width="10" height="10" fill="#5ec8ff"/><rect x="24" y="18" width="10" height="16" fill="#5ec8ff" opacity=".8"/><rect x="38" y="12" width="10" height="22" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="52" y="20" width="10" height="14" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: The outcome the taper aims at — the narrow window in which fitness minus fatigue is maximal and performance is highest.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="24" width="10" height="10" fill="#5ec8ff"/><rect x="24" y="18" width="10" height="16" fill="#5ec8ff" opacity=".8"/><rect x="38" y="12" width="10" height="22" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="52" y="20" width="10" height="14" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: A conceptual framework treating performance as the residual of a slowly decaying fitness effect and a faster-decaying fatigue effect produced by the same training. Useful for reasoning about taper timing; it is a model, not a measurement.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Load is reduced gradually across the taper (often exponentially) rather than dropped in one step, which generally yields somewhat better outcomes.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="24" width="10" height="10" fill="#5ec8ff"/><rect x="24" y="18" width="10" height="16" fill="#5ec8ff" opacity=".8"/><rect x="38" y="12" width="10" height="22" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="52" y="20" width="10" height="14" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Short-term deliberate overload producing temporary performance decline, which rebounds above baseline once load is removed. A taper is what converts it into supercompensation, provided recovery is adequate.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A very short, high-intent, low-volume effort in the last 24-72 h intended to sharpen neuromuscular readiness without generating fatigue.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Elevated muscle glycogen stores achieved by raising carbohydrate intake while training volume is low in the days before racing.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Measurable loss of adaptation from insufficient stimulus — the failure mode of a taper that is too long or that abandons intensity.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Running under the residual fatigue of a preceding station; must still be rehearsed, at low total volume, during the taper.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

43.exam_focus: Expect to be tested on the volume-down / intensity-and-frequency-held principle, the typical 1-3 week duration with ~40-60% volume reduction, the realistic magnitude of the gain, and the ability to lay out a specific race-week sequence for a HYROX athlete.

44.title: Multi-race & in-season management
44.key_concept: In-season HYROX planning replaces linear build logic with a repeating reload → mini-build → taper → race loop. A race is a maximal effort lasting roughly 55–60 min for elites and commonly 90 min to over 2 h for age-group athletes: 8 km of running split around eight stations, with the eccentric-damaging elements (sandbag lunges, wall-ball catches, burpee broad-jump landings, and the running itself) sitting alongside high-tension but concentric-dominant sled work. That damage outlasts metabolic and autonomic recovery, so readiness markers return before tissue does. The coach's job is to decide, race by race, whether the gap allows a genuine rebuild (roughly 4+ weeks), only maintenance (roughly 2–3 weeks), or pure recovery plus taper (under 2 weeks). Maintenance works because intensity preserves adaptation while volume can drop sharply. Cumulative fatigue across a block is managed by ranking races A/B/C and defending only the A races with full taper and full reload.
key_facts: Race block = repeating loop: reload → mini-build → taper → race, not one long linear plan.
Rank races A/B/C. Only A races get a full taper + full post-race reload; B/C races are trained through.

Typical inter-race gaps: <2 wk → recover + taper only; 2–3 wk → maintenance + short sharpening; ≥4 wk → real rebuild block possible. These are planning heuristics, not fixed thresholds — individual recovery varies widely.
Maintenance rule: hold intensity, cut volume (commonly ~1/3 to ~2/3) and keep frequency roughly intact → strength and VO2max are largely retained for several weeks.

Rough detraining order: plasma volume falls first (within days); anaerobic/repeat-effort capacity over ~1–3 wk; VO2max meaningfully declines from ~2–4 wk; maximal strength is the most durable (largely held for several weeks, though power and rate of force development fade sooner).
Muscle-damage markers (soreness, ↓ eccentric force, ↓ jump height) recover more slowly than HR/HRV → don't restart heavy lunge, wall-ball and running volume on HRV alone.

The eccentric-damaging race elements are sandbag lunges, wall-ball catches, burpee broad-jump landings and the 8 km of running. Sled push and pull are concentric-dominant — very high tension and locally fatiguing, but they are not a major source of eccentric muscle damage.
Post-race reload: 2–4 easy days (Z1–Z2, mobility), then easy aerobic running, then compromised running, and only then heavy eccentric station volume.
Cumulative-fatigue red flags: ↑ RHR, ↓ HRV trend, ↓ wall-ball/burpee capacity at same RPE, rising roxzone times, sleep + mood decline.

When rebuilding mid-season, raise volume gradually — ~10%/week is a common coaching rule of thumb rather than a validated injury threshold, but abrupt post-race spikes onto damaged tissue are widely implicated in in-season injury.
Recovery between races is slower in older athletes and in those with less training history — extend reloads rather than compressing them.
Skill/station technique work is cheap to maintain — low volume, low fatigue → keep it in even the tightest weeks.
44.training_link: Map your athlete's whole season on one page first, mark one or two A races, then work backwards to decide which gaps allow a rebuild and which only allow maintenance. If two races sit three weeks apart, give days 1–4 as reload, days 5–14 as one hard compromised-run session plus one heavy strength/sled session per week at reduced volume, then a 5–7 day taper — do not chase new strength PRs in that window. Reintroduce lunge and wall-ball volume later than sled work, since those carry the eccentric damage. Track wall-ball capacity and roxzone times across the block; when those drift up at the same RPE, cut a race or convert it to a C-priority pacing rehearsal.

glossary.def: A stretch of the calendar containing two or more races where full training progression is subordinated to race readiness. Load is shaped around race dates rather than a single peak.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="10" y="24" width="10" height="10" fill="#5ec8ff"/><rect x="24" y="18" width="10" height="16" fill="#5ec8ff" opacity=".8"/><rect x="38" y="12" width="10" height="22" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="52" y="20" width="10" height="14" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: A priority ranking for events. A races get a full taper and full recovery; B races get a short taper; C races are treated as hard training or pacing rehearsals.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 30h52" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="14" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/><rect x="30" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#ffb86b"/><rect x="46" y="12" width="8" height="8" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

glossary.def: Reduced-volume, intensity-preserving training that holds an existing adaptation rather than building it. Enough to stop decay, cheap enough to allow recovery.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The deliberate low-load period straight after a race, aimed at clearing muscle damage and central fatigue before any new stimulus is applied.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Incomplete recovery stacking across successive races and hard weeks, showing as flat performance at unchanged or higher perceived effort.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A short planned overload that temporarily depresses performance (days to weeks) but supercompensates after adequate recovery. It becomes non-functional overreaching — a longer decline needing weeks to months — if the recovery window is skipped.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A brief phase of race-specific, race-pace work — compromised running, station transitions, roxzone drills — with low overall volume, used when there is no time to rebuild.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.term: Residual eccentric damage (informal shorthand: 'eccentric load debt')
glossary.def: Not a formal textbook term — a working label for muscle damage from the high-eccentric race elements (sandbag lunges, wall-ball catches, jump landings, running) that lingers after metabolic and autonomic markers have normalised.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The HYROX transition area between each run and its station. Cumulative roxzone time is a sensitive in-season fatigue marker because it degrades before pace does.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

44.exam_focus: Choosing the correct in-season strategy — recover-and-taper vs maintain vs rebuild — from a given inter-race gap and race priority, and justifying it with recovery-timeline and detraining principles.

45.title: Arousal, anxiety & activation control
45.key_concept: Arousal is a neutral physiological-cognitive activation continuum from sleep to frenzy; anxiety is the negative emotional response to perceived threat, split into cognitive (worry, doubt, narrowed attention) and somatic (HR, breath rate, muscle tension, gut) components. Performance depends less on raw arousal than on whether activation sits inside that athlete's individual zone of optimal functioning — a personal band, not a universal midpoint. The inverted-U model predicts an optimum with decrement either side; IZOF and catastrophe models refine it, showing zones differ by athlete, task and interpretation, and that high cognitive anxiety on top of rising arousal can cause abrupt collapse rather than gentle decline. These are competing descriptive models rather than settled mechanism, so treat them as diagnostic lenses. Coaching goal → recognise direction of error, then activate or deactivate deliberately.
key_facts: Arousal = intensity of activation (neutral). Anxiety = unpleasant emotional state from threat appraisal (negative valence).
Anxiety splits: cognitive (worry, doubt, ↓ attentional width) vs somatic (↑HR, ↑breath rate, tension, nausea, urge to urinate).
State anxiety = right-now, fluctuating. Trait anxiety = stable dispositional tendency to perceive threat.
Inverted-U: performance peaks at moderate arousal; ↓ either side. Simple/power tasks tolerate higher arousal; complex, fine-skill tasks need lower. Descriptive pattern, not a proven mechanism.
IZOF (Hanin): each athlete has an individual optimal intensity band — may be low, moderate or high; identified by logging arousal vs performance over many sessions/races.

Catastrophe model (Hardy/Fazey): with high cognitive anxiety, over-arousal can produce a sudden performance drop rather than a smooth decline; recovery requires dropping arousal well below the crash point.
Directional interpretation: symptoms read as 'facilitative' (ready) are generally associated with better performance than identical symptoms read as 'debilitative' (panicking).
Over-arousal → rushed pacing, shallow chest breathing, over-gripping, tunnel vision, fumbled transitions. Under-arousal → flat warm-up, slow reaction, drifting focus, no urgency into stations.
Deactivate: slow nasal diaphragmatic breathing, exhale longer than inhale (~4-in / 6–8-out) → ↑ vagal influence, ↓HR; plus PMR, cue words, external focus, re-appraisal.
Activate: brisk/forceful breathing → ↑ sympathetic drive; plus primers and strides, energising self-talk, music, sharp movement prep, upright posture.

HYROX station order is fixed — SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump, Row, Farmers Carry, Sandbag Lunges, Wall Balls — each preceded by a 1 km run, so arousal plans can be rehearsed station by station.
45.training_link: Map your athlete's zone before you try to manage it: log pre-session arousal (1–10) plus mood words against actual output for 6–10 key sessions and race sims, and you will see their band rather than guessing at 'moderate'. In HYROX the error is usually over-arousal early — corral it with a fixed start routine and a paced first km, then use extended-exhale nasal breathing in the roxzone and on the sled push turnarounds. Reserve activation cues (sharp breaths, a slap, a trigger word) for the moments that genuinely need drive: the sled push, the eighth and final run, and the wall balls that close the race.

glossary.def: Global physiological and psychological activation level along a continuum from deep calm to extreme excitation. It carries no positive or negative meaning by itself.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: The thought-based component of anxiety — worry, self-doubt, catastrophising, and disrupted attention. Tends to rise earliest and can persist across a race.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: The bodily component of anxiety — racing heart, fast shallow breathing, tremor, sweat, gut distress. Typically peaks near the start and falls once the effort begins.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: Individual Zone of Optimal Functioning: the athlete-specific band of emotional intensity within which their best performances occur, established empirically from their own history.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Trait anxiety is a stable personality tendency to appraise situations as threatening; state anxiety is the momentary anxious response in a given situation.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: Whether an athlete labels their arousal symptoms as helpful readiness or harmful panic. Similar physiology, differing performance effect.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Any deliberate method used to lower arousal — extended-exhale breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, cue words, slowing the pre-station routine.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Any deliberate method used to raise arousal — fast breathing, strides or primers, energising self-talk, music, sharper movement prep.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A model in which high cognitive anxiety turns the inverted-U's gentle right-hand decline into an abrupt performance collapse that is hard to reverse mid-event.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The transition area an athlete moves through between each run and station. Its length varies by venue, which makes it the natural place to run a rehearsed breathing or cue routine.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

45.exam_focus: Correctly separating arousal from cognitive vs somatic anxiety and applying IZOF/inverted-U to diagnose over- or under-arousal in a race scenario, then selecting the matching activation or deactivation technique.

46.title: Goal setting & mental skills training
46.key_concept: Mental skills are trainable rather than fixed traits. Structure them around a three-tier goal hierarchy: outcome goals (placing, qualifying — motivating but dependent on others), performance goals (a personal time, a run split, a sled segment — self-referenced and measurable), and process goals (cadence, grip strategy, breathing pattern, wall ball tempo — controllable actions). Process goals are the only tier the athlete can directly execute moment to moment; the performance goal still runs in the background as a pacing reference she checks against, and the outcome goal belongs to the planning phase. Because arousal and fatigue narrow the range of cues an athlete can process, late-race attention falls back on whatever has been rehearsed — so simple, practised process cues carry the hardest sections. Imagery and self-talk are the delivery vehicles: imagery pre-encodes the sequence and its discomfort, instructional self-talk directs technique, motivational self-talk sustains effort. Confidence is built mainly from mastery experiences in training that replicates race demands, then stabilised by a consistent pre-performance routine.
key_facts: Goal tiers: outcome (vs others, low control) → performance (vs own standard) → process (controllable actions). Race-day attention sits on process; the performance goal stays as a pacing reference.

A focus resting solely on outcome goals is generally associated with higher cognitive anxiety and lower perceived control, especially when the field is unknown; performance and process goals are more robust to a bad wave draw.

Effective goals: specific + measurable + difficult but attainable given the athlete's ability and commitment + time-bound + written + reviewed. Vague 'do your best' instructions produce the weakest effect (Locke & Latham's goal-setting work).

Imagery quality factors (PETTLEP framework, Holmes & Collins): match the physical, environmental, task, timing, learning, emotion and perspective elements of the real thing — multisensory (noise, chalk, burning quads), real-time rather than fast-forwarded, in kit where practical, and pitched at the athlete's current ability. Perspective should suit the task; internal/first-person is the usual default for pacing and effort rehearsal, while an external view can help when checking body position. Rehearse coping (sled stalls, missed wall ball reps), not only perfect runs.

Self-talk types: instructional (technique/pacing cues — tends to help most on tasks where precision and movement quality decide the outcome, e.g. burpee broad jump rhythm) vs motivational (drive/effort — tends to help most on sustained gross-motor endurance efforts). A planned, positive self-talk strategy generally outperforms having no strategy; negative self-talk is not automatically harmful for every athlete, but it is unreliable and a poor thing to leave to chance.

Bandura's 4 sources of self-efficacy, in his proposed descending order of influence: mastery experience > vicarious experience (similar-athlete modelling) > verbal persuasion > interpretation of physiological/affective states.

Reinterpret arousal: teach that a high heart rate and heavy breathing in the roxzone can be read as a readiness signal rather than evidence of failing — the sensation is fixed, its meaning is interpreted.

Pre-performance routine = a short, fixed, rehearsed sequence of breath + cue word + first-action image. The research emphasis is on consistency of content and duration, not on any particular length; use it identically before every station in training so it transfers to race day.

Simulation training (compromised-running blocks, full or half sims) is one of the most useful mental-skills tools available: it builds mastery evidence, calibrates realistic performance goals, and pre-exposes the athlete to the specific discomfort of the later runs.
Track mental skills like physical ones — log cue adherence and self-talk quality alongside splits.

Race context: HYROX is 8 × 1 km runs alternating with 8 stations in a fixed order — SkiErg, sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jump, row, farmers carry, sandbag lunges, wall balls — with the roxzone transitions counting in total time. The fixed order is what makes cue rehearsal possible: the athlete always knows which station is next.
46.training_link: Give each athlete one performance goal per race (a target time or a run-split band) and no more than three process cues — typically one for running, one for the sled/carry group, one for wall balls — and make them say those cues aloud during simulation sessions so they are automatic by race week. Build their evidence file deliberately: log every compromised-run block and half-sim so that in the taper you can point to concrete mastery experiences instead of offering empty reassurance. When they report a racing heart rate and shaky legs on the start line, reframe it as their body arriving ready, and run them straight into the same breath-plus-cue routine they used before every station in training.

glossary.def: A goal defined by result relative to other competitors (podium, qualifier, ranking). Motivating in the planning phase but dependent on factors the athlete cannot control.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: A self-referenced standard such as a target finish time, a 1 km run split, or a wall ball set structure. Independent of the field, so it survives a slow heat or a crowded roxzone.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: A controllable action or technical focus executed in the moment — cadence, hip height on the sled, breath count on the SkiErg. The tier the athlete can directly act on while racing.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: An athlete's situation-specific belief that they can execute the actions needed to succeed at a given task. Distinct from broad trait confidence and strongest when built from personal mastery.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Deliberate multisensory simulation of a performance in the mind, including physical and emotional sensations. Used to pre-encode movement patterns, sequencing and coping responses.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: A framework for building imagery that resembles the real performance across seven elements — Physical, Environment, Task, Timing, Learning, Emotion, Perspective. The closer the match, the better the transfer.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Short internal cues that direct technique or pacing ('tall chest', 'drive the heel'). Most useful where movement quality decides efficiency.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: Internal statements that sustain effort, arousal and persistence ('this is my station', 'stay in it'). Most useful in prolonged, high-discomfort efforts.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: A consistent, rehearsed sequence of physical and cognitive actions performed immediately before a task, used to standardise attention and arousal across varying environments.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The reduction in the range of cues an athlete can process as arousal and fatigue rise (Easterbrook's cue-utilisation idea). Explains why only well-rehearsed, simple cues remain usable late in a race.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M14 12v18M14 12h12" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M30 30c8-2 16-10 30-14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/></svg>

46.exam_focus: Distinguishing outcome, performance and process goals and prescribing the right tier for a specific race-day scenario, with imagery/self-talk and Bandura's mastery-first efficacy sources as the supporting mechanisms.

47.title: Race-day mental strategies & pain coping
47.key_concept: Race day is a psychological skill executed under load. A rehearsed pre-race routine narrows arousal toward the athlete's optimal zone and removes decision-making from a chaotic call room. Once running, attention is a dial, not a switch: associative focus (cadence, breathing, split, technique cue) protects pacing and form; dissociative focus (counting, recalled rhythm, external scenery, mantra loops) tends to blunt perceived exertion when the work is fixed and safe. Segmenting the eight run–station couplets into small, winnable chunks keeps the effort psychologically finite. The back half brings rising discomfort — reframed as expected signal, not damage. After a bad station, a scripted reset (breath → cue → next chunk) is intended to stop one loss becoming three.
key_facts: Pre-race routine = fixed sequence (nutrition, warm-up, kit, activation, cue rehearsal) → ↓ decision load, ↑ predictability in the call room.

Two related but distinct arousal models: the inverted-U (performance falls off at both low and high arousal) and IZOF (Hanin), which replaces one universal optimum with an individually determined band. IZOF is the more defensible framing for coaching decisions.
HYROX is long and skill-loaded, so over-arousal at the gun plausibly costs more on run 1 pacing than mild under-arousal — treat this as a coaching heuristic, not a measured effect.

Associative attention = internal/task cues (breath, cadence, grip, sled hip angle, split) → supports pacing accuracy and technique under fatigue. Early work (Morgan & Pollock) linked it to elite endurance runners, but later evidence is mixed: athletes shift strategies with intensity rather than using one exclusively.

Dissociative attention = distraction (counting, crowd, imagery, recalled rhythm) → generally lowers RPE at a given workload; most useful in repetitive fixed-output blocks. Note: HYROX competition rules do not permit headphones/personal music devices, so any 'music' strategy must be internal.
Rule of thumb: associate when the task can go wrong (sled, burpee broad jump, wall ball depth, roxzone) — dissociate when output is locked and discomfort is the only problem.
Segmentation: 8 runs + 8 stations = 16 chunks; further chunk within a station (wall balls in sets of 10–15; ski/row per 250 m of the 1000 m) → each chunk has its own finish line.

Back half (Row → Farmers Carry → Sandbag Lunges → Wall Balls) is where pacing debt is paid; expect ↑ RPE at the SAME external power as fatigue accumulates — pre-frame this so it isn't read as failure.

Pain-coping toolkit: acceptance/reframe ('this is on schedule'), rhythmic breathing, self-talk, goal-shrinking ('next 10 reps'). The matching hypothesis (Theodorakis and colleagues) suggests instructional self-talk suits precision/technique tasks and motivational self-talk suits effort tasks; effects are real but modest.
Refocus script after a bad station: acknowledge (1–2 s) → physical reset (exhale, posture) → single process cue → attention forward to next chunk; no in-race score-keeping.

Non-first-person self-talk (second person or own name) is associated with self-distancing and lower anxiety under pressure. Catastrophizing and outcome comparison (place, rivals) are plausible contributors to pacing errors — the mechanism is well argued, the HYROX-specific effect is not quantified.
47.training_link: Rehearse the routine and the attention plan in training, not on race morning — run at least two full or half simulations where your athlete uses the exact warm-up sequence, the exact chunking (16 blocks, wall balls in sets), and the exact cues they will use in the arena. Assign attention per station in writing: associative on sled push/pull, burpee broad jump and wall ball depth; dissociative counting or a mantra on ski and row. Farmers carry sits in between — output is locked, but grip and posture still need periodic checking, so pair dissociation with a scheduled grip cue. Because headphones are not permitted in competition, any rhythm or music strategy has to be internal and practised that way. Then deliberately sabotage one rep — a no-rep call, a dropped sandbag — and make them run the refocus script, so the reset is trained rather than improvised at station six.

glossary.def: Deliberately monitoring internal or task-relevant signals — breathing, cadence, technique, splits — while working. Supports pacing precision and movement quality but raises awareness of discomfort.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Directing attention away from bodily sensation to external or unrelated content. Tends to lower perceived exertion at a given workload, at the cost of pacing and technique sensitivity.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A fixed, rehearsed sequence of actions and cues run before competing. Its proposed value is consistency and reduced decision-making, not superstition.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Breaking a long event into small, individually completable units so the athlete only ever confronts the current chunk rather than the whole race.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The classic model in which performance peaks at moderate arousal and declines when arousal is too low or too high. Criticised for assuming a single optimum common to all athletes.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Hanin's model: the arousal/anxiety band in which a given athlete performs best. It is personal — some race well keyed-up, others need calm — and is identified from that athlete's performance history, not assumed.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Reinterpreting a sensation or event so its meaning changes without denying it — e.g. burning quads read as an expected marker of race pace rather than as impending failure.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Short technical commands directed at execution ('tall chest', 'push the floor away'). Best suited to skill and form under fatigue.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: Effort- and confidence-directed phrases ('stay with it', 'you trained this'). Best suited to sustaining output in simple, high-discomfort efforts.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 8c8 12 14 18 14 23a14 14 0 0 1-28 0c0-5 6-11 14-23Z" fill="#ffb86b" opacity=".5"/><path d="M34 24c3 3 9 3 12 0" stroke="#0b1220" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/></svg>

glossary.def: A pre-planned 3–5 second sequence used after an error or bad station to interrupt rumination and return attention to the next controllable action.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

47.exam_focus: Selecting and justifying associative vs dissociative attention for a specific HYROX station or race phase, and applying a structured refocus/segmentation strategy to a described athlete scenario.

48.title: Needs analysis & athlete assessment
48.key_concept: A HYROX needs analysis is a two-sided audit: the demands of the event versus the athlete in front of you. The event is 8 x 1 km of running alternating with 8 fixed-order stations (SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump, Row, Farmers Carry, Sandbag Lunges, Wall Balls), finishing on wall balls — roughly an hour for elite athletes and commonly well over 90 minutes for typical age-group finishers. Physiologically it is a predominantly aerobic effort with repeated higher-intensity surges, and every run is performed on pre-fatigued legs. The athlete side is training history, injury history, current fitness profile, lifestyle and recovery capacity, division, race goal and time-to-race. You gather objective test data and subjective history, convert it into a profile, then find the largest gap between current capability and race requirement — the limiting quality. That gap sets the training priority order; everything else is maintained, not developed, until it becomes limiting.
key_facts: Two halves of a needs analysis: demands of the sport → then demands on the athlete. Never athlete-only.

Race structure to profile against: 8 x 1 km runs alternating with 8 stations in fixed order — SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump, Row, Farmers Carry, Sandbag Lunges, Wall Balls. Every run after the first is compromised running.

Map demands to qualities honestly by region: upper-body/trunk pulling and pushing endurance (SkiErg, Row, Sled Pull), lower-body strength-endurance under heavy horizontal load (Sled Push, Sled Pull), grip and trunk stiffness (Farmers Carry, Sandbag Lunges), unilateral leg endurance (Sandbag Lunges), repeated squat-to-overhead local muscular endurance (Wall Balls), and aerobic/threshold running underneath all of it.

Core intake blocks: training history (years, modality bias, current volume), injury history (mechanism, recurrence, current irritability), lifestyle load (job, sleep, travel, stress, nutrition), division + goal + race date, and prior race splits if any.

Assessment battery ≈ aerobic (threshold or ~5 km run test, ideally with HR), station-specific time trials (1000 m Ski, 1000 m Row, max unbroken wall-ball set), strength (heavy sled push/pull tolerance, hinge/squat competence), movement screen for lunge, hinge and overhead positions.
Limiting quality = the biggest race-relevant gap, not the weakest raw number. Judge it against target finish time, then time budget.

Split-based diagnosis: run-time drift across the 8 runs ↑ → aerobic/durability limiter; station times fine but roxzone and the first 200 m after stations poor → transition/compromised-running limiter; single station outlier (sled, wall balls) → strength or local-endurance limiter.

Roxzone time is not trivial: summed across the transitions it commonly runs to several minutes, and is generally larger in slower athletes. Treat the exact figure as something you measure from your own athlete's splits, not as a fixed published benchmark — it is often a cheap, coachable time saving that outranks fitness work early.

Priority order rule: develop 1 (max 2) qualities at a time; the rest get maintenance dosing. Maintenance works by holding intensity while cutting volume/frequency — roughly one quality session per week is a common practical dose, not a precise physiological constant.
Injury history + irritability outranks the limiter: if the limiter is sled push but the athlete has an irritable patellar tendon, tissue tolerance becomes priority 1.
Recovery capacity (sleep, shift work, life stress, training age) caps weekly volume — set the ceiling first, then allocate sessions to priorities.
Re-test on a cycle (≈every 4-8 weeks); the limiting quality is not fixed and the priority order should shift with it.
48.training_link: Before you write a single session, sit your athlete down and get the four inputs that actually change the plan: what they've trained for the last two years, what hurts and how easily, how much sleep and life stress they really have, and which division and finish time they're chasing. Then test them — a threshold run, a 1000 m Ski, a 1000 m Row, an unbroken wall-ball set and a heavy sled — and rank the gaps against that goal time, not against each other. Pull their own roxzone and run-split numbers from any previous race rather than assuming a benchmark. Build the block around the top one or two gaps, maintain the rest at reduced volume but honest intensity, and re-test in 4-8 weeks before you rewrite the priority order.

glossary.def: Structured comparison of a sport's physiological, biomechanical and tactical demands against an individual athlete's current profile. Its output is a ranked list of training priorities.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: The physical or technical attribute whose deficit costs the athlete the most race time relative to their goal. It receives the largest share of training stimulus.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Running performed on pre-fatigued musculature immediately after a station, with accumulated metabolites and reduced force capacity. It behaves as a trainable quality distinct from fresh running speed.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: How much training stress an athlete can absorb and adapt to, influenced by sleep, nutrition, life stress, training age and health. It caps prescribable volume regardless of ambition.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The HYROX transition area an athlete moves through between a run and a station. Time spent in it counts toward the finish time, so movement discipline and pacing through it are coachable performance variables.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The reduced stimulus needed to hold an already-adequate quality — typically preserving training intensity while cutting volume and frequency — so training resources can go to the limiter.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: How easily a symptomatic tissue is provoked, how severely, and how long it takes to settle. High irritability forces conservative loading regardless of what the performance profile says.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The progressive slowing of successive run splits across a race. Large drift points to aerobic durability or pacing failure rather than a deficit in top-end speed.

48.exam_focus: Given an athlete case (history, injury, splits, lifestyle, goal), identify the limiting quality and justify a ranked training priority order with correct maintenance of the non-priority qualities.

49.title: Testing & benchmarks for HYROX
49.key_concept: Testing in HYROX exists to drive decisions, not to collect numbers. A useful battery is specific (mirrors the race's compromised-running-under-load demand), reliable (same protocol, same equipment, same time of day, controlled prior 24-48 h), and valid for the quality you claim to measure. Build it in layers: an aerobic anchor (a threshold estimate plus a time-trial pace), a race-transfer anchor (run-station couplets or a partial sim), station-specific benchmarks (SkiErg/Row 1000 m, sled times, wall ball unbroken capacity), and strength/durability markers. Retest on block boundaries, not on impulse. Interpret each result as a limiter ranking — engine, station skill, strength, or roxzone economy — then aim the next block at the biggest gap.
key_facts: Test purpose = decision. No decision attached → drop the test.
Validity = measures the intended quality; reliability = repeatable (low typical error); specificity = resembles race demand. All three needed.
Standardize the controllables: warm-up, footwear, time of day, sled surface/load, 24-48 h prior load, fuelling, caffeine. Uncontrolled sled friction makes cross-venue sled times near-useless.

Race format to test against: 8 x 1 km runs alternating with 8 stations in the fixed order SkiErg → Sled Push → Sled Pull → Burpee Broad Jump → Row → Farmers Carry → Sandbag Lunges → Wall Balls. Benchmarks are only specific if the distances, loads and order match the athlete's actual division.

Aerobic markers: a 5 km TT is a solid fitness/pace anchor but is raced ABOVE threshold by most athletes — do not read it directly as threshold pace. For a threshold estimate use a ~30 min steady TT, or a lactate/ventilatory threshold test if lab access exists. HR at a fixed submaximal pace tracks drift cheaply.
Race-transfer test: 4 x (1 km run + 1 station), stations taken in race order, at race intent — a better predictor of race outcome than any isolated station PB.

Station benchmarks: 1000 m SkiErg, 1000 m Row, 50 m sled push, 50 m sled pull (fixed load/surface), 80 m burpee broad jump, 200 m farmers carry, 100 m sandbag lunge, 100 wall balls. Use the athlete's own division standard for loads and reps rather than a remembered number.
Compromised-running index: fresh 1 km TT pace vs average 1 km pace inside the couplet test. Gap ↑ → durability/station-economy limiter, not raw speed.

Strength markers that matter: heavy sled-push proxy, trap-bar/back-squat 3-5RM or e1RM, front-rack or Zercher hold time, grip endurance (a farmers hold at race load held for a minute-plus is a practical working target, not a validated cut-off).
Retest cadence: benchmark battery every 6-12 weeks (block boundary); simple monitors (submax HR, RPE at fixed pace) weekly. Retesting a slow-changing quality every 2 weeks buries signal in noise.

Treat change as real only if it exceeds the test's typical error — on the order of 1-2 % for a well-practised erg TT, and larger (often several percent) for sled, burpee and sim-based tests. Below that, call it noise. Establish your own typical error from repeat trials rather than trusting a generic figure.

Half-sim (4 runs + 4 stations) costs far less recovery than a full sim and yields most of the information; common coaching practice is 1-2 full sims per build, placed well clear of race week. Time roxzone separately — transitions are a coachable, measurable variable.
49.training_link: Open a new athlete with a 5 km TT plus a 4 x (1 km + station) couplet test using the four stations they claim to hate, and time their roxzone entries separately — you will often find the limiter is pacing discipline or transitions rather than fitness. Lock the exact protocol (loads, surface, station order, warm-up, time of day) in writing so the 8-week retest is comparable, and only change the plan when the delta beats the test's typical error. Then re-test one station-specific marker mid-block as a cheap check that the intervention is actually working.

glossary.def: The degree to which a test actually reflects the quality you intend to measure. A 1 km fresh TT is a valid speed marker but a weak validity claim for race-day compromised running.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The repeatability of a test under identical conditions, expressed as the normal spread between repeats. Change smaller than typical error is noise, not adaptation.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: How closely test conditions match competition demands — load, duration, movement pattern, fatigue state, station order and transitions.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Running performed in the fatigued, locally-loaded state that follows a station. The gap between fresh and compromised pace is a primary HYROX diagnostic.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: A repeated run + single-station pairing performed at race intent, used to expose pacing discipline and station-to-run recovery without the cost of a full simulation.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: A fixed, repeatable set of tests re-run under identical conditions at block boundaries so results are comparable over a season.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Ordering an athlete's constraints (aerobic engine, station technique, strength, grip, transitions) by their estimated cost in race minutes, to prioritize the next block.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The HYROX transition area an athlete moves through between each run and station. It carries its own running distance on top of the 8 x 1 km, is included in total race time, and is a coachable, measurable performance variable.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Monitoring = low-cost, frequent, non-disruptive (submax HR, RPE, session pace). Testing = high-cost, infrequent, maximal or near-maximal, needing taper and recovery.

49.exam_focus: Selecting the appropriate, specific and reliable test for a stated limiter and correctly converting the result — especially a fresh-vs-compromised pace gap — into the next block's training priority.

50.title: Individualising the programme
50.key_concept: Individualisation converts needs-analysis output into a repeating weekly template. Rank limiters by cost in race minutes — running under fatigue usually dominates, since the 8 km of running is the single largest time block for most amateurs — then allocate sessions to the biggest leak first. Build the week backwards from non-negotiables: one compromised-running session (run → station → run), one aerobic long run, one heavy lower-body strength day, plus grip, hinge and posterior-chain support. Remaining hours are discretionary and scale with the athlete's real availability. Strength serves the stations, not the mirror. Progress load gradually with a deload every 3rd–4th week, and let autoregulation (RPE, velocity loss, readiness) set the daily dose.
key_facts: Race shape: 8 × 1 km runs alternating with 8 stations in fixed order — SkiErg, sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jump, row, farmers carry, sandbag lunges, wall balls. Station travel distance totals roughly 2.5 km (SkiErg 1000 m, sled push 50 m, sled pull 50 m, burpee broad jump 80 m, row 1000 m, farmers carry 200 m, sandbag lunges 100 m; wall balls are counted in reps, not distance), so the athlete covers on the order of 10–11 km all-in.

Running is typically the largest single share of finishing time for amateur athletes — published field analyses commonly put it around half, though the exact split varies by division, athlete and event. Treat it as the default first limiter unless the athlete's own splits say otherwise.
Prioritise limiters by minutes lost, not by what feels weakest. Compare athlete's station splits + roxzone time vs division benchmarks.
Weekly non-negotiables: 1 compromised-run/hybrid session, 1 aerobic long run, 1 heavy lower-body strength, 1 grip/carry+pull exposure. Everything above that is optional volume.
Typical allocation by profile — runner-type: ↑ strength/station density, keep 2 easy runs; strength-type: ↑ aerobic base volume, cap heavy lifting to 2 sessions, ↓ hypertrophy work.

Aerobic distribution ~70–80% low intensity / 20–30% moderate-hard for most weeks (the broad pattern seen in endurance-athlete training-distribution research, not a precise prescription); race-specific compromised work sits in the hard bucket and is capped at 1–2×/week.
Time-poor athlete (≤4–5 h/wk): merge qualities — strength circuit finished with a run, tempo run + wall balls, sled work as both strength and conditioning. Drop isolation, not specificity.

Minimum effective dose for strength retention ≈ 1–2 heavy sessions/week at ≥80% 1RM with much-reduced volume; detraining studies consistently show maintained intensity is what preserves strength when frequency and volume fall.

Short layoffs: aerobic markers (VO2max, plasma volume) decline measurably within the first 2–4 weeks, while maximal strength typically decays more slowly over comparable periods — so aerobic work is usually the more urgent thing to protect in a compressed week. Rates vary widely with training age and how complete the layoff is.

Progression: a ~5–10% weekly increase in the key load metric (run km, sled distance, tonnage) is a practical coaching heuristic rather than a validated rule — the underlying '10% rule' has not held up well in injury-prevention trials, so treat it as a starting point and let symptoms and readiness override it. Deload every 3rd–4th week at ~40–60% volume, intensity largely retained.

Autoregulation levers, cheapest first: session RPE vs target, velocity loss cutoffs (~10–20% for strength/power work, ~20–40% where hypertrophy is the goal), pace-at-fixed-HR drift, subjective readiness/sleep, HRV trend (7-day rolling vs baseline — noisy at individual-day resolution, so read the trend, not one reading).
Reassess every 3–4 weeks with a repeated benchmark (e.g. 4 km compromised sim or 2-station + 1 km time trial) — re-rank limiters, then rewrite the template rather than tinkering weekly.
50.training_link: Start by pulling your athlete's last race or sim splits and comparing each 1 km and each station against division benchmarks — the two or three biggest gaps, plus roxzone time, become the whole basis of the template. If they only have four hours a week, don't shrink your ideal plan proportionally; rebuild it as three merged sessions (heavy lower + sled and carries, compromised intervals, one long easy run) and accept that isolation work disappears. Then hold the skeleton for three to four weeks, autoregulate volume day to day on RPE and readiness, and only rewrite the plan after the next benchmark retest.

glossary.def: Running performed immediately after a station, with pre-fatigued legs and disturbed breathing/pacing after heavy local muscular work. The specific quality HYROX rewards, and rarely trained by running volume alone.

glossary.def: Ordering an athlete's weaknesses by estimated race-time cost rather than by raw deficiency, so training hours go to the largest recoverable losses.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A fixed skeleton of session types and their placement across the week; contents change block to block, the skeleton mostly does not.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The blunting of strength or aerobic adaptation when both are trained hard in close proximity — most evident for lower-body strength and power, and smaller in trained athletes than early studies suggested. Managed by session order, separation (commonly ≥3–6 h, more if practical) and intensity spacing, not by avoiding one quality.

glossary.def: The smallest training stimulus that maintains or slightly advances a quality. The core planning tool for time-poor athletes and for in-season maintenance.
