glossary.def: Adjusting the prescribed session in real time using objective or subjective readiness markers, so planned load matches the athlete's actual capacity that day.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A planned low-volume week (roughly 40–60% of normal) that allows accumulated fatigue to dissipate so fitness gains become expressible.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The transition area between run and station, and the time accumulated moving through it. A trainable time sink — coach entry/exit routines, equipment approach and pacing into the mat.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

50.exam_focus: Expect to be given an athlete profile with splits and a weekly hour budget and asked to justify session allocation, what to cut when time shrinks, and how progression plus autoregulation are applied across the block.

51.title: Coaching decisions — applied case studies
51.key_concept: Case work is a diagnostic discipline: identify the rate-limiter, then apply the smallest intervention that moves it. HYROX performance decomposes into run economy/aerobic ceiling, station-specific strength-endurance, compromised-running tolerance, roxzone efficiency, and pacing discipline. Archetypes recur — strong-but-slow (aerobic ceiling caps everything), runner-fails-on-sleds (a force/strength deficit against a high-friction horizontal push and pull), the recurring calf (load-tolerance and tissue-capacity failure, not a flexibility problem), the first-timer peaking (taper and race-execution, not fitness). Each demands a different lever: aerobic volume, targeted heavy strength, progressive calf/tendon loading, or rehearsal plus deload. Wrong lever → training stress without transfer. Note that archetypes are a starting hypothesis for triage, not a diagnosis; athletes commonly present with mixed or overlapping limiters.
key_facts: Race format anchor: 8 × 1 km runs alternating with 8 stations in fixed order — SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jump, Row, Farmers Carry, Sandbag Lunges, Wall Balls. Diagnosis starts from where in that sequence time is actually lost.
Diagnose by profile: split the race into run time, station time, roxzone time → the biggest addressable loss is the target.
Strong-but-slow → aerobic ceiling is the usual limiter; ↑ easy-run volume + threshold work, hold strength at maintenance (1–2 quality sessions/wk with intensity kept high) to limit detraining.

Runner-fails-on-sleds → force deficit. Sleds are high-force efforts against friction with a large maximal-strength contribution — they are also metabolically brutal, so this is a strength emphasis, not a claim that sleds are 'not cardio'. ↑ heavy squat/leg press/hip-hinge + prowler intervals at or near race load.

Sled push/pull cost scales strongly with friction (floor surface, sled runners, venue) — coach technique (low body angle, short choppy steps, avoid stopping on push; hip-hinge and rhythmic arm-over-arm on pull) before adding load, since each restart means overcoming static friction again.

Recurring calf issues → most often a capacity problem; progressive calf loading (straight- and bent-knee, heavy and slow), sane run-volume progression, and review eccentric exposure from lunges and wall balls. Rule out non-training drivers (footwear change, prior injury, sleep/fuelling) before assuming pure load error.
Compromised running (running under station fatigue) is a specific trainable quality → run→station→run couplets, not isolated sessions.

First race peak → roughly 1–2 week taper, ↓ volume ~40–60% with intensity largely retained (the pattern best supported in the taper literature); rehearse pacing, transitions, wall-ball sets, and fuelling. Meaningful fitness gains in the final two weeks are unlikely, so execution is the lever.

Wall balls are 100 reps in every individual division — only ball weight and target height change (Open men 6 kg to a 3.00 m target, Open women 4 kg to 2.70 m; Pro men 9 kg to 3.00 m, Pro women 6 kg to 2.70 m). This is the classic blow-up point. Pre-plan set sizes (e.g. 25/25/20/15/15) rather than going to failure.

Pacing: the first 1 km should feel restrained — going out hard costs disproportionately in runs 5–8; roxzone discipline is comparatively free speed for most amateurs, with no change in fitness required.
Re-test the same limiter after 4–8 weeks; if the metric didn't move, revisit the diagnosis before repeating or intensifying the block.
51.training_link: When an athlete brings you a race result, don't prescribe from feel — split their time into runs, stations, and roxzone, and compare each against their peer group to find the likely limiter. If their sleds are the outlier, spend a block on heavy push/pull strength rather than adding more intervals; if their late runs collapse, look first at pacing and compromised-run couplets. Re-test the same segment in about six weeks and let the number, rather than the athlete's preference, decide whether you keep the lever or change it.

glossary.def: The physiological or technical quality most constraining race time. Training it typically yields the largest return per unit of training stress, though athletes often have more than one.

glossary.def: The transition area between run and station. Time spent there counts toward total race time and is often the cheapest performance gain.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C26 31 38 26 50 16 S66 6 72 6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="50" y1="6" x2="50" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The capacity to repeat submaximal force output with minimal decay — a dominant quality on sleds, carries, lunges and wall balls.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: How much cumulative mechanical stress a tissue can absorb before symptoms. Raised primarily by progressive loading rather than by rest or stretching alone.

glossary.def: A planned pre-race reduction in volume with intensity largely retained, to shed fatigue while preserving fitness.

glossary.def: The structured comparison of race demands against the athlete's current profile, producing a ranked list of gaps to train.

glossary.def: Second half of the race slower than the first — often evidence of a pacing error, though it can also reflect a genuine endurance ceiling.

51.exam_focus: Given a case profile (splits, history, race goal), identify the most likely rate-limiter and justify the single most appropriate intervention over plausible distractors.

52.title: Reflective practice & the growth mindset
52.key_concept: Module 1 positions the reflective coach as the professional spine of Level 2. Schön's distinction is the starting point: reflection-in-action means reading and adjusting a session while it is still running — changing a cue, capping a sled load, cutting an interval when movement quality collapses — whereas reflection-on-action is the structured review afterwards. Reviews tend to stick when they follow a simple written cycle, such as Rolfe's 'what? so what? now what?' or Gibbs' longer loop, fed by deliberate inputs: session logs, filmed station work, peer observation and athlete feedback. Dweck's mindset research then shapes how findings are interpreted: praising process and strategy rather than talent, using 'not yet' language, and treating DNFs and poor splits as information tends to build athletes who seek feedback rather than fear it. The guard-rail is honesty — growth mindset is not toxic positivity, and sleep, injury and age still bound what is achievable.
key_facts: Schön's reflection-in-action is live adjustment during the session; reflection-on-action is structured review after it ends.
Rolfe's reflective framework is three questions asked in order: what happened, so what does it mean, now what will I do.
Gibbs' reflective cycle is a longer loop — description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan — suited to bigger events like a race or an injury.
Dweck's growth mindset is the belief that abilities are developable through effort, strategy and feedback; a fixed mindset treats them as static traits.
Praising process and strategy tends to build resilience, while praising talent tends to make athletes risk-averse and fragile after setbacks.
'Not yet' language reframes a failed standard as a stage of progress — 'you can't hold 4:45 pace yet' — without lowering the standard itself.
A DNF or a bad split is information for the reflection cycle, not a verdict on the athlete or the coach.
A deliberate self-review system combines four inputs: session logs, filmed station work, peer observation, and athlete feedback loops.
Mindset shapes cue receptivity: growth-oriented athletes tend to hear correction as help, while fixed-oriented athletes may hear the same cue as criticism, which erodes adherence.
Reflection-in-action in HYROX looks like swapping a cue mid-station, capping sled load when mechanics break down, or shortening intervals when quality collapses.
Growth mindset is not toxic positivity: real constraints such as sleep debt, injury and age still limit what improvement is available, and pretending otherwise damages trust.
Peer observation works best with one narrow, agreed focus per visit — for example cue economy — rather than general impressions.
A reflection only changes practice when it ends in a written 'now what' action that is carried into the next session plan.
The reflective coach is the through-line of the whole Level 2 course: every later module (physiology, nutrition, periodization, mental performance) supplies material for the same review loop.
52.training_link: This week, close every coaching session with a two-minute written Rolfe cycle: one line on what happened, one on so what, one 'now what' action that goes straight into the next session plan. Film one station per group session — sled or wall balls are the highest-yield — and review the clip against your own cueing, not just the athlete's mechanics. Swap one session of peer observation with another coach, each watching for a single agreed focus. Then audit your language: replace talent praise ('you're a natural on the erg') with process praise ('your pacing plan held'), and reframe one athlete's recent bad split or DNF as data using 'not yet' phrasing — while openly naming any real constraint, such as poor sleep or a niggle, rather than talking past it.

glossary.def: Schön's term for thinking and adjusting while the activity is still happening — reading the session live and changing cues, loads or structure in real time.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Schön's term for structured review after the event, done deliberately and ideally in writing, to convert experience into changed future practice.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A minimal three-question reflection cycle — what? so what? now what? — designed to be fast enough to use after every session.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A six-stage reflection loop (description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan) better suited to significant events such as races, injuries or conflicts.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Dweck's term for the belief that abilities can be developed through effort, strategy and feedback, which tends to increase persistence and feedback-seeking.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The belief that abilities are innate and largely unchangeable, which tends to make setbacks feel like verdicts and correction feel like criticism.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Praise directed at strategy, effort and execution ('your transitions were disciplined') rather than at talent; it tends to build resilience where talent praise builds fragility.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Framing an unmet standard as a stage of progress rather than a fixed limit — 'not yet' keeps the standard intact while signalling it is reachable.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Relentless optimism that denies real constraints or genuine setbacks; it is a distortion of growth mindset and tends to erode athlete trust.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Having another coach watch a session with one narrow, pre-agreed focus and give structured feedback — a low-cost external input to the self-review system.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A routine, structured channel (for example a short post-session or weekly prompt) through which athletes tell the coach what landed, what confused them and how sessions felt.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: How open an athlete is to receiving and acting on technical correction; it is shaped strongly by mindset and by how the coach frames feedback.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

52.exam_focus: Expect to be asked to distinguish reflection-in-action from reflection-on-action with a session example, and to identify growth- versus fixed-mindset coach language in a scenario — for instance choosing the process-praise or 'not yet' response over talent praise or toxic positivity.

53.title: Holistic athlete development & coaching culture
53.key_concept: Holistic athlete development treats the HYROX athlete as a whole person rather than a set of training variables: physiology, psychology and social context interact, so a biopsychosocial lens tends to predict performance and adherence better than fitness metrics alone. Because most HYROX competitors are working adults, training is only one stressor among work, family, finances and sleep, all drawing on the same recovery budget — the coach programmes against total life-load, not the plan on paper. This differs sharply from youth long-term athlete development models: the adult amateur needs retention, health and sustainable progress, not talent identification. A deliberate club culture — belonging, visible progress, shared effort and celebration — is the retention engine, while athlete education multiplies the coach by teaching self-management. Aerobic base, strength reserves and station skill floors are multi-year projects, and leaderboard-only or more-is-better cultures are the classic red flags.
key_facts: The biopsychosocial model views performance and adherence as the product of interacting biological, psychological and social factors, not fitness alone.
Training is only one stressor among work, family, finances and poor sleep, and all of them draw on the same finite recovery budget.

Most HYROX competitors are working-age amateurs with jobs and families — HYROX itself reports an average participant age in the late 30s and a majority-amateur field — so retention and health, not youth talent development, are the coaching priorities.
Youth LTAD models emphasise developmental stages and talent pathways, whereas adult amateur development emphasises adherence, injury avoidance and sustainable progression.
A HYROX race is 8 x 1 km runs alternated with 8 functional stations, a demand profile that rewards multi-year aerobic and strength foundations over short-term peaking.
This lesson frames four practical levers of club retention: belonging, visible progress, shared effort and celebration rituals.

As covered in the Motivation, adherence & behaviour change lesson, self-determination theory's needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness explain why those retention levers work: belonging feeds relatedness, and visible progress feeds competence.
Athlete education is a coaching multiplier: athletes who understand why a session exists self-regulate better during the many hours the coach is absent.
Safeguarding in a community setting means clear professional boundaries, appropriate communication channels, and never exploiting the coach-athlete power imbalance.
Aerobic base, strength reserve and station skill floors are multi-year projects that race-to-race planning systematically undermines.
A leaderboard-only culture retains the top performers and quietly loses everyone else.
Treating overtraining as a badge of honour is a culture red flag that normalises under-recovery and predicts injury and dropout.

A heavy life-stress week should trigger a planned load reduction — cutting weekly training load by roughly 20-30% is a practical heuristic, not a published model, and works best when agreed with the athlete in advance.
53.training_link: This week, audit each athlete's life-load before you audit their training load: a two-minute check-in ('work, sleep, home — score each out of five') tells you whether the written session fits the day. For your busiest professionals, agree in advance which session gets cut first in a heavy week, so reductions feel planned rather than like failure. Add one visible-progress ritual — a benchmark board, a monthly re-test, a shout-out at the end of Saturday's session — and explain the why behind one programming decision to the whole group, so athletes begin self-managing. Finally, check your own culture honestly: if rest is mocked or the leaderboard is the only story your club tells, change the story.

glossary.def: A framework viewing health and performance as the product of interacting biological, psychological and social factors, rather than physiology alone.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The cumulative physiological wear produced by all stressors combined — training, work, family, finances and poor sleep all contribute to the same total.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: An informal coaching term for the sum of non-training stressors competing for an athlete's finite recovery capacity; programmed training should flex around it.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Staged frameworks built primarily around youth developmental windows and talent pathways; their emphases are largely mismatched to the adult amateur HYROX population.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Load-monitoring method (session RPE multiplied by minutes, giving arbitrary units) covered fully in the Monitoring load & readiness lesson; used here only to make life-load reductions concrete.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The policies and behaviours that protect members from harm or exploitation in a club setting: transparent coaching arrangements, agreed communication channels, clear coach boundaries and awareness of the coach-athlete power imbalance.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The technique level an athlete can reproduce under race fatigue without coaching input; raised gradually over years of deliberate practice.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The buffer between an athlete's maximal strength and the absolute demands of the stations; a larger reserve lowers the relative effort of every rep and push.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Planning only as far as the next event, so repeated tapers and recoveries crowd out the sustained blocks that build long-term capacities.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

53.exam_focus: Expect multiple-choice items asking you to identify features of a holistic development culture, distinguish adult amateur coaching from youth LTAD, and choose the correct coach response when life stress collides with the written plan; culture red flags such as leaderboard-only clubs and glorified overtraining are likely distractor material.

54.title: Exam synthesis — recovery, monitoring & injury management
54.key_concept: This synthesis day is about classification under exam pressure: given a scenario, place the athlete correctly on the recovery–fatigue continuum and choose between monitor, modify, or refer. Sleep remains the recovery intervention with the broadest, most consistent support; the rest — cold-water immersion, compression, massage — tend to offer small or context-dependent benefits, and chronic post-lifting cold immersion may blunt strength adaptations. Monitoring tools answer different questions: session-RPE (after Foster, built on Borg's effort scales) quantifies internal load cheaply; HRV and resting heart rate index autonomic status but are noisy day to day; simple wellness questionnaires often shift earliest. The ACWR is a useful teaching heuristic but statistically contested, so treat it as one signal, never a law. The functional overreaching → non-functional overreaching → overtraining syndrome continuum (per the ECSS/ACSM consensus) is distinguished by recovery timescale and performance response — not by soreness, and never by assumed laziness.
key_facts: Sleep is the recovery modality with the most consistent evidence; most other modalities (cold water, compression, massage) show small or context-dependent effects.
Regular cold-water immersion after strength sessions may blunt hypertrophy and strength adaptations, so reserve it for competition-dense phases rather than everyday training.
Session-RPE load = RPE (0–10 scale) x session duration in minutes, expressed in arbitrary units (AU).

ACWR divides acute load (typically the last 7 days) by chronic load (typically the 28-day average weekly load); the often-quoted 0.8–1.3 'sweet spot' is a heuristic and the metric is statistically contested.

Functional overreaching recovers with supercompensation within days to about two weeks; non-functional overreaching stagnates for weeks to months; overtraining syndrome persists for months and is rare.

Overtraining syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion — a physician must rule out illness (e.g. thyroid dysfunction, anaemia, infection, clinical depression) before the label applies, so the coach's job is to refer, not diagnose.

Early warning signs of non-functional overreaching include performance decline despite maintained effort, elevated resting heart rate, disturbed sleep, and mood disturbance; muscle soreness is not a reliable marker of either recovery or overtraining.
Most HYROX injuries trace back to load error — too much, too soon, on too little chronic base — rather than intrinsically 'dangerous' movements.

Typical HYROX injury map: knee (patellofemoral) pain with spikes in lunges, wall balls and running; Achilles/calf issues with sudden running volume or speed increases; low-back complaints with sled work and loaded carries under fatigue; shoulder irritation with wall-ball, sled and pressing volume.
Movement screens predict injury poorly at the individual level, so use them to inform programming and coaching priorities while relying on ongoing monitoring to manage risk.
Return-to-training logic runs range and pain-free movement first, then load, then speed and plyometric or impact work, then sport-specific density — load before speed.

A practical traffic-light rule for niggles: pain up to about 3/10 that settles within 24 hours is amber (modify and monitor); pain above that, worsening across sessions, or changing movement mechanics is red (stop and refer).
Wellness questionnaires (sleep quality, soreness, stress, mood) tend to detect fatigue shifts earlier than heart-rate-based measures, at near-zero cost.
Single-day drops in HRV or single elevated resting-HR readings are usually noise; decisions should rest on multi-day trends against an individual baseline.
54.training_link: This week, install one lightweight monitoring stack across your HYROX squad: a four-item morning wellness check (sleep, soreness, stress, mood) plus sRPE logged within 30 minutes of every session. On Sunday, review each athlete's weekly AU total against their previous month before you add sled or running volume — hunt for spikes, not magic ratios. Apply the traffic-light rule to every reported niggle in the diary, regressing stations (lighter sled, shallower lunge range, ski instead of run) for ambers. Finally, rehearse the referral conversation: pick the athlete whose numbers look flattest and decide in advance what pattern would make you send them to a physician rather than coach harder.

glossary.def: Internal-load method multiplying an athlete's post-session rating of perceived exertion (0–10) by session duration in minutes, giving load in arbitrary units.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: External load is the work prescribed or done (km, kg, metres); internal load is the athlete's physiological and perceptual response to it (HR, RPE). The same external load can produce very different internal loads.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Beat-to-beat variation in heart rhythm, commonly summarised as RMSSD, used as a proxy for autonomic recovery status; meaningful only as a trend against an individual baseline.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Acute (about 7-day) load divided by chronic (about 28-day average weekly) load, popularised as a spike detector; its predictive validity is statistically contested, so treat it as one signal among several.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Planned short-term overload producing a temporary performance dip that rebounds, often with supercompensation, within days to roughly two weeks of reduced load.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Unplanned fatigue state in which performance stagnates or declines for weeks to months despite rest, usually with mood and sleep disturbance; recovery occurs but no fitness benefit results.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Rare, severe maladaptation with performance decline lasting months; it is a diagnosis of exclusion made by a physician after ruling out medical causes.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A label applied only after other explanations (illness, deficiency, mental-health conditions) have been medically ruled out — which is why coaches refer suspected OTS rather than declare it.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Practical triage rule: green = train normally; amber = mild pain that settles quickly, so modify load or regress the station; red = significant, worsening, or mechanics-altering pain, so stop and refer.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Return-to-training principle: rebuild tolerance to heavy, slow loading before reintroducing high-velocity, plyometric, or dense race-specific work.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

54.exam_focus: Expect scenario items that make you classify an athlete along the FOR–NFOR–OTS continuum from markers like recovery timescale, resting HR and mood, then choose monitor, modify, or refer — with at least one trap where the correct answer is referring out rather than coaching or treating. sRPE arithmetic and the 0.8–1.3 ACWR band are easy quiz fodder, so know the numbers and the caveat that ACWR is a contested heuristic.

55.title: Exam synthesis — mechanics, skill acquisition & running technique
55.key_concept: This synthesis day binds three threads the assessment is likely to mix freely: mechanics (days 9–12), motor learning (27–29) and running technique (30–33). The unifying idea is impulse–momentum thinking: every station is a problem of building or preserving momentum with a limited force–time budget — a sled start demands one long, continuous impulse from standstill, wall balls and burpee jumps demand small rhythmic impulses repeated at cadence, and running rewards minimising braking impulse per step. A useful way to file faults is into kinetic-chain energy-leak families — hip drop, trunk collapse, overstriding — each exposed by a predictable station or state. The coaching layer then selects learning conditions: blocked practice with rich knowledge of performance for novices and re-learning; random-variable practice under fatigue, external cues and faded feedback for race preparation, because contextual interference tends to trade today's performance for tomorrow's retention and transfer.
key_facts: Impulse is net force multiplied by the time it acts (the area under the force–time curve) and, by the impulse–momentum theorem, equals the change in momentum it produces.

A sled start from standstill is impulse-limited: with no momentum to preserve, the athlete must accumulate a large force–time area before movement begins, so a continuous lean-and-drive beats repeated stop–start efforts.
Wall balls and burpee jumps sit at the opposite end of the impulse problem — brief impulses repeated at cadence — so every pause or reset re-pays the cost of accelerating body and ball from rest.

A useful way to file kinetic-chain faults is into three energy-leak families — contralateral hip drop, trunk collapse and overstriding — a teaching heuristic rather than a formal taxonomy, exposed respectively by single-leg work (sandbag lunges, fatigued running), anteriorly loaded stations (wall balls, sled push) and late-race running.
Blocked practice (AAA-BBB) tends to produce better performance within the session, while random practice (ABC-BCA) tends to produce better retention and transfer — the contextual interference effect.
Contextual interference is thought to work because task-switching forces the learner to reconstruct the action plan on every attempt and to elaborate on differences between tasks.

External cues, which direct attention to the movement's effect on the environment, tend to outperform internal body-focused cues for performance and learning — Wulf's constrained action hypothesis — though the advantage is fairly consistent in direction only; the effect is modest and some recent replications are mixed.

Knowledge of performance (KP) describes movement quality ('your hips rose before your chest'), whereas knowledge of results (KR) describes the outcome ('that set was 15 seconds slower') — a favourite exam confusion.
Feedback frequency should generally be faded as skill develops, because constant after-every-rep feedback breeds dependency and blocks the athlete's own error detection.

Running speed equals cadence multiplied by stride length — taken here, per this site's convention, as the distance covered per step — so at a fixed speed any cadence increase must be paid for with a proportionally shorter stride.
A modest cadence increase of around 5% — not a universal 180 steps per minute — tends to reduce overstriding, braking impulse and per-step loading, making it the safest first running-economy lever.
Reducing vertical oscillation and braking are honest but modest economy levers, and large deliberate technique overhauls often cost economy in the short term before any benefit appears.

Under fatigue, running form tends to degrade in a recognisable signature — cadence falls, ground contact time lengthens and trunk flexion increases, with stride length also shortening as pace fades — which is why restoring cadence is the first cue out of the roxzone (the transition zone), and why the compromised state must itself be rehearsed.
Race preparation should progress practice conditions from blocked and fresh towards random-variable and fatigued (run–station couplets), matching specificity of both skill and physiological state.
55.training_link: This week, run one video session per athlete and file every fault under an energy-leak family rather than a station-specific note: hip drop (lunges, fatigued running), trunk collapse (wall balls, sled), overstriding (late-race running). Fix each with one external cue, not three internal ones. Then audit your practice schedule against athlete level: give your newest athlete blocked sets of their weakest station with frequent knowledge of performance; give race-ready athletes shuffled run–station couplets with feedback only every few rounds. Finally, rehearse degradation — finish one session with a 1 km run at race pace straight into their leakiest station, and cue cadence, not stride length, when form fades.

glossary.def: The product of net force and the time over which it acts — the area under the force–time curve. By the impulse–momentum theorem it equals the change in momentum it produces.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A point in the kinetic chain where force is lost to unwanted motion (hip drop, trunk collapse) instead of being transmitted to the task.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The motor-learning phenomenon whereby interleaving tasks (random practice) worsens performance during practice but improves retention and transfer relative to blocked practice.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Repeating one task for a full set of trials before moving to the next (AAA-BBB). Low interference: strong within-session performance, weaker retention.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Interleaving tasks in unpredictable order (ABC-BCA). High interference: weaker session performance, stronger retention and transfer.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Augmented feedback about the outcome of an attempt — time, distance, success — rather than the movement itself.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Augmented feedback about the quality or pattern of the movement, e.g. 'your hips rose before your chest'.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: An attentional focus on the movement's effect on the environment ('push the floor away'), which tends to outperform internal, body-part-focused cues — an advantage fairly consistent in direction, though modest in size and mixed in some replications.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The oxygen or energy cost of running at a given submaximal speed; a lower cost means better economy.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Step rate in steps per minute; multiplied by stride length (per this site's convention, the distance per step) it gives running speed, creating a direct trade-off at fixed pace.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Initial ground contact too far ahead of the centre of mass, which increases braking impulse and per-step load.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

55.exam_focus: Expect cross-module questions that pair a station fault with the correct mechanical explanation and the correct practice-schedule or cue choice — the classic distractor pairs are force vs impulse, KR vs KP, blocked vs random, and cadence vs stride length. Be ready for simple arithmetic on impulse (force × time = change in momentum) and on speed = cadence × stride length (distance per step, per the site's convention — and watch step vs stride itself as a trap).

56.title: Exam synthesis — energy systems, thresholds & fuelling
56.key_concept: HYROX is best modelled as an aerobically-dominant event punctuated by repeated glycolytic surges: the eight runs and the aerobic 'engine' largely set the finishing time, while sled, wall-ball and burpee stations spike anaerobic demand and seed local fatigue. Endurance performance resolves into three partly-independent qualities — VO2max (the aerobic ceiling), fractional utilisation (the sustainable share of that ceiling, governed by the lactate/threshold boundaries), and economy (the oxygen cost of a given pace) — each answering to different training. Lactate is a shuttled fuel and a flux marker, not the cause of fatigue; acidosis tends to track hydrogen-ion accumulation, buffered extracellularly by bicarbonate and intracellularly by carnosine. Nutrition is periodised in parallel: daily carbohydrate matched to the work required, a brief race-week load, and in-race intake banded by duration. Treat energy availability, not merely body weight, as the health floor beneath all of it.
key_facts: HYROX (8 x 1 km runs plus 8 functional stations) is aerobically dominant overall and typically lasts around 60-90+ minutes, so the aerobic system supplies most of the total energy.
Individual stations — sled push and pull, wall balls, burpee broad jumps — provoke large anaerobic-glycolytic contributions and local muscular fatigue that then compromise the run that follows.

The three-part endurance model is VO2max (aerobic ceiling), fractional utilisation (the sustainable % of VO2max, set by the threshold boundaries) and running economy (oxygen cost at a given speed); race velocity depends on all three.

VO2max responds best to hard intervals near maximal aerobic power (roughly 3-5 min efforts); fractional utilisation to tempo and threshold work; economy to strength, plyometrics, drills and accumulated easy volume.
Lactate is a metabolic fuel shuttled from fast to slow fibres, the heart and the liver (the lactate shuttle), not a waste product that 'burns' the muscle.
Exercise acidosis tends to be driven by hydrogen-ion accumulation rather than lactate itself; blood lactate is a marker of the balance between glycolytic production and clearance.
Buffering is split by compartment: bicarbonate acts extracellularly (supplemented as sodium bicarbonate) and carnosine acts intracellularly (raised by beta-alanine supplementation).

LT1 (aerobic threshold) marks the first rise of lactate above baseline; LT2 (anaerobic threshold / MLSS) is the highest intensity at which lactate production and clearance still balance — above it lactate rises inexorably and the effort becomes unsustainable.

Compromised running feels disproportionately hard because of residual metabolic fatigue, blood-flow competition after loaded stations, and neuromuscular interference that alters gait and leg stiffness.
Durability — resistance to the decline of economy and thresholds late in a prolonged effort — is a distinct, trainable quality that fresh laboratory values do not reliably predict.

In-race carbohydrate is banded by duration: roughly none needed under ~45-60 min, ~30 g/h for ~1-2 h, up to ~60 g/h beyond that, and up to ~90 g/h (multiple transportable carbs) only for very long efforts — all requiring gut training first.
Daily carbohydrate should be periodised to the work required (higher on hard and long days, lower on easy days), with a brief race-week load topping up muscle glycogen.
The best-evidenced ergogenic supplements are creatine, caffeine, beta-alanine and sodium bicarbonate (dietary nitrate/beetroot also has good support); most other products are weakly evidenced.

Low energy availability — a commonly cited heuristic floor of about 30 kcal/kg fat-free mass per day — underlies REDs; red flags include stalled performance, frequent illness or bone-stress injuries, menstrual disturbance and poor recovery.
56.training_link: This week, audit each athlete against the three-part model rather than a single number. Give the runner-type station strength plus compromised-running bricks — heavy sled or wall balls straight into a threshold run — to attack their limiter; give the strength-type more threshold and easy aerobic volume plus economy drills. Screen fuelling by race duration: for a 75-90 minute finisher, rehearse roughly 30-60 g carbohydrate per hour in training and never debut it on race day. Run one weigh-in to set a personal sweat-rate and fluid plan, and quietly check energy-availability red flags — sleep, mood, appetite, menstrual status — in anyone chasing a lean 'race weight'.

glossary.def: The maximum rate at which the body can take up and use oxygen; the ceiling of aerobic power.

glossary.def: The percentage of VO2max an athlete can sustain, largely set by the lactate/threshold boundaries. Two athletes with the same VO2max can differ greatly here.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The oxygen (energy) cost of running at a given submaximal speed; better economy means a faster pace for the same metabolic cost.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The intensity at which blood lactate first rises above resting baseline; roughly the top of comfortable, conversational effort.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The highest intensity at which lactate production and clearance still balance; above it lactate rises inexorably and the effort is unsustainable.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Brooks's concept that lactate is transported between and within tissues to be oxidised as fuel or used for glucose synthesis, rather than being a dead-end waste product.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Running performed under the residual fatigue of preceding station work, as in HYROX, and therefore slower and harder than fresh running.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The resistance of economy and threshold to deterioration over a prolonged effort; a fatigue-resistance quality distinct from fresh fitness.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Matching daily and session carbohydrate intake to training demand — 'fuel for the work required' — rather than eating the same every day.

glossary.def: Progressively practising higher in-race carbohydrate intakes so the gut's absorption capacity adapts and tolerates them without distress.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A syndrome of impaired health and performance driven by sustained low energy availability, affecting bone, hormones, immunity and recovery.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Dangerously low blood sodium, usually caused by over-drinking fluid; distinct from dehydration and treated in the opposite way.

56.exam_focus: Expect to be asked to name the three determinants of endurance performance and match each to its training method, and to correct classic misconceptions — lactate as fuel not villain, VO2max versus economy, and hyponatraemia versus dehydration. Numerical items are likely to probe duration-banded carbohydrate targets and a sweat-rate calculation.

57.title: Exam synthesis — performance pillars, off-feet conditioning & race execution
57.key_concept: Race craft is the synthesis layer that turns fitness into a finishing time, and it rests on three ledgers a coach should hold simultaneously: running time, station time and roxzone time, because total race time is simply their sum. The format itself — eight 1 km runs alternating with eight fixed-order stations — rewards athletes who know each station's demand fingerprint: SkiErg and Row are paceable engine work, the sleds, carries and lunges tax strength-endurance, while wall balls and burpee broad jumps punish rep integrity under fatigue. Pacing doctrine tends to favour even or slightly negative run splits with strict first-run discipline, since early enthusiasm is repaid with interest as compromised running. Roxzone time is usually the cheapest time on course, because it responds mainly to rehearsal and logistics rather than added fitness. Off-feet conditioning (erg and bike work) supplies aerobic volume without impact cost, prescribed by split targets rather than feel — a practical heuristic, not a published model.
key_facts: The race structure is eight 1 km runs alternating with eight stations in a fixed order — SkiErg, Sled Push, Sled Pull, Burpee Broad Jumps, Row, Farmers Carry, Sandbag Lunges, Wall Balls; loads and rep counts are division- and season-dependent (Doubles split station work between partners and Relay formats differ again), so check the current rulebook — the format and rules lesson covers the numbers.

Demand fingerprints: SkiErg and Row are pure-engine stations (paceable, low failure risk); Sled Push, Sled Pull, Farmers Carry and Sandbag Lunges are strength-endurance stations; Wall Balls and Burpee Broad Jumps are rep-integrity stations where form breakdown costs no-reps and failure sets.

Roxzone time is usually the cheapest place on the course to save minutes: it responds mainly to transition rehearsal, station-order familiarity and logistics planning rather than to added fitness — fatigue does slow roxzone pace somewhat, but rehearsal and logistics are the dominant levers.

Community race-data analyses of published splits suggest total roxzone time of roughly four to six minutes for well-drilled athletes versus eight or more for unpractised amateurs — treat these as illustrative rather than official figures, but the gap is largely pure race craft.
First-run discipline is the core pacing rule: going out faster than goal pace on run 1 tends to cost more time later through compromised running than it ever gains.
Well-paced HYROX athletes aim for even or slightly negative run splits across the eight runs, whereas a fading positive-split profile usually signals an early pacing error rather than poor endurance.

Wall Balls and Burpee Broad Jumps are where failure sets occur, and a planned break scheme (moderate sets with short scheduled rests taken before failure) tends to beat unbroken efforts that collapse.
Runner-profile athletes typically bleed time on the sleds, lunges and carries; strength-profile athletes bleed time on the back-half runs; the hybrid profile concedes the least anywhere.
Off-feet conditioning on the SkiErg, rower and bike adds aerobic volume without impact cost, which protects tissue during high-run blocks, niggle management and return-to-training phases.
Erg work is prescribed by split targets (time per 500 m), and because power scales with roughly the cube of speed, small split improvements demand disproportionately large increases in watts.
The damper on an erg sets drag factor — how much air the flywheel works against per stroke, i.e. the gearing and feel — not the workout intensity, which comes only from the athlete's power output.

Compromised-pair (couplet) training — a station straight into a run, or a run straight into a station — is arguably the most race-specific repeatable conditioning unit short of a full simulation, because it rehearses the exact transition demand of the event.
Race-model arithmetic is simply: target time = run budget + station budget + roxzone budget; coach the cheapest gains first, which are usually roxzone and pacing errors, not fitness.
57.training_link: This week, build each athlete a one-page race model: split their target finish time into run, station and roxzone budgets, then work backwards to a per-kilometre pace and per-station split targets. Rehearse the roxzone deliberately — station-order recitation, a walked transition plan and one timed race-flow simulation — because that time is close to free. Programme one compromised-pair session matched to each athlete's weakest fingerprint (for example sled push into 400–800 m repeats at race pace for runner profiles, or station-into-run couplets emphasising back-half run pace for strength profiles). Prescribe erg sessions by 500 m split targets so the SkiErg and Row become controlled, pre-planned stations rather than emotional ones.

glossary.def: The transition area between runs and stations; time spent there counts toward the finish and is reduced mainly by rehearsal and familiarity, with fitness playing only a supporting role.

57.exam_focus: Expect items that ask you to classify stations by dominant demand fingerprint, complete simple race-craft arithmetic — splitting a target finish into run, station and roxzone budgets, or converting an erg split into time and watts — and scenario questions presenting a runner-profile versus strength-profile athlete and asking where each loses time and what to prescribe; station-order and rep-count recitation is examined from the format and stations lessons rather than here.

58.title: Exam synthesis — periodization, concurrent training & peaking
58.key_concept: Periodization is the deliberate sequencing of training emphasis across a macrocycle, and the honest reading of the comparative literature is that structure beats no structure, while differences between named models — linear, block, undulating — tend to be smaller than the effects of adherence and sensible load management. Polarised distribution describes how intensity is spread, not how phases are sequenced, and the two are often confused. A practical HYROX macrocycle runs general preparation (maximal strength plus aerobic base), specific preparation (station endurance and compromised running), competition (race simulations and a taper cutting volume roughly 40–60% while holding intensity and frequency for one to two weeks), then transition. Concurrent-training interference — endurance blunting strength adaptation, with a molecular story that remains contested — matters mainly at high endurance volumes and with poor session sequencing, and is managed through ordering, separation and off-feet modalities rather than avoided outright.
key_facts: Comparative trials tend to show that any structured periodized plan beats unstructured training, while differences between the named models are small and usually smaller than the effect of adherence.
Linear periodization progresses from high-volume/low-intensity toward low-volume/high-intensity across long sequential phases.
Block periodization concentrates one dominant quality per mesocycle (commonly accumulation, transmutation, realisation) and relies on residual training effects to hold the others.
Daily or weekly undulating periodization (DUP) varies intensity and volume targets within the week, which suits concurrent-demand sports like HYROX that must keep several qualities warm at once.
Polarised (~80% easy / ~20% hard) is an intensity-distribution strategy, not a periodization model — a classic exam confusion.
A practical HYROX macrocycle runs general prep (strength + aerobic base), specific prep (station endurance + compromised running), competition (race sims + taper), then transition.

The interference effect is the blunting of strength and hypertrophy adaptations by concurrent endurance training; the molecular explanation (often framed as AMPK–mTOR crosstalk) is plausible but not settled.
Interference matters most at high endurance volumes, when same-muscle endurance work immediately precedes strength training, and when key lifting is done glycogen-depleted.

Practical interference mitigation: lift first when strength is the priority, separate sessions by roughly six hours where possible (a heuristic, not a published law), and push some endurance volume to low-impact off-feet modalities.
The textbook taper cuts training volume by roughly 40–60% over one to two weeks while maintaining intensity and frequency, typically yielding small but meaningful performance gains of around 1–3%.
The most common taper error is cutting intensity rather than volume, which lets race-pace sharpness fade exactly when it is needed.
An A/B/C race hierarchy assigns the full taper to A races, a 3–7 day mini-taper to B races, and trains through C races as quality sessions.

Functional overreaching is a planned short-term overload that rebounds to supercompensation after recovery; a plan should schedule it deliberately with the recovery week written in advance, never discover it by accident.
Strength decays over weeks rather than days, so low-volume, moderate-to-high-intensity weekly touches are enough to hold it between races and through the competition phase.
58.training_link: This week, audit one athlete's next twelve weeks against the four-phase template: name the phase each week belongs to and check the dominant emphasis actually matches it. If they lift and run on the same day, fix the ordering — strength first when strength is the priority, or roughly six hours' separation where life allows — and move some easy volume to the SkiErg or bike if their legs are chronically heavy. Draft the race hierarchy now: one A race gets the full one-to-two-week taper, B races get 3–5 day mini-tapers, C races are trained through. Finally, write the taper arithmetic into the plan in advance — peak weekly volume, the 40–60% cut, and the short race-pace sessions that preserve intensity — so race week is executed, not improvised.

glossary.def: The full planning span (typically a season or year) containing preparation, competition and transition phases.

glossary.def: A model that concentrates a single quality per mesocycle in sequence (accumulation, transmutation, realisation), relying on residual training effects to maintain the qualities not currently emphasised.
