glossary.def: A model that varies intensity and volume targets within the week or day rather than across long phases; well suited to sports that must train several qualities concurrently.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Spending roughly 80% of endurance training time at low intensity and about 20% at high intensity; it describes the intensity mix, not the phase sequence, so it is not itself a periodization model.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The attenuation of strength and hypertrophy adaptations when high volumes of endurance training run concurrently, strongest when endurance work loads the same muscles immediately before lifting.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The period a fitness quality is retained after dedicated training for it stops; strength persists for weeks, while speed and anaerobic qualities fade faster.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A pre-race reduction of training volume by roughly 40–60% over one to two weeks while maintaining intensity and frequency, allowing fatigue to fall faster than fitness.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A planned short-term overload producing temporary performance decline that rebounds above baseline after scheduled recovery; distinct from non-functional overreaching, where the decrement persists without payoff.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Classifying races by priority to decide taper depth: full taper for A races, mini-taper for B races, and training through C races.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

58.exam_focus: Expect scenario questions asking you to choose and justify a periodization structure and macrocycle sequence for a given athlete and race calendar, plus items that separate taper volume (cut) from intensity (kept) and block from undulating models; interference questions will most likely test when it matters and how you mitigate it, not the molecular detail.

59.title: Exam synthesis — mental performance & personalized coaching
59.key_concept: Mental performance and individualisation converge on the same coaching question: what does this athlete need, and how do I know? Arousal regulation is symptom-led — over-aroused athletes (racing thoughts, rushed transitions, early surging) need down-regulation through slow, exhale-biased breathing and calming routines, while flat, under-aroused athletes need activation via up-tempo music, dynamic movement and energising cues. Goal architecture stacks outcome, performance and process goals; under pressure, process goals tend to hold up best because they stay controllable. Pain coping draws on attentional strategy — association for experienced pacers, dissociation and chunking for surviving predictable crisis points, pre-scripted as if-then plans in the spirit of Gollwitzer's implementation intentions. Individualisation runs through the needs-analysis pipeline: history, testing battery, gap analysis, priorities, programme, re-test. The synthesis is the case-study loop — symptom, most-limiting factor, targeted intervention, re-test — a practical heuristic, not a published model.
key_facts: Arousal regulation is symptom-led: identify whether the athlete is over- or under-aroused first, then match the tool — down-regulation for the jittery, activation for the flat.
Slow, exhale-biased breathing (exhale longer than inhale) tends to lower arousal, while up-tempo music, dynamic movement and energising self-talk raise it.
Over-arousal typically shows as racing thoughts, a rushed warm-up and going out too hard; under-arousal shows as flatness, low drive and sluggish transitions.

Goal architecture stacks outcome goals (the result), performance goals (own-standard targets) and process goals (controllable actions), and process goals tend to be the most robust under race pressure because they stay fully controllable.
If-then plans (implementation intentions, after Gollwitzer) pre-script responses to predicted crisis points and must be rehearsed under fatigue in training to hold up on race day.

Association (internal monitoring of effort, breathing and form) supports accurate pacing in experienced athletes; dissociation and chunking help athletes tolerate discomfort spikes but can blunt pacing judgement.
Because HYROX is a fixed sequence of 8 x 1 km runs alternating with 8 stations, crisis points are predictable and can be scripted in advance — for example run 6 or the back half of the wall balls.
The needs-analysis pipeline is the individualisation engine: athlete history, then testing battery, then gap analysis, then priorities, then programme, then re-test.

A HYROX testing battery samples three layers: aerobic field tests (threshold or race-pace running), gym strength benchmarks (for example trap-bar deadlift and loaded carries) and station benchmarks (for example 1,000 m erg times and unbroken wall-ball capacity).
Every test in the battery must map to a programming decision — a test that would not change the plan is not worth its cost in time and fatigue.
Benchmarks are commonly re-tested every 6–12 weeks or at the end of a training block: often enough to steer the programme, rarely enough not to disrupt it.

A practical ranking of individualisation levers is volume tolerance, then strength floor, then pacing discipline, then psychology — fix the most-limiting lever first (a coaching heuristic, not a published hierarchy).
Outcome goals depend partly on rivals and conditions, so they motivate the season but should be de-emphasised on race day in favour of process focus.
The case-study reasoning loop the assessment is likely to reward is symptom, then most-limiting factor, then targeted intervention, then re-test.
59.training_link: Pick one athlete this week and run the whole engine. Take a short history (training age, injuries, race results, constraints), then schedule a two-session mini-battery: one running field test at threshold or race pace, two or three gym strength benchmarks, and one or two station benchmarks their history flags. Write a one-line gap analysis ("strong, but fades from run 5") and choose the single most-limiting lever. In parallel, script the mental plan: name their two predictable crisis points, write an if-then card for each, and rehearse the breathing reset in training — never for the first time on race day. Diary the re-test six to eight weeks out before you write the block.

glossary.def: Matching an athlete's activation level to the task — down-regulating the over-aroused or up-regulating the flat — using breathing, music, movement and routine.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A goal defined by controllable actions (e.g. "hold my breathing rhythm on every run") rather than results; the most robust goal type under race pressure.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A pre-scripted response to a predicted trigger ("if X happens, then I do Y"), also called an implementation intention; it must be rehearsed under fatigue to work on race day.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: An attentional strategy of monitoring internal signals such as effort, breathing and form; supports accurate pacing, particularly in experienced athletes.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Directing attention away from bodily discomfort through external focus, counting or imagery; helps tolerate pain spikes but can blunt pacing accuracy.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Breaking a daunting whole into small units — a long wall-ball set into blocks of ten, the race into eight run-station couplets — to keep effort psychologically manageable.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The structured pipeline (history, testing, gap analysis, priorities, programme, re-test) that turns athlete information into individual programming decisions.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The selected set of aerobic, strength and station benchmarks used to profile an athlete; every test should map to a programming decision.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Comparing test results against the race's demands and the athlete's goals to identify the most-limiting factor to target first.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: How often benchmarks are repeated — commonly every 6–12 weeks or at block end — often enough to steer decisions without disrupting training.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A modifiable factor (volume tolerance, strength floor, pacing discipline, psychology) a coach adjusts per athlete; address the most-limiting lever first.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

59.exam_focus: Expect case-study vignettes fusing M9 and M10: an athlete described by symptoms and test data, where you must pick the most-limiting factor and the matched mental or programming intervention. If the assessment mirrors the platform's sibling courses (MCQ format — inferred, not verified for L2), distractors will likely be plausible generic tools that ignore the specific profile presented, so always answer from the athlete described.

60.title: Mock assessment I — full athlete case study
60.key_concept: This day is a mock assessment: one athlete, twelve linked exam-style decisions that walk the full coaching process in order — needs analysis, testing, planning, weekly design, injury-aware progression, station priorities, monitoring, a mid-block fatigue call, taper, pacing and in-race crisis — drawing on every earlier lesson. The case: Ana, 38, women's open division, first HYROX in 12 weeks. She runs a 21:40 5 km and deadlifts 120 kg — a strong-amateur profile in which running is the clear strength and force production already covers open-division demands — but her wall balls break down early, she carries a history of Achilles niggles, and with two young children her budget is five training hours per week. Answer each question before reading the model answer, and grade yourself on reasoning rather than phrasing: the defensible 'why' matters more than the exact set-and-rep choice. The real L2 assessment format is not publicly documented, so treat this as integration practice, not a format rehearsal.
key_facts: Case anchor: Ana is 38, entering the women's open division for her first HYROX, with race day in 12 weeks.
Ana's fresh 5 km time is 21:40 (4:20/km) — a clear relative strength for a first-time open-division athlete, so her performance ceiling is set elsewhere.
Ana's 120 kg deadlift means force production comfortably covers open-division sled and lunge demands, so strength is maintained, not built, in this cycle.
Wall balls are Ana's most-limiting station — reps break down early — and they close the race under maximal fatigue: in women's open she faces 100 reps with a 4 kg ball to a 2.70 m target.
Ana has a history of Achilles niggles, so every running progression is gated by tendon load tolerance, not by fitness.
Ana's two young children make her sleep unpredictable and her sessions missable at short notice, so her plan needs a designated droppable session, not a fragile seven-day grid.
Ana's budget is five hours per week — about four sessions — so minimum effective dose is the organising rule and no quality is trained twice.
Ana's twelve weeks split naturally into three four-week blocks: general prep (tendon base plus wall-ball skill), HYROX-specific prep (compromised running plus station pairings), and sharpen/taper.

The taught pacing rule of thumb — race run pace roughly 30-60 s/km slower than fresh 5 km pace, wider for weak-aerobic athletes, and a starting estimate rather than a law — puts Ana at about 4:50-5:20/km, with the lower end defensible because running is her strength.
Ana's monitoring must be low-burden: session RPE plus a three-item morning traffic light; daily HRV is skipped because broken parent sleep makes it noisy and prone to false alarms.
Ana's red-flag rule: Achilles morning stiffness lasting beyond roughly 24 hours, or pain that changes her gait, triggers an immediate running-load cut.
The exam skill this case trains is stating decision plus justification in two sentences — integration across modules, not isolated recall.
60.training_link: Run this format on your own roster this week. Pick one real athlete, write their case line in Ana's format — age, division, key numbers, constraints, red flags — then answer the same twelve questions for them in writing, two to three sentences each. Where you cannot answer (no wall-ball benchmark, no tendon history), that is a hole in your intake, not in the athlete. Then reverse it for exam prep: practise defending each decision aloud in one breath — decision plus 'because' — since that structure answers scenario questions far faster than re-deriving everything from theory under time pressure.

glossary.def: The single quality or station that caps race performance regardless of improvement elsewhere; it gets first claim on a scarce training budget.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The smallest training stimulus that still drives the target adaptation; the organising principle when weekly hours are fixed and low.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A structured comparison of the event's demands against the athlete's current profile, producing a ranked gap list rather than a generic programme.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Sequencing training blocks so each block's adaptations raise the ceiling of the next — for Ana, tendon capacity before compromised-run volume.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Running performed under residual fatigue from a preceding station; the signature HYROX demand and the reason fresh run tests over-predict race pace.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The athlete's 0-10 rating of a whole session multiplied by its duration in minutes (Foster's method); a validated, low-burden internal-load measure.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A short-term performance dip from deliberate overload that recovers — and may rebound above baseline — after planned recovery; distinguished from non-functional overreaching by being brief and planned.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The deliberate pre-race reduction of training volume — commonly around 40-60% over one to two weeks — with intensity retained, trading a little fitness for a large drop in fatigue.

glossary.def: A pre-agreed, rehearsed response to a predicted race problem ('if X happens, then I do Y'), converting an in-race crisis from a decision into a retrieval task; borrowed from implementation-intentions research.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A green/amber/red readiness triage built from a few daily items; amber modifies the session, red replaces it.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

60.exam_focus: Expect scenario items built around a described athlete — 'what would you prioritise, change, or decide, and why' — rather than isolated facts, particularly around the populations Module 10 names; since the actual assessment format is unverified, train the transferable skill of decision plus one-breath justification.

61.title: Mock assessment II — hard cases & exam-day strategy
61.key_concept: The twelve cases here are the exam's hard mode: scenario items where every option looks plausible and the credited answer is the safest defensible one — refer out of scope, reduce load, protect the athlete — and, where two options survive, the one that individualises. The exam-strategy spine is applied here rather than re-taught: nothing about the Level 2 assessment's format is officially published, so format expectations are working assumptions anchored to the same LMS's other courses (per-module multiple-choice quizzes, a pass mark around 80%, generous retakes — as experienced first-hand on the Foundation Course, not published for Level 2). Because navigation is linear you cannot preview a quiz, so bank named numbers, frameworks and definitions as you watch each module; if retakes are permitted, treat the first attempt diagnostically; and drive the final week from your due queue rather than re-reading modules.
key_facts: No official public documentation of the Level 2 assessment format exists — only the course page's marketing copy — so every format expectation should be held as a working assumption, not fact.

Verified about Level 2: digital-only, self-paced, English-only, delivered on the HYROX365 LMS, Level 1 as the prerequisite, and a published list of ten structured modules. The often-quoted figure of roughly 40 hours of material is published nowhere — it comes from totalling the LMS's own module runtimes first-hand, so file it as a working assumption.

On the same LMS, the Foundation Course places a mandatory multiple-choice quiz after each module — roughly 10–20 questions, an 80% pass mark, and unlimited retakes with an unchanged question set, as experienced first-hand on completing that course (none of this is published by HYROX365) — and Level 2 plausibly but unverifiably mirrors this.
Because LMS navigation is strictly linear you cannot preview a quiz, so capture named numbers, frameworks and expert-specific claims as you first watch each module.
The safest-defensible-answer principle: when several options look plausible, the credited one almost always refers out of scope, reduces load, or otherwise protects the athlete.
Scope of practice is a classic trap family: coaches screen and refer, and never diagnose injury or illness, treat medical conditions, or prescribe medication.

Secondary amenorrhoea, persistent cold intolerance, stalled performance despite rising volume, and pride in restriction together flag possible low energy availability (REDs) and warrant referral, not applause.

External-focus cues, which direct attention to the movement's effect on the environment, tend to outperform internal body-part cues — an advantage associated with Wulf's attentional-focus research that some evidence suggests persists, and may even grow, under fatigue.
A stalling sled usually signals intermittent impulse: re-overcoming static friction on every step costs more than keeping the sled moving with a continuous lean and long driving strides.

HYROX rulebooks generally prohibit outside assistance and enforce movement standards through no-reps, but exact standards and penalties vary by season, so brief athletes from the current rulebook rather than memory.
For a 60–90 minute race the aerobic system and threshold dominate, so a programme built on short maximal sprints with full recovery mismatches the event's energy-system demands.

Evidence on concurrent-training interference is mixed — recent meta-analytic work finds small, inconsistent effects concentrated mainly in explosive power — but a common, low-risk practical recommendation is to separate heavy strength and hard intervals by six to twenty-four-plus hours or periodise emphasis; much of what athletes report as interference is simply residual fatigue.
Pre-race anxiety responds to reappraisal of arousal as readiness, slow-exhale breathing, process goals and a rehearsed routine — not to outcome reassurance.
Final-week heuristic: work the spaced-repetition due queue and your per-module number notes; re-watching whole modules is the lowest-yield use of the last week.
61.training_link: Run these twelve scenarios as a closed-book mock this week, then mine the misses twice: once for revision, once on the gym floor. Each applied case maps to a live coaching situation, so audit your athletes against them: check whether anyone's 'discipline' is masking under-fuelling, rewrite one internal cue per session as an external one, watch one sled push for stalling impulse between steps, and re-order any training day that stacks heavy lower-body strength against hard intervals. Before the next race weekend, run the pacing arithmetic from the calc item against each athlete's target time so their run splits are agreed numbers, not vibes.

glossary.def: Exam heuristic: among plausible MCQ options, pick the one that protects the athlete, stays inside coaching scope, or reduces load — it is almost always the credited response.

61.exam_focus: Expect scenario MCQs where every distractor is plausible and the credited answer is the safest defensible one — refer out, reduce load, protect the athlete, individualise. Format-wise, apply the strategy spine rather than relearning it: assume per-module multiple-choice quizzes with a pass mark around 80% and generous retakes — an inference from the same platform's Foundation Course, not anything HYROX365 publishes for Level 2 — and bank module-specific numbers and named frameworks as you go, because linear navigation means you cannot preview a quiz.

62.title: The six pillars of HYROX performance
62.key_concept: Fitness is not a general trait; it is sport-specific physical readiness — the particular qualities an event demands, in the proportions it demands them. Rank one group of trained athletes by 1RM deadlift, by 10 km time and by HYROX finish and you get three different orders, so 'fit' describes nothing until the test is named. The six pillars — strength, endurance, speed, power, coordination and flexibility/mobility — are a needs-analysis vocabulary for naming those qualities, essentially the classical biomotor abilities of the periodisation literature with power broken out from strength. Treat it as a coaching taxonomy, not a validated factor structure: the pillars overlap (power is the force-velocity product, with strength the capacity behind the force term) and their boundaries are conventions of practice. Its value is corrective. Coaches who read HYROX as strength plus endurance programme heavy lifting and long runs, leaving movement rate, expressed power, accuracy under fatigue and usable range unaddressed — precisely the qualities that separate close finishers. Day 17 identifies which quality costs an athlete time; the pillars are the menu it selects from.
key_facts: Fitness in this framework means sport-specific physical readiness: the qualities an event actually requires, weighted as that event weights them. Transfer is partial rather than absent — central adaptations such as cardiac output, stroke volume and plasma volume carry across endurance modes, while muscle-specific, positional and technical qualities do not — so fitness for one sport is a weak predictor of readiness for another. The needs analysis therefore has to be written for HYROX specifically rather than borrowed from running or from the gym.

The six pillars are strength, endurance, speed, power, coordination and flexibility/mobility — recognisably the classical biomotor abilities of the periodisation literature, with power separated out from strength. This is a coaching checklist, not a validated model of human fitness: power is arithmetically force times velocity, with strength the capacity behind the force term; coordination is inseparable from economy; and mobility is a precondition for expressing several of the others. The overlap is a feature — it forces the coach to look at the same athlete from six angles.

Reading HYROX as strength plus endurance is the error the checklist exists to catch. That framing produces heavy lifting and long aerobic work and nothing at all for movement rate, expressed power, precision under fatigue or joint range — four of the six pillars left untrained by omission rather than by decision.

Strength is the capacity to produce force, and it does three jobs in a race rather than one. It moves the fixed external loads — driving a loaded sled 50 m, holding the farmers handles, standing out of a loaded lunge — and it lowers the fraction of maximum every rep demands, so joint positions and technique survive further into the race (day 21 for why they degrade, day 37 for dosing). It also raises the load tolerance of tendon, ligament and other connective tissue, which is much of what decides whether a compromised position under fatigue is merely slow or actually injurious: the safety case for strength, which stands separately from the performance case.

Endurance is the ability to keep producing work as duration extends, and the capacity itself answers to accumulated exposure — hours of running, ergometer and cycling volume — rather than to a technical correction; how much of that capacity reaches the clock is a separate, economy question, and economy does respond to erg technique and to heavy strength and plyometric work (day 19). It is not a quality only slower finishers need: an athlete taking two hours works continuously for twice as long as one taking sixty minutes, so the requirement scales with the time on the clock rather than thinning out at the sharp end. Its clearest race expression is the standard rather than the stopwatch — the wall balls are judged identically on rep 1 and rep 100 (100 reps in every individual division), and endurance decides how much of the athlete's rep-1 quality is still available at rep 100.

Speed is the rate at which a movement is executed — a distinct question from endurance, which asks only that work continues. HYROX is not won on top-end speed, but raising the maximal ceiling lowers the relative intensity of any fixed submaximal pace. Note the honest limit of that argument: the relative-intensity logic is sound, whereas the stronger claim that maximal-speed work directly improves submaximal running economy is better supported for heavy strength and plyometric training (day 19) than for sprinting itself.

Speed is a station and transition quality, not only a running one. Reps per minute at the burpee broad jump and wall balls, hand speed on the sled-pull rope, and the pace at which an athlete covers the 15 roxzone traverses (day 15) are all expressions of the same pillar — and the transition ones are the cheapest to improve, because they need a rehearsed routine and a pre-made decision rather than any new physical adaptation. They are not metabolically free, though: part of a traverse is genuine aerobic recovery (day 17), so moving through it faster raises average race intensity and is paid back on the following kilometre unless the engine has moved too. Pace the roxzone; do not sprint it.

Power is the product of force and velocity, so it asks not how much force an athlete can generate but how fast they can generate it. It is the one pillar the race reports back in physical units, because the SkiErg and rower read out watts — but read them carefully: average watts held across 1000 m is overwhelmingly sustained aerobic power output, an endurance quality at that duration. The neuromuscular pillar shows in the opening strokes, in peak watts, and in holding the same average watts at a lower stroke rate, which means more force produced per stroke.

The clearest race moment for explosive force production is breaking a stationary sled: limiting static friction exceeds kinetic friction and the mass has to be accelerated from rest, so it takes more force to start the sled than to keep it moving. Strictly, the instant of the break is a maximal-force and rate-of-force-development problem — velocity, and therefore mechanical power, is zero at rest — while power in the force-times-velocity sense is what accelerates the sled once it is moving. Because each 50 m is 4 x 12.5 m lengths, the athlete solves that problem four times (the start plus three turnarounds), and covering the concentric-dominant lengths in between is a strength-endurance problem; the same start-then-sustain pattern appears in every stand-out from a sandbag lunge.

Coordination is the organisation of a movement so that it is accurate and metabolically cheap at the same time. It looks like a non-issue in HYROX, since no station demands a complex skill — but speed and load raise the control demand while accumulated fatigue lowers the control available (altered recruitment, blunted proprioceptive feedback, compensatory patterns). Demand rising as capacity falls is why accuracy gives way wherever the athlete works closest to their limit, rather than uniformly across the race.

Most no-reps and penalties are coordination failures under fatigue rather than knowledge failures. The athlete knows the wall-ball depth and target standard and knows the burpee broad jump needs a two-foot take-off; they simply stop delivering them as precision degrades. Wall balls and the burpee broad jump carry by far the largest exposure because of their rep counts and strict standards — and the burpee broad jump is station 4, which is why this is not only a closing-minutes problem.

Flexibility is the range available at a joint; mobility is the portion of that range the athlete can actively access and control under load. The practical criterion is not a goniometer reading but the movement standard — enough hip, knee and ankle range to still hit wall-ball depth on rep 90, and enough hip extension to keep running tall instead of folding forward. Usable range is also the safety margin, since an athlete who reaches a fatigued position at the very edge of their available range has nothing in reserve when mechanics degrade; there is no validated 'sufficient range' threshold for HYROX, so judge it against judged reps and against the positions fatigue forces, not against a norm table.

The pillars are interdependent and unequally weighted, and those are two different points. Interdependence: every pillar reaches the result only through the others — a force reserve is unusable in a position the athlete cannot hold, a high movement rate is worth nothing if the reps it produces are not counted, and range that is never loaded quickly is range the race never sees. Weighting: running is roughly half the clock for most age-groupers, so endurance carries the largest share — yet the pillar costing an individual athlete the most time is often a lighter-weighted one, and distinguishing weight from limiter is exactly what day 17 profiling exists to do.
62.training_link: Run the pillars as a pre-block audit, not as six weekly sessions. Score each one for the athlete in front of you: relative strength against the division's sled, sandbag and farmers loads; a threshold anchor plus long-run history for endurance; a flying 20-30 m for the top-end speed ceiling, adding a 400 m or 600 m only if you also want the speed-endurance ceiling — different tests, and a 400 m does not measure maximal speed; countermovement jump height and peak erg watts for power; filmed judged reps taken past rep 70 for coordination; and a loaded overhead-squat and lunge screen for usable range. Most athletes show one clear hole and two soft spots. Bias the block at the hole, hold the rest at maintenance dosing (day 37), and re-score at the block boundary. Then triangulate: day 17 tells you which quality the race splits blame, the audit tells you whether the gym data agrees. When the two disagree, believe the race.

62.exam_focus: Expect to name and define all six pillars precisely — including power as force times velocity rather than as a synonym for strength — and to argue why HYROX is not adequately described as strength plus endurance, typically by mapping a named pillar onto a specific station failure (a sled that will not start, wall-ball no-reps, a staggered burpee take-off, a collapsed running posture) and explaining how a missing pillar limits the expression of the others.

63.title: Motor units & muscle fibre types
63.key_concept: The motor unit — one alpha motor neuron plus every muscle fibre it innervates — is the smallest parcel of voluntary force the nervous system can address, because its firing is all-or-none: reach threshold and every fibre in the unit contracts, or nothing does. That leaves exactly two ways to grade force. Recruit more units, in the broadly fixed small-to-large order described by Henneman's size principle, or fire the already-recruited ones faster (rate coding). Almost everything we label 'fibre type' follows from which neuron owns the fibre: small, easily excited, slowly conducting neurons run few, small, oxidative, fatigue-resistant fibres, while large, high-threshold, fast-conducting neurons run many large, glycolytic, forceful, fatigable ones. Human fibres sit on a continuum from Type I through IIa to IIx, with hybrids at every boundary and proportions that differ between muscles, between people and between sports. HYROX is unusually unkind to specialists at either end: it asks for Type I fatigue resistance across 8 km of running and Type II force output on the sleds, inside the same hour or two.
key_facts: A motor unit is a single alpha motor neuron together with all the fibres it innervates. In adult limb muscle every fibre answers to exactly one motor neuron — specialised muscles such as the extraocular group contain multiply innervated fibres and are the textbook exception — while each neuron commands many fibres. Firing is all-or-none, so there is no such thing as recruiting half a unit: the unit rather than the fibre is the real currency of force production.

With all-or-none units, force can only be graded two ways: recruiting additional units, and increasing the discharge frequency of those already recruited (rate coding). Recruitment is commonly reported as complete somewhere between about 50% MVC in small hand muscles and 85–90% MVC in large limb muscles, above which rate coding does the remaining work; discharge rates commonly rise from roughly 5–10 Hz at recruitment into the 30–50 Hz region at maximal effort. Treat all these figures as approximate and muscle-specific.

Innervation ratio — the number of fibres a single motor neuron supplies — varies by orders of magnitude between muscles. Textbook estimates run from a few dozen fibres per neuron in the small muscles that steer the eye to well over a thousand in the large muscles of the calf and thigh; sources disagree on the exact values, so treat them as order-of-magnitude approximations. The trade-off is fixed either way: the fewer fibres a neuron owns, the finer the force gradation each additional unit buys; the more it owns, the larger and coarser the increment.

Neural properties covary with motor neuron soma size. Small neurons have low excitation thresholds — they switch on first and easily — but thinner, more slowly conducting axons. Large neurons need much more synaptic drive, conduct faster, and innervate more and larger fibres. 'Easily excitable' and 'fast-conducting' therefore sit at opposite ends of the same axis, which is a common exam trap.

Henneman's size principle: units are recruited in a broadly fixed order from smallest and most excitable to largest, and de-recruited in reverse. The coaching consequence is blunt — the high-threshold units cannot be reached at all without high external force, genuinely high movement velocity, or enough fatigue in the low-threshold units to drag them in; and even then they are added on top of the low-threshold units, never instead of them, so they can never be trained in isolation. It also means Type I units are working on every run and every station of a HYROX and are never rested.

The fibres of one motor unit are scattered across a territory within the muscle and intermingled with the fibres of other units, often of other types, rather than grouped in a block. A needle biopsy therefore samples a mosaic, which is precisely why single-site fibre-type percentages carry real sampling error and should never be quoted to the decimal point.

Human limb fibres are classified as Type I, IIa and IIx after the myosin heavy chain isoform they express (MyHC-I, IIa, IIx). 'Type IIb' is the older histochemical label: the true MyHC-IIb isoform is expressed in small mammals, and the human fibre it was mapped onto is IIx, sometimes written IId/x. Expect older textbooks and histochemical staining plates to say IIb where IIx is meant.

Most properties run in one direction from I → IIa → IIx: twitch speed slow → fast; fatigue resistance very high → low; peak force low → high; fibre cross-sectional area small → large; mitochondrial density, myoglobin and oxidative enzyme activity high → low; intramuscular lipid high → low; phosphagen (ATP-PCr) stores low → high; myosin ATPase and glycolytic enzyme activity low → high. Two lines break the pattern: capillary density is high in both I and IIa and low only in IIx, and resting glycogen — often listed as rising across the same order — differs only modestly between fibre types and is inconsistently reported. IIa is genuinely intermediate on fatigue resistance, force, mitochondrial density, myoglobin and oxidative capacity, but sits with IIx on twitch speed, fibre size and glycolytic/ATPase activity: a fast fibre with an oxidative back end, which is why it is the workhorse of a HYROX race.

How fast a fibre shortens tracks how fast its myosin head splits ATP — the relationship Bárány (1967) established across muscles of widely differing speeds. That is what made ATPase histochemistry a workable way to sort fibres by contraction speed decades before myosin isoforms could be typed directly, and it is also why the fastest fibres exhaust a high power output so quickly: they spend ATP at the rate they contract.

The three-bin scheme is a convenience. Hybrid fibres co-expressing more than one isoform (I/IIa, IIa/IIx) are common, so fibre type is better read as a continuum. Proportions vary between muscles (soleus is strongly Type I dominant as a postural muscle, commonly reported above 70%; triceps brachii sits comparatively fast), between individuals (vastus lateralis Type I proportions in published samples span roughly 15–85%), and between athlete populations, with endurance cyclists and distance runners highest in Type I and sprinters lowest. Those population differences are mostly self-selection layered on top of a largely inherited typology — twin and family data attribute a substantial share of fibre-type variance to genetics — so training reshuffles proportions within an athlete rather than rebuilding a sprinter's profile into a cyclist's.

What training reliably moves is the IIx↔IIa balance. Almost any sustained training — resistance, endurance, sprint and ballistic work alike — reduces the IIx share and raises IIa; IIx content reliably climbs only when training is reduced, through disuse, immobilisation, detraining or the 'IIx overshoot' commonly seen after a taper, so explosive work may blunt the loss relative to high-volume endurance work but should not be taught as preserving IIx. Whole conversion between Type I and Type II in humans is far less established, and published percentage changes in Type I after endurance blocks should be read as illustrative of a direction, not as constants to programme against. Fibre size is the other axis, moved independently of type: resistance work enlarges fibre cross-sectional area with the larger gains typically in the Type II fibres, so two athletes with identical fibre-type percentages can differ substantially in the force each pool actually produces.

The fastest-moving adaptations here are neural, not histochemical: lower recruitment thresholds, higher discharge rates and reduced antagonist co-activation appear within weeks. Motor neuron pools receive both excitatory and inhibitory input, and reciprocal inhibition of the antagonist is part of why a well-coached movement is more economical than a braced, co-contracted one. Structural changes to axon diameter and myelination are plausible but weakly evidenced in already-trained adults.

Fibre typology influences recovery between hard efforts, not just peak output: more fast-twitch-dominant athletes tend to show larger power decrements across repeated high-intensity bouts and to restore output more slowly between them. The direction of that effect is reported consistently, but its size varies with the population and the test protocol — bout duration, rest length and exercise mode — so no single percentage should be carried around as a constant. Use it to decide how far apart to space hard sessions, and measure the athlete's own decrement rather than assuming a number.
63.training_link: You cannot biopsy an athlete, so infer typology from behaviour and hold it as a hypothesis. Run a repeat-effort test on fixed rest — six 50 m sled pushes, or six 20 s maximal bike sprints — and record the decrement from first bout to last. A large fall with a long tail points toward a fast-twitch-dominant athlete and a small, flat profile toward a slow-twitch one, but no validated field test for fibre typology exists, so use the decrement to schedule, never as a measurement of composition. For the fast-twitch-dominant athlete, space hard interval and sled sessions further apart, lengthen the rests inside them, and add sub-threshold volume to build the oxidative side of their Type II pool. For the slow-twitch-dominant athlete the risk inverts: tempo running with no high-force or high-velocity exposure erodes IIx and, more immediately, detrains recruitment of the high-threshold units the sleds need, so keep short maximal-intent work in every week.

glossary.def: A single alpha motor neuron together with every muscle fibre it innervates; in adult limb muscle each fibre belongs to just one unit. It is the smallest quantum of voluntary force the nervous system can command, because all its fibres contract together or not at all.

glossary.def: The property that a motor neuron either reaches its firing threshold and produces a full action potential or produces none at all. Force cannot be graded within a unit, only between units and by discharge frequency.

glossary.def: The orderly recruitment of motor units from smallest and most excitable to largest and least excitable as force demand rises, with de-recruitment in reverse order. It is why high-threshold units require high force, high velocity or accumulated fatigue to be reached, and why they are never recruited in isolation.

glossary.def: Grading force by altering the discharge frequency of motor units that are already recruited. It becomes the dominant mechanism once recruitment within a muscle is complete.

glossary.def: The molecular variant of the myosin motor protein a fibre expresses — MyHC-I, IIa or IIx in human limb muscle. It is the modern basis of fibre-type classification and the reason fibre types are named as they are.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 8v24M70 8v24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M10 14h26M10 26h26M70 14H44M70 26H44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="28" y="17" width="24" height="6" rx="3" fill="#ffb86b"/><path d="M30 17v-3M36 17v-3M42 23v3M48 23v3" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: The rate at which the myosin head splits ATP during cross-bridge cycling. Faster-shortening fibres split it faster (Bárány, 1967), the relationship that let histochemical ATPase staining classify fibres by speed.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 8v24M70 8v24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M10 14h26M10 26h26M70 14H44M70 26H44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="28" y="17" width="24" height="6" rx="3" fill="#ffb86b"/><path d="M30 17v-3M36 17v-3M42 23v3M48 23v3" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: The fastest, most forceful and most fatigable human fibre type, low in mitochondria, capillaries and myoglobin and reliant on phosphagen and glycolytic supply. Frequently labelled 'IIb' in older literature, though true MyHC-IIb is a small-mammal fibre.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="10" width="9" height="24" rx="2" fill="#5ec8ff"/><rect x="25" y="22" width="9" height="12" rx="2" fill="#5ec8ff" opacity="0.45"/><rect x="46" y="24" width="9" height="10" rx="2" fill="#ffb86b" opacity="0.45"/><rect x="59" y="8" width="9" height="26" rx="2" fill="#ffb86b"/><path d="M40 6v28" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A fibre co-expressing more than one myosin heavy chain isoform, most often I/IIa or IIa/IIx. Their prevalence is the main reason fibre type is better treated as a continuum than as three discrete bins.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="12" y="10" width="9" height="24" rx="2" fill="#5ec8ff"/><rect x="25" y="22" width="9" height="12" rx="2" fill="#5ec8ff" opacity="0.45"/><rect x="46" y="24" width="9" height="10" rx="2" fill="#ffb86b" opacity="0.45"/><rect x="59" y="8" width="9" height="26" rx="2" fill="#ffb86b"/><path d="M40 6v28" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The region of a muscle across which one motor unit's fibres are distributed. Because territories overlap and fibres of different units and types are intermingled, any single biopsy site samples a mosaic rather than a pure population.
