63.exam_focus: Expect to define the motor unit, explain the two mechanisms of force gradation and lay out the Type I / IIa / IIx property contrast — including the IIb-versus-IIx naming correction and why myosin ATPase activity tracks shortening velocity. Applied items typically ask which fibre-type shifts training does and does not produce, and how a fast-twitch-dominant HYROX athlete's week should be spaced differently.

64.title: Muscle mechanics — contraction types, force-length, force-velocity & strength curves
64.key_concept: Everything an athlete feels under load reduces to one mechanism: myosin heads binding actin, pivoting toward the centre of the sarcomere, and being detached again by ATP. Whole-muscle force is a question of how many cross-bridges are attached at once, and three separable things set that number — the filament overlap allowed by the muscle's current length (force–length), the speed at which it is changing length (force–velocity), and how much contractile tissue sits behind the tendon (physiological cross-sectional area, which pennation raises at the cost of shortening velocity). Layer changing joint moment arms on top and you get the strength curve of an exercise: how the force the athlete can produce changes through the range — ascending when capability rises toward lockout, descending when it falls away, bell-shaped when it peaks mid-range. Felt difficulty is the mismatch between that capability curve and the demand the load imposes. The point most often taught wrongly is that isometric force is 'maximal': it is maximal only relative to concentric actions, because maximal eccentric force exceeds it. Getting that hierarchy right — eccentric > isometric > concentric — is what makes the model usable at the sled and at the wall.
key_facts: Muscles shorten by sliding, not by shrinking filaments. Thin (actin) filaments are drawn over thick (myosin) filaments toward the centre of the sarcomere, so the I band and H zone narrow while the A band — the length of the thick filament — is unchanged. That band observation, reported independently by two research groups in 1954, is the original evidence for the model.

Cross-bridge cycle, in the order most often got backwards: ATP binding to the myosin head detaches it from actin; hydrolysis to ADP + Pi re-cocks the head into its high-energy position; calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin and shifts tropomyosin off the binding site; phosphate release triggers the power stroke that drags actin toward the M line; ADP leaves; the next ATP detaches the head again. One ATP per cycle.

It takes ATP to let go, not only to pull: with none available the head cannot detach and the muscle locks into the attached rigor state, of which rigor mortis is the extreme case. Relaxation costs ATP too, because calcium must be pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum — commonly estimated at something around a quarter to a third of contractile ATP turnover, with estimates varying by fibre type and method. Because the bill is charged per cycle, a gripped farmers handle or a braced sandbag does no external work yet still costs real energy.

Four muscle actions are conventionally named: isometric (tension, no net length change), concentric (shortening, positive external work), eccentric (lengthening under tension, so the load does work on the muscle) and isokinetic (length changing at constant velocity). Be precise about the fourth — isokinetic is a velocity condition rather than a distinct action, since the underlying action is still concentric or eccentric. A single sled-push stride uses only two of them: concentric hip, knee and ankle extension driving through an isometric locked-arm and braced-trunk link, with almost no eccentric component and nothing isokinetic about it.

Isokinetic work is a dynamometer condition rather than a gym method: holding limb velocity constant requires a machine that varies its resistance moment by moment to match whatever force is applied, which is why it survives mainly in testing and rehabilitation settings. SkiErg and rower flywheels do accommodate applied force — drag rises with handle speed — but the limbs still accelerate and decelerate within every stroke, so calling erg work isokinetic is loose at best.

Eccentric actions produce the highest force for the lowest metabolic cost per newton, because fewer attached cross-bridges are needed and those attached are forcibly detached while bearing high strain, with titin and connective tissue carrying part of the load. They also carry the largest damage and soreness cost — which is why sandbag lunges and burpee broad jump landings, not the concentric-dominant sleds, tend to dominate the days after a race.

Architecture decides the force–velocity trade-off before training does. Fusiform muscles run fibres along the line of pull — long fibres, many sarcomeres in series, high shortening velocity and large excursion — while pennate muscles attach fibres at an angle, packing more and shorter fibres into the same volume for a larger physiological cross-sectional area (PCSA, roughly muscle volume ÷ fibre length) and more force, at the cost of excursion and speed. Only the component along the tendon is transmitted, a factor of cos θ — about a 6% loss at 20° — which the PCSA gain comfortably repays. The quadriceps and calf that drive the sled push are pennate.

Force–length: active force peaks on a plateau where actin–myosin overlap is optimal and every myosin head is within reach of a binding site. Shorter than that (ascending limb), thin filaments from the two halves of the sarcomere double-overlap and interfere with one another and calcium sensitivity falls, and at the shortest lengths the thick filaments collide with the Z discs they are being drawn toward; longer (descending limb), overlap and therefore available cross-bridges fall away roughly linearly. Classic single-fibre work placed the optimum near 2.0–2.2 µm, but those are isolated-preparation figures and should not be quoted as in vivo human values.

In an intact muscle the measured force–length curve is active plus passive. Passive tension from titin, the extracellular matrix and the tendon rises steeply on the descending limb, so total force at long lengths does not collapse the way the active curve does. That passive contribution is one reason a lengthened muscle still transmits very high force, and part of why eccentric actions are so strong.

Force–velocity (Hill, 1938): concentric force falls as shortening velocity rises, because fewer cross-bridges are attached at any instant. Zero velocity gives the highest force on the concentric side of the curve — but maximal ECCENTRIC force exceeds maximal isometric force, commonly reported around 1.2–1.8× in isolated preparations and often only about 1.0–1.3× in voluntary human efforts because of neural inhibition. The lengthening branch is not a mirror image of the shortening branch: force rises steeply just past zero velocity and then largely plateaus, so eccentric force is close to velocity-independent in voluntary human efforts even though isolated preparations show it continuing to climb. 'Isometric is maximal force' is true only if eccentric actions are excluded, and that is a standard exam trap.

Power = force × velocity, so it is zero at both ends of the curve — no force at maximal unloaded velocity, no velocity at isometric — and peaks at an intermediate velocity, commonly around a third of maximal shortening velocity in isolated muscle. The maximal-strength / strength-speed / power / speed-strength / speed vocabulary simply labels positions along that curve; the terms describe the intent of a set, have no agreed load boundaries, and the single-muscle optimum does not transfer directly to a multi-joint barbell task.

Strength curves describe the exercise, not the muscle: they are the product of force–length, changing joint moment arms and the resistance's own lever arm, which is also why a constant external load never means a constant muscle tension. Three broad shapes recur. Ascending — capability rises toward extension, so a deadlift is hardest off the floor and eases past the knee, and most squat and press variations behave the same way. Descending — capability falls toward full contraction, so a chin-up or a supported row is hardest in the final few centimetres. Bell-shaped — most single-joint work peaks mid-range, the biceps curl being the standard example, hardest where the load's moment arm is longest. Equipment decides as much as anatomy: a leg extension on a plain lever arm gets harder toward full extension, in the short and weak range of the quadriceps, whereas a cammed machine follows whatever profile its designer chose.

HYROX mapping: the drive out of a wall ball and the leg action of the sled push are ascending-pattern exercises — capability rises toward end-range extension — except that the sled never gets easy, because friction is roughly constant across the 50 m, so end-range extension must still produce useful force on every stride. Sled pull, SkiErg and rower are descending-pattern for the upper body: capability falls as the rope or handle finishes toward the body, in the shortened range where the lats, posterior shoulder and elbow flexors are weakest, while the demand stays constant.
64.training_link: Work backwards from where in the range the athlete actually fails. The sled push demands force at end-range hip and knee extension because friction does not fall away as the joints open — precisely where a barbell squat unloads — so the primary dose is sled work at race load over race distance, with accommodating resistance on squats and presses as a secondary way of keeping tension high where the bar goes light. The pulling stations fail near the body, in the shortened range, so build strength there: brief loaded holds at the finish of rows and chin-ups, and rope pulls at race cadence. Load long muscle lengths deliberately — squats and split squats at or below judged depth — because wall balls and lunges are decided at the bottom. The push is concentric-dominant, so it tolerates more frequent repetition than lunge or landing work. Then audit station splits: matching a strength curve is a rationale, not demonstrated transfer.

glossary.def: The contractile unit of a myofibril, running from one Z line to the next and containing interdigitating thick (myosin) and thin (actin) filaments. Whole-muscle shortening is the sum of many sarcomeres shortening in series.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 8v24M70 8v24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M10 14h26M10 26h26M70 14H44M70 26H44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="28" y="17" width="24" height="6" rx="3" fill="#ffb86b"/><path d="M30 17v-3M36 17v-3M42 23v3M48 23v3" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: The repeating sequence in which a myosin head binds actin, executes a power stroke on phosphate release, is detached by ATP binding and re-cocked by ATP hydrolysis. One ATP is consumed per cycle, so the cost of a rep is set by how many cycles it takes.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 8v24M70 8v24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M10 14h26M10 26h26M70 14H44M70 26H44" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="28" y="17" width="24" height="6" rx="3" fill="#ffb86b"/><path d="M30 17v-3M36 17v-3M42 23v3M48 23v3" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: The strongly bound actin–myosin configuration that persists when no ATP is available to detach the head. It explains rigor mortis and makes the point that ATP is required for relaxation as much as for contraction.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 6 C12 22 26 32 72 34" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M8 4v32h68" fill="none" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: The combined cross-sectional area of all a muscle's fibres measured perpendicular to their own line of pull, approximated by muscle volume divided by fibre length. Maximal force is proportional to PCSA rather than to anatomical girth.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h60" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M16 20l7-10M26 20l7-10M36 20l7-10M46 20l7-10M56 20l7-10" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M16 20l7 10M26 20l7 10M36 20l7 10M46 20l7 10M56 20l7 10" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M20 30a12 12 0 0 1 4-9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.4"/></svg>

glossary.def: The angle between a muscle's fibres and the tendon or aponeurosis they pull on. Greater angles pack more fibres into a given volume for more force, but reduce excursion and shortening velocity and transmit only cos θ of the fibre force to the tendon.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h60" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M16 20l7-10M26 20l7-10M36 20l7-10M46 20l7-10M56 20l7-10" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M16 20l7 10M26 20l7 10M36 20l7 10M46 20l7 10M56 20l7 10" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M20 30a12 12 0 0 1 4-9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.4"/></svg>

glossary.def: The dependence of active muscle force on sarcomere length: a plateau at optimal actin–myosin overlap, with force falling on the ascending limb (thin-filament double overlap, reduced calcium sensitivity and eventually thick-filament contact with the Z discs) and on the descending limb (declining overlap).
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 6 C12 22 26 32 72 34" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M8 4v32h68" fill="none" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: Force transmitted by a muscle–tendon unit without active cross-bridge cycling, arising from titin, the extracellular matrix and the tendon. It rises steeply at long muscle lengths and adds to the active force there.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 6 C12 22 26 32 72 34" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M8 4v32h68" fill="none" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: The inverse relation between concentric force and shortening velocity, extended on the lengthening side where eccentric force exceeds maximal isometric force and then plateaus rather than continuing to climb in voluntary efforts. Force is highest eccentrically, next isometrically, and lowest at high shortening velocities.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="26" cy="21" r="11" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M26 21V13M26 21l7 5" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M44 14h24M44 21h18M44 28h12" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round"/></svg>

glossary.def: Not a fourth type of muscle action but a velocity condition: the underlying action is still concentric or eccentric, performed at a constant limb velocity, which in practice requires a dynamometer that varies its resistance to match the force applied. It belongs to testing and rehabilitation rather than to ordinary gym training.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="24" y="8" width="32" height="9" rx="4" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M20 12.5h-10M60 12.5h10" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M14 9l-4 3.5 4 3.5M66 9l4 3.5-4 3.5" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/><rect x="18" y="24" width="44" height="9" rx="4" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M14 28.5h-6M66 28.5h6" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M10 25l4 3.5-4 3.5M70 25l-4 3.5 4 3.5" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: How the force an athlete can produce changes across an exercise's range of motion — ascending, descending or bell-shaped. It is set by muscle force–length, changing joint moment arms and the resistance's own lever arm, so it is a property of the exercise and its equipment rather than of the muscle.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 6 C12 22 26 32 72 34" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M8 4v32h68" fill="none" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

64.exam_focus: Expect to sequence the cross-bridge cycle correctly, to define all four muscle actions, and to place the eccentric, isometric and concentric cases on the force–velocity curve — in particular to state that maximal eccentric force exceeds maximal isometric force, which in turn exceeds any concentric force. Expect also to identify an exercise's strength curve (ascending, descending or bell-shaped) and justify which HYROX station it maps to.

65.title: Oxygen transport — from atmosphere to mitochondria
65.key_concept: Oxygen reaches a mitochondrion by falling downhill in pressure, and every component of the delivery system exists to keep that descent steep enough to matter. Air is a mixture, so by Dalton's law each gas exerts its own partial pressure independently, and diffusion follows that pressure difference rather than the percentage in the mixture — which is why altitude costs performance although the oxygen fraction of air is unchanged. Sea-level barometry places the top of the cascade near 159 mmHg; humidification, carbon dioxide dilution and continuous pulmonary extraction bring it to roughly 100 mmHg in the alveolus, and it falls again through arterial blood, muscle tissue and finally the mitochondrion. Effort has no purchase on the composition or the pressure of that air: what climbs is consumption, and the body meets it by moving blood and gas faster. Oxygen crosses the alveolar membrane under Fick's law, travels almost entirely on haemoglobin, and is released where warmth and acidity lower affinity; carbon dioxide returns mostly as bicarbonate. The Fick principle closes the chain — oxygen uptake equals cardiac output multiplied by the arterial–venous oxygen difference, one central term and one peripheral.
key_facts: Dalton's law: the total pressure of a gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures of its constituents, each behaving as though the others were absent. Dry air is close to 78% nitrogen, 20.9% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide, so at a sea-level barometric pressure near 760 mmHg the partial pressure of oxygen is about 0.209 x 760 ≈ 159 mmHg. Diffusion is driven by that pressure, never by the fraction: the oxygen percentage of the atmosphere is effectively the same at a coastal venue and on a mountain, and what falls with elevation is the pressure term. At roughly 2000 m, standard barometric pressure is near 596 mmHg, giving a dry inspired PO2 of about 125 mmHg — a reduction of roughly 21% in driving pressure with the gas mixture unchanged. Every downstream altitude consequence (lower arterial saturation, lower oxygen content, a higher heart rate at a given pace) descends from that single piece of arithmetic.

The cascade, with typical resting sea-level figures presented as approximations rather than constants: atmospheric PO2 about 159 mmHg; humidified tracheal gas about 149 mmHg; alveolar gas about 100–105 mmHg; arterial blood about 95–100 mmHg; mixed venous blood returning to the lung about 40 mmHg; resting muscle tissue roughly 20–40 mmHg, falling into single figures in hard-working muscle; and mitochondrial PO2 lower still, commonly quoted in the region of 1–5 mmHg. Alveolar PO2 sits below atmospheric for four separable reasons: water vapour at body temperature contributes about 47 mmHg and displaces the other gases; carbon dioxide entering the alveolus dilutes them further; pulmonary capillary blood strips oxygen continuously; and each tidal breath mixes into a much larger resident lung volume instead of replacing it. Approximating alveolar PO2 as inspired PO2 minus arterial PCO2 divided by the respiratory exchange ratio gives roughly 149 − 40/0.8 ≈ 99 mmHg. Taken across the tissue bed as a whole, the descent from arterial blood at 95–100 mmHg to a mitochondrial PO2 of roughly 1–5 mmHg is by far the largest in the chain — the arterial-to-tissue step alone, at 55–80 mmHg, exceeds any single pulmonary step, and it is that gradient which pulls oxygen out of the capillary. Keep the two currencies separate, though: the arterial–venous oxygen difference does not measure a pressure step at all, but the oxygen CONTENT removed from blood across the tissue bed, in mL per 100 mL — and content, not pressure, is what the peripheral term of the Fick principle is expressed in.

Barometric pressure and the oxygen fraction are properties of the venue, not of the athlete, so the pressure at the top of the cascade is identical at rest and at maximal effort — a misconception worth killing explicitly, because athletes routinely reason as though effort improved the supply. Intensity moves only the consumption side of the ledger, and the body meets it with flow: a larger cardiac output moving blood past the alveolar membrane and the muscle capillary more often, and a larger alveolar ventilation refreshing alveolar gas faster (how that ventilation is regulated is day 66). Two secondary effects do steepen the gradient at each end without touching the starting point — alveolar PO2 rises modestly as hyperventilation lowers alveolar PCO2, and mixed venous PO2 falls as extraction increases — so the pulmonary gradient generally widens during exercise rather than narrowing. The coaching consequence: training buys transport and extraction, never a richer atmosphere, so an altitude deficit is a race-model problem, not a fitness problem to be fixed in taper week.

Fick's LAW of diffusion and the Fick PRINCIPLE are separate statements from the same physiologist, and conflating them is a standard exam error. The law governs transfer across a membrane: rate rises with the available surface area and the partial pressure gradient, falls with membrane thickness, and is scaled by each gas's own diffusion constant (proportional to solubility, inversely proportional to the square root of molecular weight). The lung is built to exploit it — several hundred million alveoli give a total exchange surface commonly estimated around 70 m2, with published values spreading roughly 50–100 m2 by method, and the blood–gas barrier at its thinnest is well under one micrometre. The law also explains the asymmetry between the two gases: oxygen crosses on a gradient of roughly 60–65 mmHg while carbon dioxide has only about 6 mmHg (mixed venous near 46, alveolar near 40), yet carbon dioxide is roughly 24 times more soluble in the fluid it must cross and, after correcting for its greater molecular weight, diffuses on the order of twenty times faster. Small gradient, easy clearance.

A red cell spends roughly 0.75 s in a pulmonary capillary at rest, and equilibration with alveolar gas is normally complete within about the first third of that — which is why the lung is not the limiting step for most athletes. At maximal cardiac output, transit time falls toward roughly 0.25 s. Capillary recruitment and distension blunt that fall by increasing the total capillary volume available, and equilibration usually still completes, but the safety margin narrows: this is why a subset of highly trained athletes show measurable arterial desaturation at maximal effort (exercise-induced arterial hypoxaemia), and why altitude, a thickened membrane or lung pathology bites hardest at high outputs rather than at rest. Teach it as a shrinking reserve, not as a routine failure.

Roughly 98% of arterial oxygen is bound to haemoglobin and about 2% is physically dissolved in plasma; the dissolved fraction alone could not fund resting metabolism, let alone a race. Each haemoglobin molecule carries four haem groups — each an iron-containing porphyrin ring binding one oxygen molecule — set within a four-subunit globin protein whose cooperative conformational change generates the sigmoid curve. At a haemoglobin concentration near 15 g/dL and a binding capacity around 1.34 mL O2 per gram, arterial blood carries close to 20 mL of oxygen per 100 mL. Total haemoglobin MASS, not merely concentration, is therefore a genuine performance variable rather than trivia: it sets arterial oxygen content, which multiplies cardiac output to give delivery. Iron status matters for the same reason, because iron deficiency constrains haemoglobin synthesis long before frank anaemia appears on a report. Diagnosis and treatment are medical decisions — screen and refer, do not prescribe.

The oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid, and each half of the shape does a distinct job. The flat upper portion — saturation stays above roughly 90% while PO2 remains above about 60 mmHg — protects arterial loading against modest falls in alveolar PO2 at the lung. The steep lower portion, roughly 10–40 mmHg, means small further falls in tissue PO2 release large quantities of oxygen at the muscle. At rest, arterial saturation is about 97–98% and mixed venous about 75%, so roughly a quarter of the carried oxygen is unloaded per circuit; at maximal exercise venous saturation falls far lower and extraction rises to around 75–85%. Get the direction right: a RIGHT shift means REDUCED haemoglobin–oxygen affinity and therefore MORE offloading at any given PO2, produced by raised H+ (lower pH), raised temperature, raised 2,3-DPG and raised PCO2, with P50 — the PO2 at 50% saturation, normally about 26–27 mmHg — rising accordingly. The Bohr effect names the pH and carbon dioxide arm specifically; temperature and 2,3-DPG act through separate mechanisms. A left shift is the reverse and favours loading. The arrangement is self-regulating: hot, acidic working muscle unloads oxygen where it is wanted, while the cooler, less acidic lung loads it. Myoglobin, a single-subunit intracellular carrier with one haem, has a much higher affinity (P50 around 2–3 mmHg) and a hyperbolic rather than sigmoid curve, so it accepts oxygen from haemoglobin at low tissue PO2 and buffers supply at the start of a contraction.

Carbon dioxide leaves in three forms, and the proportions matter. Most of it — roughly 60–70% — travels as bicarbonate: CO2 diffuses into the red cell, carbonic anhydrase hydrates it to carbonic acid within milliseconds, and that dissociates to H+ and HCO3−. The bicarbonate is exported into plasma in exchange for chloride through the red cell's anion exchanger, the chloride shift, which keeps electrical neutrality and prevents bicarbonate accumulating inside the cell and stalling the reaction. Roughly 20–25% is carried as carbamino compounds, bound chiefly to the terminal amine groups of the globin chains rather than to the haem iron, and only about 5–10% is dissolved. The H+ released in the process is buffered largely by haemoglobin itself. The Haldane effect is the reciprocal of the Bohr effect and should be learned as a pair with it: deoxygenated haemoglobin binds both H+ and carbon dioxide more readily, so unloading oxygen in the muscle simultaneously increases the blood's capacity to carry carbon dioxide away, while re-oxygenating haemoglobin in the lung drives carbon dioxide off. Bohr describes what CO2 and acid do to oxygen carriage; Haldane describes what oxygen does to CO2 carriage. The two reinforce one another at the muscle and reverse together at the lung — they are not opposing effects.

The heart is two pumps in series, not one. The right side receives systemic venous blood and drives the low-pressure pulmonary circuit; the left ventricle receives oxygenated blood and drives the high-pressure systemic circuit, with valves enforcing one-way flow through each. Stroke volume is the blood ejected per beat, and cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume: typical resting values are around 5 L/min from a stroke volume of roughly 60–100 mL, rising to about 20–25 L/min in trained athletes and beyond 30 L/min in elite endurance athletes, with maximal stroke volumes of roughly 150–200 mL or more. All of those are population approximations that vary with body size, posture and measurement method. Worked example: an age-group athlete on run 5 at 172 bpm with a stroke volume of 118 mL is producing 172 x 118 = 20,296 mL/min ≈ 20.3 L/min; at an arterial oxygen content of 19.5 mL per 100 mL that is roughly 203 dL/min x 19.5 ≈ 3,960 mL of oxygen delivered per minute. After a block that raises stroke volume to 132 mL, the same 20.3 L/min needs only about 154 bpm — the whole point of central training. Note the caveat on the classic account: stroke volume is usually described as rising to a plateau somewhere around 40–60% of VO2max, but in highly trained endurance athletes stroke volume frequently keeps climbing toward maximal effort, attributed to superior ventricular compliance and diastolic filling. Treat the plateau as the general pattern, not a law. The adaptations behind a larger stroke volume are plasma volume expansion (fast, within days to weeks), greater end-diastolic filling, eccentric ventricular hypertrophy and improved contractility.

Blood is roughly 55% plasma and 45% formed elements, of which over 99% are red cells; plasma is about 90% water, the remainder plasma proteins, electrolytes, hormones, nutrients and metabolites, and it also transports heat toward the skin. Haematocrit — the red-cell fraction of blood volume — typically runs around 40–45%, with a lower usual range in women. Two honest nuances follow. First, dehydration raises haematocrit and haemoglobin concentration by removing plasma, which is haemoconcentration and not improved oxygen-carrying capacity: total haemoglobin mass is unchanged, viscosity rises, and the lost plasma volume reduces filling and stroke volume, so delivery actually falls. A high reading after a hard hot session is a warning, not a win. Second, the mirror image: a haematocrit that drops a few points early in a heavy aerobic block is usually dilutional, because plasma volume expands within days to weeks while red-cell mass follows far more slowly — evidence the training is working rather than of anaemia, though persistent findings alongside stalled progress warrant referral.

Where the blood goes changes as much as how much of it there is. At rest, skeletal muscle takes only about 15–20% of cardiac output while splanchnic and renal beds take roughly half; at high intensity, muscle can claim 80–85%. Three mechanisms do it: local metabolic vasodilation in active muscle (falling PO2 with rising CO2, H+, potassium, adenosine and temperature), sympathetic vasoconstriction in gut, liver and kidney, and capillary recruitment within the working muscle, which simultaneously increases the surface area for diffusion and lengthens red-cell transit through the tissue. Reduced splanchnic perfusion is part of why gastrointestinal symptoms surface at race intensity. The competitor that matters on a hot race day is skin: thermoregulatory flow claims litres per minute from the same finite cardiac output, so cooling and locomotion are drawing on one budget (the further blood-flow competition from hard-working respiratory muscles is day 21).

Extraction is the second half of the peripheral story. The arterial–venous oxygen difference runs roughly 5 mL per 100 mL at rest — about 25% of the arterial content — and roughly 15–17 mL per 100 mL at maximal exercise, widened by capillary density and recruitment, mitochondrial density and oxidative enzyme activity, myoglobin content, and the local right shift of the dissociation curve. The Fick principle assembles the whole lesson into one equation: VO2 = cardiac output x arterial–venous oxygen difference. It splits aerobic capacity cleanly into a central delivery term and a peripheral extraction term, and those two answer to different training — the central term to sustained aerobic volume and threshold work through plasma volume and ventricular filling, the peripheral term to capillarisation and mitochondrial adaptation. At sea level in healthy athletes, VO2max itself is generally considered limited more by delivery than by extraction, whereas submaximal endurance, threshold pace (day 19) and between-station recovery (day 20) lean heavily on the peripheral term.

HYROX application. The race opens by asking the delivery chain to feed a small muscle mass hard: the SkiErg is station 1 and the row station 5, and upper-body ergometry at a given oxygen uptake produces a higher heart rate, higher blood pressure and higher ventilation than leg work — the elevated heart rate reflecting a LOWER stroke volume rather than a larger pump output, since a smaller active muscle mass returns less blood to fill the ventricle (day 14 on the early-race heart-rate spike). Peak oxygen uptake in arm-dominant work is typically well below leg values, because there is less muscle to extract into, so the peripheral term is small and the effort is expensive centrally. The sleds are concentric-dominant and high-force, and sustained tension there transiently impairs local perfusion, so delivery is briefly throttled at exactly the moment demand peaks. Wall balls close the race at 100 reps in every individual division, with no run afterwards to clear on. Across the 15 roxzone traverses, delivery is being defended by a rising heart rate against a falling plasma volume, and extraction has little reserve left to widen — which is the transport-side floor under the durability picture on day 22.
65.training_link: Two terms of the Fick principle are yours; the atmosphere is not. Central: sustained aerobic volume and threshold work (day 19) expand plasma volume within days to weeks, improve ventricular filling and drive eccentric hypertrophy, so the cardiac output an athlete needs on run 6 arrives at a lower heart rate. Peripheral: capillarisation, mitochondrial density and myoglobin widen the arterial–venous oxygen difference, and that is the term that repays a sled push over the following kilometre. Screen the input side rather than guess at it — if aerobic progress stalls with unexplained fatigue and a rising heart rate at fixed pace, refer for a full blood count and ferritin, and never prescribe iron yourself. Programme upper-body aerobic work so the SkiErg and row are not the first time the chain has fed a small muscle mass hard. In heat, protect plasma volume, acclimatise across several sessions and re-model the race, because skin and muscle draw on one finite output.

glossary.def: The pressure a single gas in a mixture would exert if it alone occupied the volume — its fractional concentration multiplied by total pressure. It, and not concentration, is the quantity that drives diffusion across a membrane, which is why altitude lowers the oxygen driving pressure while leaving the oxygen fraction of air unchanged.

65.exam_focus: Expect to walk the oxygen cascade with typical partial pressures all the way to the mitochondrion, to give four reasons alveolar PO2 sits below atmospheric, to state the Fick principle and defend its central and peripheral terms as separate training targets, and to name the three forms of carbon dioxide carriage with the chloride shift. Four recurring traps: confusing Fick's LAW of diffusion with the Fick PRINCIPLE; reversing the dissociation curve, when a right shift means reduced affinity and greater offloading with the Bohr effect naming the pH and carbon dioxide arm specifically; mixing up the Bohr and Haldane effects, which are reciprocal rather than opposed — Bohr describes what carbon dioxide and H+ do to oxygen carriage, Haldane what oxygen does to carbon dioxide carriage, and the two reinforce each other at the muscle and again, in reverse, at the lung; and treating a high haematocrit as improved oxygen-carrying capacity when it may be haemoconcentration.

66.title: Exercise intensity domains & the ventilatory response
66.key_concept: Every cardiorespiratory response exists to keep ATP resynthesis matched to ATP hydrolysis. Because ATP turnover climbs steeply with power output, and because the pathways resupplying it differ in rate and sustainability, physiology does not change smoothly across intensity — it changes in bands. The intensity-domain model defines those bands by how the body behaves over time at a fixed workload, not by a percentage of some maximum. Below the first lactate threshold (moderate) lactate sits at or near resting values and VO2 reaches steady state within a few minutes. Between LT1 and the maximal metabolic steady state (heavy) lactate rises but stabilises at an elevated plateau, and VO2 reaches a delayed, inflated steady state. Above the maximal metabolic steady state (severe) nothing stabilises: VO2 drifts toward VO2max and the bout ends in task failure. A fourth extreme or sprint band sits above the intensities at which VO2max is attainable at all. Ventilation tracks these transitions closely enough to locate them non-invasively, which is what turns the framework into a coaching tool rather than another zone chart.
key_facts: Domains are defined by what a fixed intensity does over TIME, not by a share of a maximum — moderate: blood lactate at or near baseline; heavy: elevated but plateauing; severe: rising continuously with no steady state until task failure. That behavioural definition is what separates the model from an ordinary zone chart.

Boundaries: the first lactate threshold separates moderate from heavy; the maximal metabolic steady state separates heavy from severe. Day 19 covers LT1 and LT2 themselves and their field proxies — this lesson is about what happens either side of them.

MMSS, MLSS and critical power/speed describe the same boundary region from different tests and are not interchangeable; critical power typically sits slightly above MLSS. Treat any of them as an estimate of the heavy/severe boundary rather than a measurement of it.

An extreme (sprint) band sits above severe. Here the effort ends so quickly — well before the oxygen-uptake response has time to climb to VO2max — that performance is set by how much force the neuromuscular system can produce and how long the phosphagen pool sustains it, with the rate of oxygen delivery essentially irrelevant to the outcome.

The entire cascade — heart rate, stroke volume, ventilation, vasodilation, capillary recruitment and oxygen extraction — exists for one purpose: matching the rate of ATP resynthesis to the rate of ATP hydrolysis (day 18 for the pathways doing the resynthesising). ATP turnover rises steeply with power output while the free ATP pool itself is worth only a second or two of maximal work, so fatigue is what a failed match looks like.

VO2 kinetics by domain: moderate reaches steady state in roughly 2–3 min from the primary component alone; heavy reaches a delayed and elevated steady state; severe never stabilises, drifting up toward VO2max until the athlete stops.

The VO2 slow component appears only above LT1 and emerges after roughly 1.5–3 min of constant work: oxygen cost keeps rising although speed has not changed. It is associated with progressive recruitment of higher-threshold, less economical motor units (day 63), with respiratory-muscle work, rising muscle temperature and catecholamines also proposed — the full mechanism is still debated.

Three-phase ventilatory response at onset: (I) an immediate feedforward jump that can begin before the first stride, from central command and the abrupt rise in cardiac output; (II) a continued steep rise over roughly the next two minutes as neural drive plus limb mechanoreceptor and metabolic feedback add to it; (III) a slower chemoreceptor-modulated settling into steady state in moderate and heavy, or an unbroken climb in severe. Numbering conventions differ between texts — the mechanisms matter more than the labels.

Ventilation rises close to linearly with intensity, then breaks upward. Bicarbonate buffering of H+ liberates extra, non-metabolic CO2 so VCO2 climbs disproportionately to VO2, and rising H+ stimulates chemoreceptors directly — the carotid bodies at the carotid bifurcation are the dominant peripheral sensor in humans (aortic bodies contributing), while central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to H+ generated in brain extracellular fluid as CO2 crosses the blood–brain barrier. All converge on the brainstem respiratory centres, with group III/IV muscle afferents (day 21) adding metaboreceptor feedback.

Ventilatory equivalents: VE/VO2 (litres of air per litre of O2 consumed) and VE/VCO2. VT1 = the point where VE/VO2 turns up while VE/VCO2 is still flat or falling; it marks the START of the isocapnic buffering region, which runs from VT1 up to VT2/RCP. VT2/RCP = the point where VE/VCO2 also turns up, i.e. the END of that region, where buffering can no longer hold pH and ventilation outruns CO2 production. The region — not VT1 itself — is where the extra ventilation is matched by the non-metabolic CO2 that bicarbonate buffering liberates, so arterial CO2 is held roughly constant.

VT1 ≈ LT1 and VT2/RCP ≈ LT2 are practical approximations, not identities. Gas exchange and blood lactate measure different things, threshold detection is protocol- and assessor-dependent, and in a given athlete the two can be separated by a margin large enough to change a pace prescription — always state which method produced the number.

Heart rate rises near-linearly with intensity (sympathetic drive and catecholamines at the SA node, with parasympathetic withdrawal dominating early), but it is a weak intensity proxy: it lags a step change by tens of seconds, so a 2-minute severe effort is over before HR arrives; it drifts upward at fixed work with heat, dehydration and falling plasma volume; and arousal, caffeine and upper-body work raise it independently of running intensity. The textbook account has stroke volume plateauing somewhere around 40–60% VO2max, leaving HR as the main lever for further cardiac output — but in highly trained endurance athletes SV often continues to rise toward maximal effort, so treat the plateau as the general pattern rather than a universal law.

Race mapping: for a well-paced athlete the eight 1 km legs sit in the heavy domain, while the sleds (concentric-dominant, high-force) and the burpee broad jumps force repeated severe excursions, each repaid on the following kilometre and across the 15 roxzone traverses. Wall balls — 100 reps in every individual division — are the exception: they are the eighth and final station, so their severe excursion has no following run and no following traverse to be repaid on, which is why a blown pacing plan surfaces there as fragmented sets rather than as a slow split (day 16). Fatigue also lowers the boundaries themselves (day 22), so an athlete who spends the opening kilometres in severe cannot simply drop back into a steady state later.
66.training_link: Prescribe from behaviour, not from a percentage. A ramp test locates candidate intensities; only a constant-load trial tells you which domain one of them is actually in, so confirm with a probe: 30 minutes at the pace you believe is the athlete's ceiling, sampling pace, breathing and, if you have a meter, lactate at ten and thirty minutes. Stable readings with pace held means heavy; a reading that keeps climbing, or a pace that collapses, means that pace was severe and the race model built on it (day 16) is wrong. Anchor the heavy–severe boundary with day 19's time-trial proxy and re-anchor it every block. Then write sessions in domain language: easy volume clearly below LT1; threshold work in upper heavy where a steady state still exists; severe intervals short enough that the rising VO2 is the stimulus rather than the failure. In-race, coach pace and breathing rhythm — heart rate lags the sled by tens of seconds and drifts through the second half, so it reports where the athlete has been, not where they are.

glossary.def: A band of intensity within which the physiological response to constant work follows a characteristic time course. Domains are bounded by thresholds rather than by fixed percentages of VO2max or maximum heart rate, so the same percentage can fall in different domains for different athletes.

glossary.def: Intensities above the maximal metabolic steady state, where no steady state exists — lactate climbs continuously, VO2 rises toward VO2max, and the bout ends in task failure. Above it sits the extreme or sprint band, in which the bout is over before oxygen uptake has time to reach VO2max, so performance is decided by neuromuscular force production and phosphagen availability.

glossary.def: The highest intensity at which the metabolic responses to constant work still level off instead of climbing to their limits. It is estimated in practice by MLSS or by critical power/speed protocols, which are related but non-identical constructs.

glossary.def: The delayed additional rise in oxygen uptake that develops after roughly the first two minutes of constant work above LT1, so the oxygen cost of an unchanged workload keeps increasing. It is associated with progressive recruitment of higher-threshold, less efficient motor units, though the full mechanism remains contested.

glossary.def: Ventilation expressed per unit of gas exchanged — VE/VO2 is litres of air breathed per litre of oxygen consumed, VE/VCO2 per litre of carbon dioxide produced. Their inflection points allow thresholds to be located from expired gas alone.

glossary.def: The intensity at which VE/VO2 begins to rise while VE/VCO2 is still flat or falling, taken as a gas-exchange estimate of LT1 and as the lower end of the isocapnic buffering region. The two thresholds usually land close together but are measured by different means and need not coincide.

glossary.def: The stretch of intensity between VT1 and VT2/RCP in which the extra ventilation is matched by the non-metabolic CO2 that bicarbonate buffering of H+ liberates, so arterial CO2 is held roughly constant. It is a region with two ends, not a single point.

glossary.def: The higher breakpoint at which VE/VCO2 also begins to rise, marking the end of isocapnic buffering — ventilation now climbs faster than CO2 production because bicarbonate buffering can no longer hold pH. Used as a gas-exchange estimate of LT2.

66.exam_focus: Expect to name the four intensity domains, the boundary separating each pair, and the lactate and VO2 behaviour that defines them at a constant work rate. Applied items typically ask you to identify a domain from a described time course, to explain the two ventilatory inflection points and the region between them, or to justify why heart rate alone cannot prescribe or police HYROX intensity.

67.title: Hormonal responses to exercise
67.key_concept: Hormones are chemical messengers secreted by glands into the circulation; they reach every tissue but act only where a receptor for them exists. That clause carries most of the physiology. The receptor — its number, affinity and downstream signalling — governs the response, and receptor expression is itself altered by training, so a given blood concentration has no fixed effect. Two signalling speeds are examinable: steroid hormones (testosterone, cortisol, oestrogen) are lipophilic, travel protein-bound and act on intracellular receptors to change gene transcription over hours to days; peptide hormones and catecholamines bind membrane receptors and act through intracellular signalling cascades in seconds to minutes. The trap sits one step further on. Transient post-session rises in testosterone and growth hormone are real and easy to measure, but they predict subsequent hypertrophy and strength gain poorly or not at all — mechanical tension, effort close to failure and accumulated volume-load are the established drivers. Endocrinology earns its place in HYROX coaching through sleep, total stress load, fuelling and acute readiness, not through chasing spikes.
key_facts: The endocrine signal is only one input, and not the decisive one for the muscle. A loaded fibre responds mainly to LOCAL messages — mechanotransduction at the sarcolemma and costameres, autocrine/paracrine growth factors, satellite-cell and immune signalling — which act only on the fibres that did the work. Circulating hormones bathe every tissue equally, which is precisely why they cannot explain why only the trained limb grows.

The receptor, not the ligand alone, sets the response: number, affinity and post-receptor signalling all matter, and all are modifiable. Androgen-receptor content in loaded skeletal muscle responds to resistance training, though the time course is untidy — several studies report a fall in the hours immediately after a session followed by a rise over the following days, so a single time-point measurement is easy to over-read.

Read the acute profile as information about the session, not as the adaptation to it. Central drive and the contracting muscle both signal the endocrine glands, and what is released encodes two things at once: the degree of physiological disturbance (the catecholamine and cortisol arm) and the metabolic state of the work (the insulin/glucagon arm — insulin falling and glucagon rising as exercise draws on blood glucose). That is precisely why an acute hormone measurement is a decent index of what a session cost and a poor predictor of what it will build.

Speed distinction (a favourite exam item): steroid → lipophilic → crosses the membrane → intracellular/nuclear receptor → altered gene transcription → new protein, hours to days. Peptide (GH, IGF-1, insulin) and catecholamine → membrane receptor → intracellular signalling cascade — cAMP for catecholamines via G-protein-coupled receptors, JAK/STAT for GH, receptor tyrosine kinase and PI3K-Akt for insulin and IGF-1 — → existing proteins switched on or off, seconds to minutes. Catecholamines are fast because they modify proteins that already exist; steroids are slow because they build new ones.

Testosterone comes predominantly from the Leydig cells of the testes in men, with a small adrenal-cortical contribution (about 5%); in women the ovaries and the adrenal cortex both contribute, much of it via peripheral conversion of androgen precursors, with circulating concentrations typically about an order of magnitude lower. Its actions extend well beyond the training response: androgen signalling drives development of reproductive tissue and secondary sexual characteristics, and across adult life it is a maintenance signal for skeletal muscle and for bone — androgen deficiency is associated with reduced bone mineral density in both sexes, which is why a low reading alongside a bone stress injury is a referral trigger rather than a curiosity. It is lipophilic, so roughly 96–99% travels bound — loosely to albumin, tightly to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) — leaving only a few per cent free (commonly quoted as 1–4%, typically about 2% in men, with real assay and population variation). Carrier binding slows hepatic and renal clearance and damps swings in the free concentration; because albumin binding is weak, albumin-bound hormone is conventionally counted as bioavailable, so 'bioavailable' is a wider category than 'free'. Total testosterone counts free plus bound; free testosterone (the unbound fraction) and bioavailable testosterone (free plus the loosely albumin-bound fraction, which dissociates readily and is accessible to tissue) are separate measurements again, and the three can move differently when SHBG shifts. Circulating testosterone also follows a diurnal rhythm that is HIGHEST in the early morning and drifts down across the day.

Heavy, large-muscle-mass, moderate-to-high-volume resistance work produces a transient rise in circulating testosterone, generally peaking around the end of the session and settling back toward baseline within roughly an hour. The size of the excursion scales with muscle mass recruited, load — the protocols that reliably produce it use heavy work, commonly cited above roughly 85% 1RM, though the response is graded rather than a threshold — and total work completed; training status matters too, with experienced lifters (often quoted as beyond about two years of consistent resistance training) showing larger responses than novices, largely because they can actually complete that kind of session. Note precisely what this describes: the conditions that move the hormone, not the conditions that build the muscle. The acute rise is far smaller in women — yet women hypertrophy at broadly similar RELATIVE rates to men, which was an early clue that the spike is not the mechanism.

The acute anabolic hormone hypothesis is not supported. Post-exercise elevations in testosterone, GH and IGF-1 have repeatedly failed to predict subsequent hypertrophy or strength gain (West, Phillips and colleagues, and the replications and reviews that followed); one analysis even reported the acute CORTISOL response as a weak positive correlate of lean-mass change, the opposite of a simple anabolic/catabolic model. The honest boundary: this refutes acute ripples inside the normal range, not testosterone itself — sustained supraphysiological concentrations from exogenous administration clearly increase muscle size and strength, even without training. Weeks of markedly elevated concentration and an excursion lasting tens of minutes to about an hour are different phenomena. Rest intervals are the clearest test case: short inter-set rest (roughly 30–60 s) reliably produces a LARGER acute GH response than long rest, and often though less consistently a larger testosterone response, yet controlled trials comparing about 1 min with about 3 min report equal or GREATER hypertrophy and strength with the longer rest, because short rest cuts the reps completed and therefore the volume-load. Choose rest from the volume-load and movement quality you intend to achieve, or from a competition demand, never from the hormonal response.

Endurance training and testosterone: intense endurance exercise can raise it acutely, while some long-term endurance-trained men show lower resting concentrations than untrained comparisons. Much of that work is cross-sectional, and low energy availability plus chronic training and life stress are plausible mediators (day 23 covers the energy-availability arm and the bone consequences). It should not be read as endurance training being inherently harmful.

Growth hormone (somatotropin) is released from the ANTERIOR pituitary under hypothalamic control — GHRH stimulating, somatostatin inhibiting — in pulses, with the largest pulses in the early, slow-wave-dominant part of the night; laboratory sleep restriction blunts that nocturnal profile (day 4). High-lactate, short-rest work produces the largest acute exercise-induced GH release. Distinguish GH's OWN actions — lipolysis and a glucose-sparing, anti-insulin effect — from its growth actions, which are largely mediated by IGF-1.

IGF-1 is produced by the liver in response to GH and is also expressed locally within muscle. It promotes amino-acid uptake and protein synthesis, drives satellite-cell proliferation and inhibits apoptosis (programmed cell death). Circulating and locally expressed IGF-1 are not the same story: hepatic output changes slowly, over many hours to more than a day, and falls with sustained low energy availability, whereas local expression tracks the tissue that was actually loaded. The axis is also not muscle-only — GH and IGF-1 act on bone and on tendon and cartilage matrix, supporting the remodelling that follows mechanical loading, which is the relevant arm in a HYROX build where running volume and the eccentric exposure of sandbag lunges and burpee-broad-jump landings (day 39) both draw on connective-tissue turnover. Note that this is a permissive maintenance role, not a case for chasing an acute GH excursion.

Catecholamines: adrenaline and noradrenaline are secreted by the adrenal MEDULLA, and noradrenaline is additionally released from sympathetic nerve terminals as a neurotransmitter. Cortisol draining from the cortex into the medulla induces PNMT, the enzyme that methylates noradrenaline to adrenaline — which is why medullary output is predominantly adrenaline (commonly cited around 80%). Effects: ↑ heart rate and contractility, vasoconstriction in non-essential beds with vasodilation in working muscle, bronchodilation, glycogenolysis and lipolysis, and enhanced skeletal-muscle contractile function via Na+/K+ pump activation — with arousal and central drive rising in parallel from central noradrenergic activity rather than from circulating adrenaline, which does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier. Release is ANTICIPATORY — it begins before the gun, alongside the feedforward phase-1 ventilatory jump of day 66 — and plasma half-life is short (on the order of 1–3 min), so concentrations fall quickly once work stops.

Cortisol is the principal glucocorticoid, released from the adrenal CORTEX under HPA-axis control (CRH → ACTH → cortisol), with a diurnal rhythm peaking about 30–45 min after waking and troughing late in the evening. It drives gluconeogenesis from amino acids, glycerol and lactate; raises proteolytic enzyme activity and restrains protein synthesis; and is anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory. It is necessary rather than villainous — it supplies glucose across a 60–110 min race and maintains the tissue responsiveness that catecholamines act through. The acute response scales with intensity, total work and how strongly glycolytic the session is: high-volume, short-rest, large-muscle-mass work produces the biggest excursions, and prolonged efforts raise it through the demand for hepatic glucose output. The catabolic effect is not uniform across the muscle either — type II fibres appear more susceptible than type I (day 63), so the force-producing qualities the sleds and wall balls draw on are the ones chronic elevation erodes first. The problem is chronic elevation with insufficient recovery, not its presence.

The testosterone:cortisol ratio is an intuitively attractive index of anabolic-to-catabolic status and a poor monitoring tool in practice. Both hormones are pulsatile and strongly diurnal, so sampling time and the previous day's training dominate the number; inter- and intra-individual variation is large; assays differ; and the ratio has repeatedly failed to predict performance or to separate functional from non-functional overreaching. The alternative is not a better blood marker but the load-and-readiness monitoring set already established in day 6; nothing in the endocrine literature displaces it.
67.training_link: Take four things from this material into a HYROX build and leave the fifth behind. Protect sleep first: the largest nocturnal GH pulses sit in the early slow-wave hours (day 4). Second, audit TOTAL stress, not training stress alone — work, travel and family load drive the same HPA axis, and chronic activation degrades recovery, immune function and availability to train (day 6). Third, fuel to the work done; sustained low energy availability has documented endocrine consequences (days 23–24). Fourth, treat start-line arousal as a coaching variable in its own right — the anticipatory sympathetic rise arrives before the gun whether you plan for it or not, so the job is reaching the line activated but not over-aroused (day 45). Build the warm-up backwards from the first three minutes of the race, and judge it by how the opening kilometre and the SkiErg feel, not by a hormonal rationale. What you leave behind is choosing rest intervals or session times to chase a spike: set rests from the race demand — work under incomplete recovery across 15 roxzone traverses, concentric-dominant sleds and 100 wall balls — and from the volume-load you intend to complete.

67.exam_focus: Expect to separate steroid from peptide/catecholamine signalling by receptor location, mechanism and time course; to state where each hormone is produced and what it does — including PNMT's role in making medullary output predominantly adrenaline, the anterior-pituitary GH → hepatic IGF-1 axis, testosterone's maintenance role in muscle and bone, and the total/free/bioavailable testosterone distinctions. The discriminating item is applied: given a training recommendation justified by an acute testosterone or growth-hormone 'spike' (short rests, exercise order, evening sessions), evaluate it correctly — name mechanical tension, effort and accumulated volume-load as the actual drivers, note that short rest raises the acute GH response while reducing volume-load, and identify the testosterone:cortisol ratio as an unreliable monitoring tool relative to the day 6 approach.

68.title: Thermoregulation & heat strain
68.key_concept: Heat strain is an accounting problem before it is a physiological one. Metabolic rate sets heat production, the four exchange avenues set heat loss, and the difference is stored — stored heat is what raises tissue temperature. Because only roughly a fifth to a quarter of energy turnover leaves the body as external work, most of what a hard-working athlete produces is heat, and production scales with metabolic rate. Relative intensity therefore sets the core temperature an athlete plateaus at whenever the environment can still carry the heat away; when it cannot — warm, humid, still air — nothing plateaus and every extra minute adds stored heat directly. Once skin temperature approaches or falls below ambient, conduction, convection and radiation stop helping and evaporation carries the entire load; evaporation is driven by the water vapour-pressure gradient between skin and air, so the moisture already in the air — not dry-bulb temperature alone — decides whether sweat cools or merely drips. Meanwhile skin blood flow and muscle blood flow bid for the same cardiac output. In a self-paced race the athlete resolves all of this behaviourally: rising skin temperature and thermal discomfort inflate perceived exertion and pull work rate down long before core temperature reaches anything dramatic.
key_facts: Heat storage = heat production − heat loss. Body temperature rises only while storage is positive, so the sign of that term, not any single measurement, is what a coach is managing.

Human mechanical efficiency is low — only about 20–25% of energy turnover emerges as external work, so heat production tracks metabolic rate almost directly. In a compensable environment relative intensity sets the core temperature the athlete settles at; in an uncompensable one — a warm, humid, still hall — storage keeps accumulating and duration matters as much as intensity. Both apply in HYROX: the sled push, sled pull and burpee broad jump are the peak heat-production segments, and wall balls (100 reps in every individual division) arrive when accumulated storage is already highest.

Four avenues of exchange: conduction (direct contact with a cooler surface), convection (heat carried away by moving air or water), radiation (electromagnetic exchange with surrounding surfaces and bodies) and evaporation (phase change of sweat). The first three follow the skin-to-environment temperature gradient and reverse direction — becoming heat GAIN — once the surroundings are warmer than skin.

Evaporation is effective because of the latent heat of vaporisation: converting water to vapour at skin temperature absorbs roughly 2.4 kJ per gram (on the order of 580 kcal per litre). Only sweat that actually evaporates removes heat — sweat that drips off or is wiped away costs fluid and returns nothing.

Evaporation is driven by the water vapour-pressure gradient between wet skin and the air, so it is the ambient water vapour pressure that sets evaporative capacity. Humidity is the usual proxy, but always read it together with air temperature: the same relative humidity is a far bigger problem in hotter air, because saturated air at 35 °C holds around two-thirds more water vapour than saturated air at 26 °C and the skin-to-air gradient collapses accordingly. Air movement matters because it strips away the near-saturated boundary layer sitting against the skin; in still air that layer approaches saturation and evaporation stalls. Wet-bulb globe temperature indices weight the wet-bulb term most heavily for exactly this reason.

Competing demand: cutaneous vasodilation for heat loss and locomotor muscle perfusion for oxygen delivery draw on one finite cardiac output, so heat imposes a genuine cardiovascular cost on top of its perceptual one (see day 65 on delivery, and day 21 on cardiovascular drift).

Behavioural thermoregulation is the first line of defence. In the framing developed by Schlader and colleagues, ambient heat raises skin temperature, which feeds thermal perception and cardiovascular strain, which raise perceived exertion, which lowers self-selected work rate — a chain that operates well before core temperature approaches any putative limit. In a self-paced race it shows up as pacing, not collapse. Core and skin temperature are separate variables, and skin is the underrated one: a measure that lowers thermal discomfort can buy back work rate even when deep-body temperature is barely touched, which is why cold ingested fluid and external skin cooling earn their place in a hot hall.

Field data undercut the idea of a fixed 'critical core temperature'. Measurements around 41 °C have been published in elite road cycling competition (Racinais and colleagues) in athletes who finished and were fine. Treat critical core temperature as a contested laboratory construct; do not teach any number as a safe threshold, and never clear or condemn an athlete on a thermometer reading rather than on signs.

Individual determinants of heat tolerance: higher body fat and higher BMI are associated with poorer performance on heat tolerance testing, higher VO2max and a higher surface-area-to-mass ratio with better (Lisman and colleagues). Note the confound: when body mass AND metabolic heat production are matched, large differences in body fat produce little or no difference in core-temperature rise or sweat loss in compensable conditions (Dervis and colleagues). The field association is driven mainly by greater total mass and absolute heat production, lower aerobic capacity and poorer economy — not by adiposity acting on its own.

Movement economy is a determinant of heat strain in its own right, separate from aerobic fitness: a less economical athlete spends more energy — and so liberates more heat — to hold the same external speed, so economy shifts the thermal load even between athletes with matched aerobic capacity. Technical work on running, ski, row, burpee and sled mechanics is therefore also heat management.

Heat acclimation/acclimatisation adaptation set: plasma-volume expansion (early, and among the first to decay), earlier sweat onset, higher sweat rate, more dilute sweat, lower core temperature and heart rate at a fixed workload, and improved thermal comfort. Induction typically runs 5–14 daily exposures of roughly 60–90 min at modest intensity, with adaptations decaying over the following weeks unless topped up. Day 25 carries this as a one-line definition only.

Heat-illness spectrum: heat exhaustion presents as an inability to continue with dizziness, nausea, weakness and often collapse, but with an intact sensorium; exertional heat stroke is distinguished by central nervous system dysfunction — confusion, disorientation, irrational or aggressive behaviour, ataxia, seizure, loss of consciousness. Exertional heat stroke is a medical emergency: call emergency medical services immediately AND begin aggressive whole-body cooling on the spot — cold-water immersion where available, otherwise continuous cold water, ice packs to neck, axillae and groin, and fanning. Cool first, transport second, because outcome tracks how fast core temperature comes down. Rapid cooling is recognised first aid, not treatment; what sits outside coaching scope of practice (day 1) is diagnosis, medication, and the decision to stop cooling or clear the athlete — as injury management generally does (day 7).

Cooling has reasonable support at both ends. Pre-cooling (cold-water immersion, cooling vests, ice-slurry ingestion of roughly 5–10 g/kg before the start) improves endurance performance in the heat; per-cooling during exercise performs at least as well in meta-analysis (Bongers and colleagues) — its limitation is delivery in competition, not size of effect. In a HYROX hall the realistic levers are pre-race cooling, a shortened warm-up in minimal kit, cold fluid at the 15 roxzone traverses (day 25 covers the drinking plan) and anything that lowers thermal perception.
68.training_link: Treat the hall as a measurement, not a hope. Get your athlete in early enough to feel it: note whether any air is genuinely moving over the run loop, and read humidity alongside temperature — a still 26 °C hall at 70% humidity is a harder thermal problem than a dry, breezy 30 °C course, and cool-gym splits will lie to them. Reset the race model before the gun rather than discovering it on run five (day 16): a few seconds per kilometre off the opening two runs and a slightly softer sled push cost less than the back-half collapse they prevent. Build heat exposure into the final weeks — roughly five to ten easy 60–90 min sessions in genuinely warm conditions, kept away from key quality days — then rehearse the controllables: minimal warm-up kit, cold fluid or an ice towel in the holding pen, and one cold mouthful at a named roxzone (day 25). Finally, agree the emergency plan out loud before you need it: who calls, where the ice and water are, and that cooling starts immediately rather than after the ambulance arrives.

glossary.def: The accounting relationship in which stored heat equals heat produced minus heat lost. Body temperature rises only when storage is positive, so the coaching levers are either lowering production (pacing, economy) or raising loss (evaporation, airflow, cooling).

glossary.def: The heat liberated by energy turnover that does not appear as external work — the large majority of it, given human mechanical efficiency of roughly 20–25%. It scales with metabolic rate, which is why relative intensity sets the temperature an athlete plateaus at whenever the environment can still dissipate the load, and why duration bites hardest when it cannot.

glossary.def: Collective term for conduction, convection and radiation. All three follow the temperature gradient between skin and the surroundings, and all three reverse into heat gain once the environment is warmer than the skin.

glossary.def: Heat removed when sweat changes phase from liquid to vapour at the skin surface. The only avenue that still works when ambient temperature meets or exceeds skin temperature, and the only one that credits sweat which actually evaporates rather than drips.

glossary.def: The energy required to convert liquid water to vapour without changing its temperature — roughly 2.4 kJ per gram at skin temperature. This is the physical reason sweating is such a powerful cooling mechanism relative to the small mass of fluid involved.

glossary.def: The difference in water vapour pressure between wet skin and the surrounding air; the actual driving force for evaporation. Moist air flattens the gradient, which is why a humid warm hall can defeat cooling more thoroughly than a hotter dry environment — and why the same relative humidity is far more punishing in hotter air.

glossary.def: Down-regulation of work rate, and other voluntary heat-avoiding behaviour, driven by skin temperature and thermal discomfort acting through perceived exertion. The first and most powerful line of defence, and in a self-paced race the reason heat shows up as slower splits rather than as physiological failure.

glossary.def: The laboratory idea that voluntary exhaustion occurs at a reproducible core temperature. Contested: field measurements in competition have recorded values around 41 °C — roughly a degree above the laboratory figure — in athletes who finished uneventfully, so it should be taught as a construct under debate rather than a threshold to plan around, and never as a safe/unsafe cut-off.

glossary.def: Two labels for repeated heat exposure that differ only in setting — 'acclimation' for artificially induced exposure (heat chamber, hot room, deliberately overdressed sessions), 'acclimatisation' for living and training in a genuinely hot climate. The adaptation set is the same either way and is defined on day 25; what the distinction buys a coach is that an induction block can be manufactured at home rather than requiring travel, and that both routes decay within weeks unless topped up.

glossary.def: The severe end of the heat-illness spectrum, marked by central nervous system dysfunction — confusion, ataxia, irrational behaviour, seizure or unconsciousness — during or shortly after exertion. A medical emergency: call emergency services and start aggressive whole-body cooling immediately. Cool first, transport second, because outcome tracks how fast core temperature falls. Cooling is first aid; diagnosis, medication and clearing the athlete belong to medical staff.
