68.exam_focus: Reasoning from the heat-balance equation — why low mechanical efficiency makes intensity the driver of heat production, why evaporation becomes the only useful avenue in a warm hall, and why the skin-to-air vapour-pressure gradient rather than dry-bulb temperature governs it — and then applying behavioural thermoregulation, the individual determinants of heat strain, and the heat-exhaustion versus exertional-heat-stroke distinction (cool first, transport second) to a HYROX race plan and to a coach's scope of practice.

69.title: Body fluids, sodium & the dehydration evidence
69.key_concept: Water is roughly 45-75% of body mass -- conventionally about 60% in lean young men and about 50-55% in women, with lower values in older and higher-fat athletes. It is a range rather than a constant because adipose tissue holds far less water per kilogram than lean tissue, so body-water percentage tracks leanness. Distribution matters more than the total. About two-thirds of body water is inside cells; of the extracellular third, most is interstitial and only a minority is plasma. Plasma is the smallest of the three major compartments and the one that acutely decides stroke volume, skin blood flow and therefore pace. Sweat is a hypotonic secretion -- the gland puts out a near-isotonic fluid and then reclaims sodium and chloride in the duct -- so sweating concentrates what remains: extracellular sodium rises, water is drawn out of the cells down the osmotic gradient, and plasma volume is partly defended. That is why sodium's contribution to performance is mostly indirect. Underneath day 25's practical plan sits a genuinely contested evidence base -- laboratory trials show decrements from around 2% body-mass loss, field data often do not, and a coach should be able to name why the two disagree.
key_facts: Total body water is roughly 45-75% of body mass -- conventionally about 60% in lean young men and about 50-55% in women, with lower values in older and higher-fat athletes. It varies with age (it declines), sex (lower on average in women, largely via body composition) and adiposity -- adipose tissue is markedly lower in water content per kilogram than lean tissue, so body-water percentage tracks leanness.

Two athletes of identical mass therefore do not have identical reserves: the same absolute sweat loss represents a larger fraction of total body water in the higher-body-fat athlete, so a 2%-of-body-mass rule is not an equally severe stress for both.

Teach the compartments as FRACTIONS, not as one person's litres: about two-thirds of total body water is intracellular; the extracellular third is mostly interstitial and plasma, splitting roughly three-quarters to one-quarter once the small transcellular fraction (synovial, cerebrospinal, gastrointestinal and ocular secretions) is set aside. Textbook litre figures describe a reference individual only.

Plasma is the smallest of the three MAJOR compartments (transcellular fluid aside, which is smaller still but is not a circulating reserve) and the acutely decisive one -- it is the fluid that sets circulating volume, so small absolute shifts out of plasma have disproportionate cardiovascular consequences.

Plasma osmolality is defended within a narrow band, conventionally about 285-295 mOsm/kg. Sodium with its accompanying anions is the principal determinant of extracellular osmolality; water crosses cell membranes passively down osmotic gradients, so wherever the solute goes, water follows.

As sweating concentrates the extracellular space, rising extracellular sodium pulls water from the intracellular compartment, partially defending plasma volume and hence stroke volume, cardiac output and skin blood flow (day 68). The same osmotic rise is sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors, generating thirst and vasopressin release, which reduces renal water loss.

The sodium-potassium ATPase exports three sodium ions and imports two potassium ions per ATP hydrolysed, maintaining the resting membrane potential that makes action potentials -- and therefore motor-unit recruitment and muscle contraction (day 63) -- possible. Its running cost is substantial, commonly estimated at roughly a fifth to a third of resting energy turnover depending on tissue and method.

Sweat is HYPOTONIC to plasma: the gland secretes a near-isotonic fluid and reabsorbs sodium and chloride as it travels up the duct, so whatever an individual's sweat sodium concentration (day 25), it sits far below plasma's ~135-145 mmol/L. Sweating alone therefore tends to RAISE plasma sodium concentration, and sodium loss is not the usual route to exercise-associated hyponatraemia -- excess intake of dilute fluid is (day 25). Duct transit time is also why sweat runs saltier at high sweat rates and more dilute with heat acclimation, so a single test value is not a fixed personal constant.

Sodium supplementation evidence is MIXED. The systematic review by Heffernan and colleagues (2019, ~15 trials, ~385 participants) found roughly a third of trials supporting improved sodium balance, more so in the heat, and roughly a third showing no benefit; there is no consistent ergogenic effect in healthy athletes in temperate conditions. A high-dose pre-exercise sodium beverage (around 160 mmol/L) has some support for improving exercise tolerance in hot conditions. Established roles are indirect: plasma-volume maintenance (Sawka and colleagues), better post-exercise retention at roughly 40 mmol/L and above, possibly reduced perceived exertion in the heat (Sims and colleagues), and assistance with intracellular-to-extracellular fluid shifts (James and colleagues).

The kidney matches sodium excretion to intake across a wide range -- shown decades ago in heat-acclimatised outdoor workers (Malhotra, 1960), where sweat and urinary losses tracked intake. Chronic salt loading in a temperate climate therefore mostly produces expensive urine. It also means a single sweat-sodium value partly reflects habitual diet and acclimation state.

Not all body-mass loss during exercise is fluid loss: oxidising stored substrate consumes mass and releases metabolic water, and water bound to glycogen is freed as glycogen is used. Day 25's field simplification of 1 kg to about 1 litre remains the correct practical tool; the caveat is that a small part of the measured change is not a fluid deficit of the same size.

The proportion of laboratory studies reporting a performance decrement climbs steeply with the size of the deficit -- around 2-3% the results are close to a coin flip, and beyond 4% a decrement becomes the common finding, particularly in hot or still conditions. Even at those larger deficits, cool, well-ventilated, self-paced protocols still return null results, which is itself part of the disagreement.

Field data cut the other way: across 643 marathon finishers, percentage body-mass change was INVERSELY related to finishing time -- the fastest lost the most (Zouhal and colleagues, 2011) -- and long-course triathlon fields show the same pattern, with some finishers well beyond 5% (Wharam and colleagues, 2006). That is heavily confounded -- fast finishers are on course for less time, stop less often, drink less, and are typically leaner and fitter -- so it is evidence that laboratory protocols overstate the field effect, NOT evidence that dehydration improves performance. A real cost nonetheless exists at the muscle: dehydration accelerates muscle glycogen use and raises heart rate, core temperature and perceived exertion at a fixed workload (Logan-Sprenger and colleagues), so the disagreement is about magnitude and threshold in the field, not about whether fluid loss does anything at all.
69.training_link: Measure three things and stop guessing at the fourth. First, starting state: a week of first-morning nude body mass gives a stable baseline, so on race morning you know whether the athlete is already down a kilogram before the gun -- that is the deficit day 25's pre-race protocol exists to prevent, and the one you genuinely control. Second, classify the sweat: white crusting on kit and skin, plus a bad history in hot halls, justify a sweat-sodium test to place the athlete in a band, not to prescribe milligrams. Treat repeated cramping as a prompt to look, not as a diagnosis -- the electrolyte explanation for exercise-associated cramp is contested and the neuromuscular-fatigue explanation (load, pace, novelty) is at least as likely, so review the training and pacing before the salt. Third, plan roxzone intake capped at measured sweat rate (day 25). What you should not do is chase individualised replacement to the milligram, or load salt for weeks in a temperate climate -- the kidney simply excretes it. And tell the athlete plainly that 2% is a planning line, not a trapdoor, so they neither panic mid-race nor ignore it entirely.

glossary.def: All water in the body, roughly 45-75% of body mass -- conventionally about 60% in lean young men and about 50-55% in women, with lower values in older and higher-fat athletes. Higher in leaner and younger athletes because lean tissue is far more water-rich than adipose tissue, which is why the same litre deficit is a different physiological insult in two athletes of equal weight.

glossary.def: A small, separately listed category of extracellular water held behind epithelial layers -- synovial, cerebrospinal, ocular, pleural and gastrointestinal secretions. glossary.def: Solute concentration expressed per kilogram of solvent (mOsm/kg), defended in plasma within roughly 285-295 mOsm/kg. Osmolarity is the near-equivalent term expressed per litre of solution; the two are used loosely but osmolality is the physiologically preferred measure.

glossary.def: The membrane pump that exports three sodium ions and imports two potassium ions per ATP, sustaining the resting membrane potential behind every action potential and muscle contraction. Its continuous operation accounts for a substantial share of resting energy expenditure.

glossary.def: Sweat leaves the secretory coil near-isotonic and has sodium and chloride reclaimed as it passes up the duct, so what reaches the skin is more dilute than plasma and removes proportionally more water than sodium. Pure sweating therefore raises plasma sodium concentration -- dehydration by sweating is a concentrating process, not a diluting one. Less duct time at high sweat rates means saltier sweat; heat acclimation moves it the other way.

glossary.def: Water produced when carbohydrate and fat are oxidised, released alongside the water previously bound to stored glycogen. It is one reason measured body-mass loss during exercise slightly overstates the true fluid deficit.

69.exam_focus: Explaining where body water sits, why plasma volume is the compartment that matters acutely and how sodium osmotically defends it, then reconciling the laboratory and field dehydration literatures -- naming the confounds on both sides -- without overstating either.

70.title: Movement screening & physical testing
70.key_concept: Movement competency is the ability to perform fundamental patterns optimally, and optimally must mean something specific: pain-free, with joint alignment, muscular coordination and postural control a coach will accept. Kritz and Cronin's model proposes the chain that follows — a muscle disproportionately strong, weak, mistimed or short unbalances the support around a joint, the pattern distorts, and joint function and output fall with it. Hold that as a coaching model for organising observation, not a validated mechanism. In a HYROX athlete the patterns worth watching are a loaded lunge with a rotational component, an upper-body push, an upper-body pull, a hip-dominant bend and gait, seen from front and side inside a fixed 10-20 minute window two or three times a year. The Functional Movement Screen standardises that description usefully; its composite out of 21 does not forecast injury. And because the race demands explosive station work, 8 km of running, sustained high-force output and technique that survives fatigue, mechanical output is sampled separately, in an order that decides whether the numbers mean anything.
key_facts: Movement competency = the capacity to perform fundamental patterns optimally, where optimal is operationalised as pain-free, with joint alignment inside acceptable bounds, coordinated and correctly timed muscular contribution, and postural control held through the range. Kritz and Cronin's movement-competency work proposes the causal chain: muscles that are disproportionately strong, weak, poorly timed or short disrupt the balance of support around a joint, which produces a faulty pattern, which degrades joint function and output. Treat it as a model that structures what you look for — the same faulty-looking pattern can equally arise from unfamiliarity, skill, pain avoidance or limb proportions.

The high-yield patterns for a HYROX athlete: a loaded lunge with a rotational component (sandbag lunges, 100 m of them, arrived at already fatigued), an upper-body push, an upper-body pull, a hip-dominant bend (sled pull, row finish, farmers pick-up) and gait. Observe each from both the front and the side — one plane alone hides either frontal-plane collapse or sagittal compensation; this is the multi-plane discipline of day 10, which also sets out the screen-versus-analysis distinction and the compensation vocabulary the 0-3 scale depends on. Keep the whole screen to a fixed window of roughly 10-20 minutes per athlete and repeat it only two or three times a year: competency is a slow-moving quality, and screening it monthly buys noise. That is deliberately the opposite cadence to the weekly monitoring of day 49.

A static posture screen is the cheapest observation available: unshod, with the ankle, knee, hip and shoulder landmarks visible, and with a fixed vertical or horizontal reference in the field of view so alignment is judged against something rather than an eyeballed plumb line. From the front you are reading side-to-side level at head, shoulders and hips, knee and ankle alignment and foot position; from the side, head carriage, thoracic curve, anterior versus posterior pelvic tilt, and whether the knees sit habitually flexed or hyperextended. Note limb dominance alongside the findings, because small and consistent side-to-side differences are the norm in trained adults and carry no diagnostic weight on their own. The honest caveat, which the movement-competency literature states plainly: static posture is easy to assess, but its relationship to dynamic movement quality is unclear (Kritz and Cronin, 2008), and no better case exists for reading it as an injury indicator. So it is a hypothesis generator, never a diagnosis — anything noticed standing still must be confirmed or discarded in a loaded, dynamic pattern before it earns programme time.

The Functional Movement Screen (Cook and colleagues) is seven tests: deep squat, hurdle step, in-line lunge, shoulder mobility, active straight leg raise, trunk stability push-up and rotary stability — two of which are essentially mobility items rather than movement tasks. Each is scored on a 0-3 ordinal scale (3 = performed without compensation, 2 = performed with compensation, 1 = unable to perform, 0 = pain provoked), giving a composite out of 21; most reasonably trained adults land in the mid-teens and a clean 21 is rare. Five of the seven items are scored on each side separately and only the lower of the two sides enters the composite, so the asymmetry must be recorded alongside the item score — it is invisible in the total by construction. Three clearing tests (shoulder impingement, spinal extension press-up, spinal flexion posterior rocking) are run pass/fail, and pain on a clearing test drops the associated item to 0.

The composite cut-off of 14 or less (<=14) — at or below it, supposedly elevated injury risk — is the single most contested claim attached to this screen. It originates in small, specific cohorts (Kiesel and colleagues' work in professional American football and later in firefighters). Subsequent systematic reviews and meta-analyses (Dorrel and colleagues, 2015; Moran and colleagues, 2017; Bunn and colleagues, 2019) report pooled sensitivity of roughly 0.2-0.3 against a specificity of roughly 0.85 — the composite labels most uninjured athletes correctly but misses around three-quarters of those who go on to be injured, which is fatal for a screen whose job is to rule risk out. Note what is and is not being criticised: scored by trained raters, the composite's inter-rater reliability is generally acceptable; it is the predictive validity that fails. Do not repeat the cut-off to an athlete as a risk statement.

Why a composite fails as a matter of measurement, not just evidence: summing seven ordinal ratings discards exactly the information that carries meaning. A 14 built from seven 2s (mild global compensation) and a 14 built from three 3s, two 2s, a 1 on the in-line lunge and a 0 on the hurdle step (9 + 4 + 1 + 0 — one failed pattern, asymmetrical, plus a painful one) demand completely different responses. The sum also treats ordinal ranks as if they were interval units and gives every test equal weight, when a painful hurdle step and a stiff shoulder are not interchangeable.

The examinable measurement point: a screen meant to rule problems out needs high sensitivity, and its usefulness collapses further when the base rate of the outcome is low. Take a squad injury rate around 10% with the pooled figures above — the large majority of flagged athletes will never be injured, and most of the injuries that do occur will arise in athletes the screen passed, so the flag barely moves your estimate off the base rate. That is how a test can be reliable, respectably specific, and still useless for the decision it is being used to make.

Used properly, the screen is genuinely valuable: it is a standardised, reasonably reliable way to DESCRIBE movement competency in shared language, to structure a coach-athlete conversation about a specific pattern, and to track change in that pattern over months against the athlete's own earlier footage. Record the item scores and the asymmetries, not just the total. A score of 0 — pain reproduced — is a referral trigger under scope of practice (day 1), not a corrective-exercise cue.

Pattern-to-race mapping: overhead position and squat depth underpin 100 wall balls in every individual division and the loaded take-off of burpee broad jumps; split-stance stability underpins sandbag lunges and the sled push, where the sled is concentric-dominant and foot placement narrows toward instability as fatigue builds; shoulder mobility plus trunk stability underpin SkiErg arm drive and posture under the farmers carry; hip mobility and anti-rotation control underpin stride mechanics (days 30 and 33) and limit energy leaks across the carries and the 15 roxzone traverses.

Because the race asks for explosive station work, 8 km of running, sustained high-force output and technique that survives fatigue, one battery has to sample several qualities in a single session (the pillar vocabulary of day 62) — which is what makes the order decisive: reactive and explosive power first, then maximal strength, then strength endurance, and complex multi-joint tests before simple single-joint ones. The reason is contamination, not tradition — residual fatigue degrades a power measure far more than an endurance measure, so an out-of-order battery produces a jump height that is largely a measurement of the previous test. A power number collected after heavy lifting or an erg piece is not comparable with the same athlete's rested number and should not be entered in the log as if it were.

Standardise and ramp: identical warm-up (duration and modalities), identical equipment, cueing and environment, a controlled interval from warm-up to first effort, and submaximal attempts building to maximal ones for both safety and accuracy. Allow inter-test recovery long enough to restore phosphagen availability — phosphocreatine resynthesis is roughly half complete within about 30 seconds but takes on the order of 3-5 minutes to approach completion, so allow at least 2-3 minutes between maximal power efforts and 3-5 minutes before and between maximal strength attempts, with much shorter rests acceptable for submaximal endurance items. Retest on a periodic cycle of roughly a couple of months, aligned to block boundaries, and judge change against the test's own error (day 49).

The mechanical menu, chosen so each entry answers a question the race asks: a bilateral squat or hinge to establish whether force capacity is even in the conversation (back squat, deadlift, front squat); a unilateral lower-body test, because much of the race's high-force work happens on one leg at a time (single-leg squat and split-stance variants); an overhead push, to check force can still be expressed in the position wall balls demand (overhead press, with a bench press if the horizontal push is also wanted); and a pull, to check the same for a hinged, hands-loaded position (pull-up or chin-up, row variants). Power is sampled separately — a paused concentric-only squat jump and a countermovement jump for the lower body; for the upper, a seated medicine-ball throw from a fixed bench position and a short maximal SkiErg effort held to roughly 6-10 seconds (fix and record the stroke count) so that the phosphagen system supplies most of the ATP, since glycolytic contribution rises steeply beyond about 10 seconds and is the dominant supplier well before 30 (day 18). Take the smallest set that covers force, unilateral force and power in both halves of the body, and note that prescribing the lifts themselves belongs to day 37.

Eccentric utilisation ratio (EUR) = countermovement jump divided by concentric-only squat jump, used as an index of how much an athlete gains from the stretch-shortening cycle; values around and slightly above 1.0 are typical across sports (McGuigan and colleagues), and the familiar low/normal/high bands are rules of thumb rather than validated norms. Four cautions: it is a ratio, so a low value can mean a poor countermovement jump OR an unusually strong squat jump, and it does not isolate elastic function; the squat jump is hard to standardise because athletes smuggle in a small countermovement, inflating the denominator; the value differs depending on whether it is computed from jump height or peak power, so the version must always be stated; and it depends on measurement method (force plate versus jump mat). Track it within-athlete against their own baseline, alongside the raw jump heights, never as a cross-sectional classification.
70.training_link: Run the movement screen once at the start of a build and once mid-season, in the same short slot, filmed from front and side so you compare footage rather than memory. Write down three things per pattern: what failed, whether it failed on one side only, and whether anything hurt. Those notes outrank any total, and pain converts the finding from a training problem into a referral (day 1). On a separate day, run the mechanical battery in order — jumps, then heavy low-rep lifting, then the strength-endurance items — with 2-3 minutes between power efforts and 3-5 minutes before maximal attempts, and an identical warm-up every time. Repeat roughly every couple of months at a block boundary, next to the race-specific benchmarks of day 49. Screening tells you how the athlete moves; the benchmarks tell you what that movement costs them across 8 km, eight stations and 15 roxzone traverses.

glossary.def: The ability to perform fundamental movement patterns optimally — pain-free, with acceptable joint alignment, coordinated and well-timed muscular contribution, and postural control retained through the range. A construct about movement QUALITY, distinct from the tissue-capacity screens of day 38 and the performance benchmarks of day 49.

glossary.def: A brief unshod observation of standing alignment from the front and the side (head, thoracic, lumbar, hip, knee, ankle and foot), judged against a fixed reference line. Cheap and easy to standardise, but its link to dynamic movement quality is unclear, so it functions as a source of hypotheses to test under load rather than as a finding to treat.

glossary.def: A seven-item standardised screen (deep squat, hurdle step, in-line lunge, shoulder mobility, active straight leg raise, trunk stability push-up, rotary stability) developed by Cook and colleagues, each item rated 0-3 with 0 reserved for pain. Five items are scored bilaterally with the lower side entering the composite, and three pass/fail clearing tests can force an item to 0 on pain. Best understood as a common descriptive language for movement competency and a way to track a single pattern over time.

glossary.def: One number formed by adding several ordinal ratings, as in the FMS total out of 21. The sum treats ranks as interval units, weights every item equally, and discards which pattern failed, whether the failure was asymmetrical and whether it was painful — so two identical composites can describe athletes needing opposite interventions.

glossary.def: Of the athletes who go on to sustain the outcome, the proportion the screen flagged in advance — true positives divided by all eventual cases. A test used to rule a problem out needs it high; when it is low, most of the events arise in athletes the screen passed, whatever cut-off is chosen. Distinct from positive predictive value, the proportion of FLAGGED athletes who actually go on to be injured, which additionally depends on the base rate. Its partner term, diagnostic specificity, is the proportion of those who stay healthy that the screen correctly passes — not the training-specificity sense of 'specificity' defined on day 49.

glossary.def: How common the outcome is in the population being screened. When the base rate is low, even a respectably specific test yields mostly false positives, so a flag adds little to what you already knew — the reason plausible-looking screening cut-offs routinely fail in practice.

glossary.def: A vertical jump from standing with hands fixed, using a self-selected downward dip immediately reversed into the jump. Because the dip pre-loads muscle and tendon, it reflects the athlete's combined muscular and stretch-shortening-cycle output.

glossary.def: A vertical jump from a held, standardised squat position with a deliberate pause before the drive, intended to dissipate stored elastic energy so that predominantly concentric output is measured. Hard to standardise: any small unloading or dip before take-off contaminates it, so depth, pause length and cueing must be fixed and recorded.

glossary.def: CMJ divided by SJ, used as an index of benefit gained from the stretch-shortening cycle. Being a ratio, it cannot distinguish a poor countermovement jump from an exceptional squat jump; it differs when computed from peak power rather than jump height; and its conventional bands are heuristics, not norms. Interpret within-athlete against their own baseline, with the raw jump values alongside.

glossary.def: The ordering of tests inside one session so that the quality most vulnerable to residual fatigue is measured first: reactive/explosive power, then maximal strength, then strength endurance, with complex multi-joint items ahead of simple single-joint ones. Violating it yields a number that partly measures the preceding test.

70.exam_focus: Defining movement competency and stating the causal chain the literature proposes without overselling it; running a defensible screen (which patterns, both viewing planes, a fixed short window, two or three times a year) and reading a static posture finding as a hypothesis rather than a diagnosis; above all, dismantling the FMS composite as an injury predictor on measurement grounds — ordinal summation destroying pattern, asymmetry and pain information, plus pooled sensitivity of roughly 0.2-0.3 set against a low base rate, while conceding that its inter-rater reliability among trained raters is acceptable and its specificity respectable, so the failure is specifically predictive validity — and still using the screen for description, conversation and pattern tracking, with a score of 0 treated as a referral. Then sequencing a within-session battery correctly, justifying the sequence by fatigue contamination and phosphocreatine resynthesis, and interpreting a ratio measure such as EUR against the athlete's own baseline.
